skills.Example of the Skill: Imagine interviewing is like being a detective who asks people about their day to figure out what makes them happy or frustrated, just like Sherlock Holmes asking questions to solve a mystery.
skills.How the Skill is Carried Out Daily: In a UX Research job, interviewing is done by talking to real users, either in person or online, and asking them about how they use an app or website. The researcher listens carefully, takes notes, and tries to understand what users like, what confuses them, and what problems they face. This involves making users feel comfortable (psychological safety), making decisions about what to ask (decision-making), taking responsibility for the process (ownership), and working with others to make sure everyone’s ideas are heard (service leadership, self-organization, empowerment).
skills.Importance of the Skill: Interviewing is important in UX Research because it helps teams learn what users really need and want. This information is used to make products easier and more enjoyable to use, which means happier customers and better results for the company.
skills.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

skills.Example of the Skill: Imagine survey design is like making a treasure map for your friends. You have to ask the right questions and give clear directions so they can find the treasure (the answers you need).
skills.How the Skill is Carried Out Daily: In a UX Research job, survey design is used every day to figure out what users like or don’t like about a website or app. UX researchers decide what questions to ask, how to ask them, and who should answer them. They use decision-making to pick the best questions, take ownership to make sure the survey is clear, use service leadership to help the team understand users, create psychological safety so people feel comfortable answering honestly, organize themselves to keep the survey on track, and empower others to share their opinions.
skills.Importance of the Skill: This skill is important because good survey design helps UX researchers get accurate and helpful feedback from users. This feedback helps the team make better decisions about how to improve the website or app, making it easier and more enjoyable for everyone to use.
skills.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

skills.Example of the Skill: Imagine you just built a new board game. Usability testing is like asking your friends to play it while you watch. If they get confused or stuck, you know what to fix. It’s like being a detective, looking for clues about what makes the game fun or frustrating.
skills.How the Skill is Carried Out Daily: In a UX Research job, people do usability testing by inviting users to try out a website or app. They watch how users move around, ask questions, and take notes on where users get confused or make mistakes. They use decision-making to choose what to test, take ownership of the process, lead the sessions, make sure everyone feels safe to share honest feedback, organize the tests, and help the team use the results to make things better.
skills.Importance of the Skill: Usability testing is important because it helps UX Researchers find out what real users need and what problems they face. This means the final product is easier and more enjoyable to use, which makes customers happier and helps the company succeed.
skills.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

skills.Example of the Skill: Imagine you’re the captain of a team on a treasure hunt. Your job isn’t to find the treasure alone, but to make sure everyone on your team works together, shares clues, and feels safe to speak up if they have an idea—even if it sounds silly.
skills.How the Skill is Carried Out Daily: In a UX research job, this skill is used every day by planning and leading meetings, asking good questions, making sure everyone’s voice is heard, and helping the team decide what to do next based on what they learn. It also means making sure people feel safe to share their honest thoughts, and encouraging everyone to take responsibility for their part of the work.
skills.Importance of the Skill: This skill is important because it helps the team learn more about users, make better decisions, and create products that people actually want to use. If the team doesn’t work well together or people are afraid to speak up, important ideas might be missed, and the final product won’t be as good.
skills.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

skills.Example of the Skill: Imagine you want to know which type of paper airplane flies the farthest. You make a plan: you’ll fold three different designs, throw each one five times, and measure how far they go. That plan is your experiment design—like making a recipe before you start cooking.
skills.How the Skill is Carried Out Daily: In a UX Research job, people use experiment design to figure out the best way to test if a website or app is easy to use. Every day, they decide what questions to ask users, how to set up tests, and how to make sure the results are fair and useful. They work with others, take responsibility for their tests, make sure everyone feels safe sharing ideas, and organize themselves to get the work done.
skills.Importance of the Skill: Experiment design is important in UX Research because it helps teams learn what users really need and what works best. Good experiment design leads to better products, happier users, and smarter decisions. Without it, teams might guess instead of knowing what to improve.
skills.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

skills.Example of the Skill: Research analysis is like being a detective who looks at clues to solve a mystery. Imagine you’re trying to figure out which ice cream flavor is the most popular at school. You ask your friends, write down their answers, and then look for which flavor comes up the most. That’s research analysis!
skills.How the Skill is Carried Out Daily: In a UX (User Experience) Research job, people do research analysis every day by talking to users, watching how they use apps or websites, and collecting their feedback. They organize all this information, look for common problems or things people like, and then share what they find with the team. They use decision-making to choose what to focus on, take ownership of their work, lead by helping others understand users’ needs, make sure everyone feels safe to share ideas (psychological safety), organize their own tasks, and feel empowered to make suggestions.
skills.Importance of the Skill: Research analysis is important in UX research because it helps the team understand what real users need and want. This means the team can make better decisions about how to design apps or websites, making them easier and more enjoyable for everyone to use. Without good research analysis, the team might guess what users want and end up making things that don’t really help people.
skills.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

skills.Example of the Skill: Imagine you have a big pile of different colored socks, and you want to sort them. Affinity mapping is like putting all the red socks in one pile, all the blue socks in another, and so on, so it’s easier to find what you need.
skills.How the Skill is Carried Out Daily: In a UX Research job, people use affinity mapping by writing down user feedback or research findings on sticky notes, then grouping similar notes together on a wall or board. They look for patterns or common themes, which helps them understand what users need or what problems they have. This process involves decision-making, working together, making sure everyone feels safe to share ideas, and organizing the work as a team.
skills.Importance of the Skill: Affinity mapping is important in UX Research because it helps teams make sense of lots of information, find the most important problems to solve, and make better choices about how to improve products for users. It makes sure everyone’s ideas are heard and helps the team work together more effectively.
skills.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

skills.Example of the Skill: Imagine you’re on a soccer team and your coach says, “We keep losing because we don’t talk to each other on the field.” That’s like a problem statement—it’s pointing out exactly what’s wrong, like shining a flashlight on the problem so everyone can see it.
skills.How the Skill is Carried Out Daily: In product management and user experience jobs, people write problem statements every day to help their teams know what to focus on. They talk to customers, look at data, and ask questions to find out what’s not working. Then, they write down the problem in simple words so everyone on the team can work together to solve it. This means they need to make decisions, take responsibility, listen to others, and make sure everyone feels safe to share ideas.
skills.Importance of the Skill: Problem statements are important because they help business analysts and product owners make sure the team is solving the right problem. If the team doesn’t know what the real problem is, they might waste time building things nobody needs. Clear problem statements help everyone work together, make better decisions, and create products that actually help people.

practices.Difference between Practices and Skills:
Practices:
1. A practice requires working with other people
1. A practice never stops being built; you never become an expert in a practice, but the behaviors of a practice become more permanent over time
1. A practice is rooted in beliefs and behaviors
1. A practice can be measured through what other people believe about you
1. A practice cannot be concretely measured through deliverables
1. A practice is an intentional choice someone makes to do
1. You learn how to get good about your practice by reflecting to yourself
1. A practice can be measured through what you believe about yourself
1. You learn how to get good about your practice by reflecting with others
Skills:
1. A skill enables you to make a deliverable
1. A skill is measured through how many times you have applied it
1. A skill is rooted in  knowledge and theory
1. A skill applies to a specific activity
1. A skill is expected to be performed in specific job functions
1. A skill is something someone can become an expert in it with a lot of experience
1. A skill you can perform yourself
1. A skill can be practiced by applying it to work you deliver or duties you perform
1. A skill is required in specific jobs, people may not have a choice to perform the skill if the job requires them
1. A skill gets practiced by doing work and performing duties

What they both have in common: 
1. A practice and a skill can be lost if  not continued to be practiced
1. A practice and a skill require willingness to perform
practices.Practice Level 0 Definition:
1. You are not aware of what makes up the practice
1. You are not willing to practice it
1. You tried to practice it, but stopped
practices.Practice Level 1 Definition:
1. You believe it's valuable to practice the practice
1. You are willing to practice it
1. You have knowledge about the components of the practice
1. You've started practicing with others and reflecting
practices.Practice Level 2 Definition:
1. You've seen growth in your own practice through reflection
1. You are starting to work on changing habits
practices.Practice Level 3 Definition:
1. Your habits are starting to become automatic in your practice with others
1. You’re so practiced in it, that you are a role model to others in the practice
1. You can and do advocate for the practice when working with others

practices.What Mindset Do You Have When You Practi: At its core, Shared Ownership comes from believing a team is stronger when responsibility is spread around. You trust that other people are capable, even when they are still learning, and you are willing to let go of control so they can lead. You also stay honest with yourself about where you can grow, and you treat every teammate's contribution as genuinely valuable.
practices.What Habits Do You Hold When You Practic: In everyday work, this looks like handing off meaningful work instead of hoarding it, and encouraging people who try even when they fall short. You set clear expectations so others can run with the work, admit your own mistakes openly, and make room for teammates to lead on things you could easily have kept for yourself.
practices.Practice Description: Shared Ownership is the idea that the work belongs to everyone on the team, not just whoever was handed a task. When a team practices it, people step up for problems even when they are not officially theirs, and they trust each other to carry real responsibility. It is built from smaller habits like humility, delegation, and a growth mindset, and it deepens over time until sharing the load feels natural. On a healthy team, no one says 'that is not my job.'
practices.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practices.What Mindset Do You Have When You Practi: Empowerment starts with believing that people rise to the trust you place in them. You accept that you do not have all the answers, and that a newer teammate can still produce something great. You value what each person brings, and you would rather someone learn by doing than step in and take over.
practices.What Habits Do You Hold When You Practic: This shows up when you let people solve problems on their own and tell them you believe they can. You recognize effort out loud, even honest attempts that did not work, and you resist the urge to jump in and control the outcome. You listen closely and reflect people's ideas back before adding your own.
practices.Practice Description: Empowerment is about helping the people around you do their best work by trusting them, not managing them. A team that practices it gives people real room to make decisions and figure things out, and treats everyone as capable regardless of title or experience. It grows from habits like letting go of control, listening well, and celebrating effort. The goal is a team where people feel capable and believed in.

practices.What Mindset Do You Have When You Practi: Shared Leadership rests on the belief that everyone can lead and that supporting others is part of your job. You set aside ego and the need to be the smartest person in the room, you assume others hold real wisdom, and you show up as your genuine self instead of performing a role.
practices.What Habits Do You Hold When You Practic: Day to day, this looks like being honest and direct while staying kind, understanding people's needs before acting, and offering steady encouragement. You do not interrupt or dismiss others, you acknowledge where they are right even in disagreement, and you make space for the person best suited to lead in the moment.
practices.Practice Description: Shared Leadership means leadership is something the whole team takes turns holding, not a title one person owns. On a team that practices it, whoever is best suited to guide a given moment steps up, and everyone works to serve the team's success rather than their own status. It is built from qualities like humility, honesty, empathy, and care. The result is a team that can lead itself.
practices.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

1. A practice never stops being built; you never become an expert in a practice, but the behaviors of a practice become more permanent over time
1. A practice is rooted in beliefs and behaviors
1. A practice can be measured through what other people believe about you
1. A practice cannot be concretely measured through deliverables
1. A practice is an intentional choice someone makes to do
1. You learn how to get good about your practice by reflecting to yourself

Skills:
1. A skill enables you to make a deliverable
1. A skill is measured through how many times you have applied it
1. A skill is rooted in  knowledge and theory
1. A skill applies to a specific activity
1. A skill is expected to be performed in specific job functions
1. A skill is something someone can become an expert in it with a lot of experience
1. A skill you can perform yourself
1. A skill can be practiced by applying it to work you deliver or duties you perform
1. A skill is required in specific jobs, people may not have a choice to perform the skill if the job requires them
1. A skill gets practiced by doing work and performing duties

1. A practice and a skill can be lost if  not continued to be practiced
1. A practice and a skill require willingness to perform

practices.What Mindset Do You Have When You Practi: Psychological Safety comes from believing that everyone belongs and has something worth hearing, even the newest person in the room. You believe people learn by trying and failing, that fresh contributions are welcome no matter someone's experience, and that respectfully challenging the way things work makes the work better.
practices.What Habits Do You Hold When You Practic: In practice, this looks like pausing so quieter voices can speak, listening fully before responding, and sharing your own mistakes and uncertainties so others feel safe to do the same. You invite questions, welcome disagreement, and treat every person as a full member of the team.
practices.Practice Description: Psychological Safety is the shared sense that it is safe to speak up, ask questions, admit mistakes, and challenge ideas without being embarrassed or punished. Research on strong teams, from Amy Edmondson to Google's own studies, points to it as the single biggest factor in how well a team performs. It grows in stages: feeling included, then safe to learn, then safe to contribute, then safe to challenge. When it is present, people bring their whole selves and their best thinking to the work.
practices.Where Can I Learn More?: Amy Edmondson on psychological safety (Harvard, author of The Fearless Organization): https://amycedmondson.com/psychological-safety/

practices.What Mindset Do You Have When You Practi: Agility rests on the belief that plans are really just guesses that should change as you learn. You would rather figure things out alongside your teammates and your users than perfect a plan on your own, and you treat failure as a fast, useful way to learn what to do next.
practices.What Habits Do You Hold When You Practic: This shows up when you ship small, working results to get real feedback, adjust direction as soon as new information arrives, and help teammates let go of outdated plans. You stay in close contact with customers to find the right path instead of assuming you already know it.
practices.Practice Description: Agility is a way of working that favors learning and adjusting over sticking rigidly to a plan. Rather than trying to answer every question up front, an agile team puts small results in front of real people, learns from the response, and changes course quickly. The idea traces back to the Agile Manifesto and its values, like favoring working results and close collaboration with customers. In short, you make progress by doing, not just by planning.
practices.Where Can I Learn More?: The Agile Manifesto, the founding values of agile work: https://agilemanifesto.org/

practices.What Mindset Do You Have When You Practi: This practice rests on the belief that the team's combined judgment usually beats any single person's, and that a decision only holds when people have had a genuine say. You stay open to changing a decision when the situation changes, rather than clinging to your first call.
practices.What Habits Do You Hold When You Practic: In everyday work, this looks like gathering input from the group, checking your assumptions out loud, and giving people time to reflect and respond before you lock anything in. You adjust decisions as you learn, and you steer toward a choice the whole team can get behind.
practices.Practice Description: Collective Decision Making is how a team makes choices together so people actually support them, instead of one person deciding for everyone. A team that practices it draws on the knowledge already in the room and gives people time to weigh in before committing. It relies on habits like building consensus, checking assumptions, and staying flexible as situations change. Decisions made this way tend to stick, because the people carrying them out helped shape them.
practices.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practices.What Mindset Do You Have When You Practi: Continuous Improvement comes from believing that growth is always possible and that failure is a lesson rather than a verdict. You see feedback as a gift that shows you where to get better, and you pay attention to how your own actions affect the people around you.
practices.What Habits Do You Hold When You Practic: This shows up when you regularly step back to reflect on how things went, seek out feedback and act on it instead of getting defensive, and treat fast failures as chances to learn. You watch your own impact on others and make small, steady changes to how you work.
practices.Practice Description: Continuous Improvement is the habit of a team getting a little better all the time by reflecting honestly and acting on what it learns. Instead of repeating the same mistakes, the team treats every sprint and every setback as a chance to adjust how it works. It grows from habits like reflection, self-awareness, seeking feedback, and failing fast. Over time, small improvements add up to a team that keeps getting stronger.
practices.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I do not judge myself or others, I operate without dominance or arrogance
practice-components.Component Description: Humility means treating yourself and everyone around you as equals, with no need to dominate or prove you are the smartest in the room. On a team it frees you to admit you do not have all the answers and to stay open to being wrong, which is exactly what lets a group share ownership and take turns leading. It is quiet, but it is the ground that Shared Ownership and Shared Leadership grow in.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe your way is not the only right way, and that every person, no matter how new, has something to teach you. Being wrong is not a threat; it is a chance to learn.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You hold back quick judgment, own your mistakes out loud, and give credit to others instead of taking it for yourself.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I seek to discover ways I am lying to myself.
practice-components.Component Description: Honesty in self is the inner work of catching the small ways we all fool ourselves, the hidden biases and the convenient excuses. It is not comfortable, but it keeps you self-aware and growing, and it is what makes you trustworthy enough to share ownership and help lead a team.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe self-deception is a normal human habit worth catching, and that facing your blind spots honestly is what makes you better over time.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You question your own assumptions, check your real motives, and reflect honestly on where you fell short instead of explaining it away.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I operate without deception or hiding.
practice-components.Component Description: Honesty toward others means being straight with your teammates, without spin and without quietly sitting on the truth. It can feel risky in the moment, but it is what builds the trust a team leans on to make good decisions and share leadership.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe people deserve the truth, and that hiding it, even to be nice, does more harm than good in the long run.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You say what you really think, give feedback that is direct but kind, and do not withhold information the team needs.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I acknowledge the truth in others' words often, even when I think they could be wrong or have a different perspective
practice-components.Component Description: Acknowledgement is recognizing the truth in what someone says, even when you do not fully agree. It shows people they were actually heard, which keeps conversations open and helps a team share ownership, empower each other, and lead together instead of talking past one another.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe there is usually something valid in another person's view, even when it is incomplete.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You name what is right in someone's point before you respond, rather than jumping straight to disagreement.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: When events don't turn out how I expected, I am quick to adjust the path I am taking, and I encourage others to do so too
practice-components.Component Description: Adaptability is changing course quickly when the situation shifts, and helping your teammates do the same. It is at the core of working in an agile way, where plans are expected to change as the team learns, and it feeds the practices of Agility, Collective Decision Making, and Continuous Improvement.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe plans are really just guesses that should change as you learn, not promises set in stone.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You adjust your approach as soon as new information arrives, and you help teammates let go of plans that no longer fit.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: The Agile Manifesto, the founding values of agile work: https://agilemanifesto.org/

practice-components.Assessment Question: I prioritize figuring out decisions with my teammates instead of developing perfect plans before I act.
practice-components.Component Description: This is the agile habit of solving problems together with people rather than perfecting a plan alone up front. It comes straight from the Agile Manifesto value of individuals and interactions over processes and tools, and it is a building block of the Agility practice.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe the best decisions come from working things out with people, not from planning in isolation.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You bring questions to your teammates early and decide together instead of finishing a plan first and handing it over.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: The Agile Manifesto, the founding values of agile work: https://agilemanifesto.org/

practice-components.Assessment Question: I prioritize getting the results into the hands of users and customers so that I can get feedback before I adjust.
practice-components.Component Description: This is the agile focus on shipping something real and usable so you can learn from real feedback, rather than waiting for everything to be perfect. It reflects the Agile value of working software over comprehensive documentation, and it is one of the habits that make the Agility practice real.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe honest feedback on something real beats endless planning every time.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You get small, working results in front of users quickly and use what you learn to steer the next step.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: The Agile Manifesto, the founding values of agile work: https://agilemanifesto.org/

practice-components.Assessment Question: I work with and talk to customers in order to determine the direction, rather than try to answer all questions up front.
practice-components.Component Description: Customer collaboration means working shoulder to shoulder with customers to shape the direction, instead of trying to lock down every answer at the start. It comes from the Agile value of customer collaboration over contract negotiation, and it keeps the Agility practice pointed at what people really need.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe the customer is a partner in figuring out what to build, not just someone you deliver to at the end.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You talk with customers regularly and let what you hear steer the work as it unfolds.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: The Agile Manifesto, the founding values of agile work: https://agilemanifesto.org/

practice-components.Assessment Question: I believe that everyone on the team, even the interns, have valuable perspective and decision-making abilities.
practice-components.Component Description: Inclusive safety is the first stage of psychological safety in Timothy Clark's model: everyone is accepted and belongs, so they can bring their whole self to work. It is the base layer the whole Psychological Safety practice is built on, and research from Amy Edmondson and Google's Project Aristotle ties it directly to how well teams perform.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe every person on the team, whatever their role or experience, belongs and has real value.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You include everyone in the group, welcome newcomers warmly, and make room for every voice.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Timothy Clark's 4 Stages of Psychological Safety (LeaderFactor): https://www.leaderfactor.com/learn/psychological-safety-timothy-clark/

practice-components.Assessment Question: I believe that everyone should learn by doing and failing
practice-components.Component Description: Learner safety is Clark's second stage of psychological safety: people feel safe to ask questions, try things, and make mistakes while they learn. It is what turns a team into a place where people grow instead of hiding what they do not know, and it strengthens the Psychological Safety practice.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe mistakes are part of learning, not something to be punished.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You ask questions openly, admit what you do not know, and treat failures as lessons rather than embarrassments.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Timothy Clark's 4 Stages of Psychological Safety (LeaderFactor): https://www.leaderfactor.com/learn/psychological-safety-timothy-clark/

practice-components.Assessment Question: I believe that everyone has something valuable to contribute on teams, even if they have little to no experience.
practice-components.Component Description: Contributor safety is Clark's third stage: people feel safe to take part as full members and use their skills to make a real difference. It moves someone from watching to genuinely contributing, and it is a key part of building Psychological Safety on a team.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe people do their best work when they are trusted to contribute, no matter their experience level.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You hand people real work and real autonomy, and you actively invite their contributions.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Timothy Clark's 4 Stages of Psychological Safety (LeaderFactor): https://www.leaderfactor.com/learn/psychological-safety-timothy-clark/

practice-components.Assessment Question: I believe in the power of people challenging the current ways that things work, or challenging current decisions, for the benefit of finding new ways to move forward.
practice-components.Component Description: Challenger safety is Clark's fourth and hardest stage: people feel safe to question the status quo and float new ideas without fear of being punished. It is the precondition for innovation and risk-taking, and it is the top layer of the Psychological Safety practice.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe respectfully challenging ideas makes the work better, and that healthy dissent is a sign of a strong team.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You speak up with different views, invite pushback on your own ideas, and never punish someone for disagreeing.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Timothy Clark's 4 Stages of Psychological Safety (LeaderFactor): https://www.leaderfactor.com/learn/psychological-safety-timothy-clark/

practice-components.Assessment Question: I rely on the voice of the team to build a consensus based on knowledge they have at the moment
practice-components.Component Description: Consensus is building a decision from the shared knowledge of the whole team, so people actually support the outcome. It sits at the heart of the Collective Decision Making practice, where a choice the group shaped together tends to stick far better than one handed down.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe the team's combined judgment is usually better than any single person's.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You gather input from the group and steer toward a decision people can genuinely get behind.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I ask others and let others take lead on things that I could own.
practice-components.Component Description: Delegation is handing real ownership to someone else, even for work you could do well yourself. It spreads responsibility and gives people room to grow, which is exactly how the Shared Ownership practice takes hold on a team.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe letting others carry meaningful work builds a stronger team than doing it all yourself.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You hand off real work, set clear expectations, and then let people run with it.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I focus myself and others on progressively learning lessons after failure and actions; I recognize the “power of yet” trusting that there’s always opportunities to improve (“I don’t get this...yet” “I can’t do this...yet.”)
practice-components.Component Description: A growth mindset, a term from psychologist Carol Dweck, is the belief that abilities grow with effort and practice, captured in the little word 'yet.' It turns setbacks into fuel instead of verdicts, and it underpins both Shared Ownership and Shared Leadership by keeping people willing to stretch.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe skills are built, not fixed, so 'I can't do this' becomes 'I can't do this yet.'
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You take on challenges, learn from what goes wrong, and encourage others to keep growing too.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Carol Dweck's growth mindset (Stanford Center for Teaching and Learning): https://ctl.stanford.edu/students/growth-mindset

practice-components.Assessment Question: I purposefully want to provide space for others to own things
practice-components.Component Description: Willingness is genuinely wanting to make room for others to take ownership, not just tolerating it. It is the open, generous spirit behind the Shared Ownership practice, and it shows up as looking for chances to step back rather than hold on.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe the team gets stronger the more people truly own the work.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You look for openings to step back and let someone else take the lead.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I prioritize letting events play out over trying to take control over outcomes
practice-components.Component Description: Letting go of control means resisting the urge to manage every outcome and trusting both the process and the people. It can feel uncomfortable, but it is what empowers others and lets a team share ownership instead of funneling everything through one person.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe you do not need to control everything for things to turn out well.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You step back, avoid micromanaging, and let people and situations play out.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I work to build a shared understanding of outcomes so that people can own work
practice-components.Component Description: Expectation setting is making the goal clear and shared, so everyone knows what success looks like and can own their part. In agile work the picture keeps sharpening as you go, so this is less a one-time briefing and more an ongoing habit that makes Shared Ownership and Collective Decision Making possible.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe people can only own work well when the goal is clear and genuinely shared.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You align on what 'done' looks like early, and you keep checking that everyone still shares the same picture.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I encourage myself and others to see my abilities as a meaningful contribution to the team; I believe people bring value no matter what their skill level is, including myself
practice-components.Component Description: Esteem is valuing your own contributions and everyone else's, whatever the experience level. It builds the confidence people need to speak up and take part, feeding the practices of Shared Ownership, Empowerment, and Continuous Improvement.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe everyone brings value, including yourself, no matter their skill level.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You affirm people's contributions and help them see their own worth on the team.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I do what I said I would do by the time agreed upon. If something will prevent me from doing what I said, I make a new agreement. I only agree to things when I can commit to doing them.
practice-components.Component Description: Commitment is reliably doing what you said you would, and renegotiating openly and early when you truly can't. It is the backbone of trust, and it is what lets a team share ownership, share leadership, and make decisions together knowing people will follow through.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe your word is a promise, so you only agree to what you can genuinely deliver.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You follow through on what you commit to, and you raise a new agreement early the moment something changes.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I repeat back what people have shared and acknowledge their views before responding
practice-components.Component Description: Active listening means fully taking in what someone says and reflecting it back before you respond. It makes people feel heard and heads off misunderstandings, which is why it shows up across so many practices, from Empowerment and Shared Leadership to Psychological Safety, Collective Decision Making, and Continuous Improvement.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe understanding someone comes before being understood.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You paraphrase what people said and acknowledge their view before adding your own.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I seek to understand and meet the needs of others
practice-components.Component Description: Care is genuinely seeking to understand and meet the needs of the people you work with. It is the heart of service leadership and a core part of the Shared Leadership practice, where leading means helping others succeed.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe part of your job is to help your teammates do their best work.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You ask about others' needs and take real action to support them.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I consistently seek to understand other perspectives before judging or concluding in interactions with others.
practice-components.Component Description: Empathy is understanding another person's perspective before you judge or conclude. It builds real connection and leads to better decisions, and it is one of the qualities that makes Shared Leadership work.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe everyone has reasons behind their actions that are worth understanding.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You put yourself in others' shoes and ask about their perspective before you react.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I get satisfaction from regularly offering attention, appreciation, and encouragement
practice-components.Component Description: Kindness is regularly offering attention, appreciation, and encouragement to the people around you. Small acts add up to a warmer, safer team, which is why kindness is woven through the Shared Leadership practice rather than treated as a soft extra.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe kindness is a real strength that makes teams work better, not a nice-to-have.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You notice and appreciate people often, and you offer encouragement freely.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I prioritize the mindset that I do not have all of the right answers in teamwork, and tell myself that others can produce great things, even when they don’t have experience
practice-components.Component Description: Removing ego is setting aside the need to be right or the smartest in the room, so the team's best ideas can win. It clears space for real collaboration and shows up across Shared Ownership, Empowerment, Shared Leadership, and Psychological Safety.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe you do not have all the answers, and that others are fully capable of producing great things.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You let go of being right, invite better ideas, and share the credit.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I provide positive reinforcement to others, even when they have tried and failed
practice-components.Component Description: Encouragement is giving people positive reinforcement, including, and especially, when they try and fall short. It keeps people motivated to keep learning and taking risks, which is how Shared Ownership and Empowerment take root.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe effort deserves recognition even when the result is not there yet.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You cheer people on, especially after a setback, and you point out what they did well.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I participate in discussions and decisions. I don’t go along with things just to avoid conflict. I am a valuable contributor to the team.
practice-components.Component Description: Participation means genuinely taking part in discussions and decisions instead of staying quiet to dodge conflict. Your voice is part of the team's strength, and speaking up is how Shared Ownership and Shared Leadership actually happen day to day.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe your input matters, and that going silent to avoid friction quietly hurts the team.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You speak up in discussions and share your real view rather than just going along.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I have the ability to pause, wait for alignment, exercise self-control
practice-components.Component Description: Patience is the ability to pause, wait for alignment, and hold your own reactions in check. It gives the team space to catch up and contribute, and it steadies the practices of Shared Ownership, Empowerment, Shared Leadership, and Continuous Improvement.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe good outcomes are worth waiting for, and that rushing usually backfires.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You slow down, wait for others to align, and manage your own impulses.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I do not interrupt or dismiss others when they share their views
practice-components.Component Description: Responding well means letting people finish and taking their views seriously, instead of interrupting or brushing them off. It protects the open, safe conversation that Shared Leadership depends on.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe every person deserves the space to be heard fully.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You wait for people to finish, and you respond to their actual point instead of dismissing it.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I recognize the wisdom of others. I acknowledge the ways other people are right even when there's disagreement.
practice-components.Component Description: Respect is recognizing the wisdom in others and where they are right, even when you disagree. It keeps disagreement healthy rather than personal, and it runs through Shared Ownership, Empowerment, and Shared Leadership.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe others hold wisdom worth honoring, even when you see things differently.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You acknowledge where others are right and treat them well straight through a disagreement.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I consistently shows up as myself. I am not different on my team as I am with other people. I can accept who I am and not try to seem more competent, knowledgeable, or skilled than I actually am.
practice-components.Component Description: Consistency is showing up as your genuine self, the same with your team as anywhere else, without pretending to be more than you are. That steadiness builds trust over time and is part of what makes Shared Leadership believable.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe being real and steady matters more than looking impressive.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You act the same across settings and never put on a front to seem more skilled than you are.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I recognize efforts in others on the team out loud and in public, even when they didn’t do something perfectly, or failed in something
practice-components.Component Description: Celebration is recognizing people's efforts out loud and in the open, even when the work was not perfect. It reinforces the behaviors a team wants more of, and it is one of the ways the Empowerment practice comes alive.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe recognizing effort openly builds a stronger, more motivated team.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You call out and celebrate good efforts publicly, including honest attempts that came up short.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I want people to figure things out on their own, and believe in their capabilities to do so without my intervention, and tell them so
practice-components.Component Description: Autonomy is trusting people to figure things out for themselves, and telling them plainly that you believe in them. It is central to the Empowerment practice, where people grow fastest when they are given room to run.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe people grow and do their best work when they are trusted with real independence.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You give people space to solve problems on their own and you tell them you trust them to.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I am able to change my decisions in the context of situations that change, and operate with flexibility in the decisions I make based on judgment calls
practice-components.Component Description: Judgment formation is making decisions with flexibility, adjusting them as the situation changes instead of clinging to your first call. It keeps the Collective Decision Making practice grounded in reality rather than in yesterday's assumptions.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe good judgment means adapting a decision to the moment, not being rigid for its own sake.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You revisit and update decisions as new information and situations come to light.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I check my assumptions when in the process of making decisions to give people time to reflect and respond whenever possible
practice-components.Component Description: Buy-in is checking your assumptions and giving people real time to reflect and respond, so a decision has genuine support behind it. It prevents the false agreement that quietly sinks projects, and it makes Collective Decision Making actually work.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe decisions only stick when people have had a genuine say in them.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You test your assumptions and build in time for others to weigh in before anything is locked.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I rely on failing as the opportunity to learn what I can do differently in the future
practice-components.Component Description: Failing fast is treating failure as a quick, cheap way to learn what to do differently, rather than a disaster to avoid. It is core to working in an agile way and drives both the Agility and Continuous Improvement practices.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe a fast failure is a lesson, not a defeat.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You try things quickly, learn from what does not work, and adjust without dwelling on it.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: The Agile Manifesto, the founding values of agile work: https://agilemanifesto.org/

practice-components.Assessment Question: I actively pay attention to how my behaviors affect others so that I can reflect on how to work on changing my own behaviors
practice-components.Component Description: Self-awareness is paying attention to how your behavior lands on others, so you can reflect on it and change. It is the starting point for personal growth and a key part of Shared Leadership and Continuous Improvement.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe your impact on others is worth watching and worth improving.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You notice the effect you have on people and reflect on how to adjust your own behavior.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I rely on user-centered and team-centered feedback on a continuous basis to learn how I need to improve
practice-components.Component Description: Feedback is leaning on regular input from users and teammates to learn how to get better. It is the engine of Continuous Improvement, and it also feeds Shared Leadership and Collective Decision Making by keeping the team honest about how things are really going.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe feedback is a gift that shows you exactly where to grow.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You seek out feedback often and act on it instead of getting defensive.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I constantly look inwards and evaluate my emotions and how I showed up, making a note about where / how I could improve.
practice-components.Component Description: Reflection is regularly looking inward at how you felt and how you showed up, and noting where you want to improve. It turns raw experience into real growth, which is why it anchors the Continuous Improvement practice.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe growth comes from honestly reviewing how you did, not just moving on.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You take time to reflect on your emotions and actions and write down what to change next time.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I believe that everyone has the ability to make decisions and want them to decide rather than make the decisions myself
practice-components.Component Description: Transferring power is believing everyone can make decisions and actively wanting them to, rather than keeping the calls to yourself. It spreads leadership across the team and supports Shared Ownership, Shared Leadership, and Psychological Safety.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe decision-making should be shared, not hoarded by one person.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You hand real decisions to others and encourage them to decide rather than deciding for them.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I actively prioritize pausing in conversations to ensure that people in the room are able to provide input and voice
practice-components.Component Description: Pause is deliberately stopping in a conversation so everyone in the room gets a chance to speak. It is a small habit with a big payoff, protecting the Psychological Safety that lets Empowerment, Shared Leadership, and Collective Decision Making thrive.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe the quietest voices often hold the input most worth waiting for.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You pause in discussions and directly invite people who have not spoken to share.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I prioritize sharing my true feelings and my mistakes, fears, and struggles to others for the benefit of building teammate confidence.
practice-components.Component Description: Vulnerability is openly sharing your feelings, mistakes, and struggles to build trust and give others permission to do the same. Timothy Clark describes psychological safety as a culture of rewarded vulnerability, so this is a cornerstone of the Psychological Safety and Shared Leadership practices.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe showing your real self, struggles included, makes the whole team stronger.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You admit mistakes and share your worries openly, which makes it safe for others to do the same.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Timothy Clark's 4 Stages of Psychological Safety (LeaderFactor): https://www.leaderfactor.com/learn/psychological-safety-timothy-clark/

practice-components.Assessment Question: I ask others how they want to be served and supported instead of supporting them in the way I want to be supported.
practice-components.Component Description: Approach is asking people how they actually want to be supported, instead of helping them the way you would want to be helped. That small shift makes support genuinely useful and is part of Empowerment, Shared Leadership, and Psychological Safety.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe support works best when it fits the other person, not you.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You ask how someone wants to be helped before you jump in.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

practice-components.Assessment Question: I value trust in myself and trust in others to carry out work.
practice-components.Component Description: Trust is believing in yourself and others to carry the work, and then acting on that belief. It is the foundation that lets a team share ownership and take risks together, and researchers like Patrick Lencioni and Amy Edmondson put it at the root of nearly every strong team, which is why it touches so many practices here.
practice-components.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe people are capable and will follow through, and you are willing to extend trust first.
practice-components.Associated Habits of the Component: You rely on others to do their part without hovering, and you prove trustworthy yourself.
practice-components.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

activities.Activity Description: Wireframing is sketching the bare-bones layout of a screen, showing where things go without color or polish. It is about structure, not looks.
activities.Why Is This Activity Important?: Starting rough lets the team test and change ideas cheaply before anyone builds a finished-looking design.
activities.How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens during the Implement work and produces wireframes that grow into prototypes. Teams often wireframe together in a workshop so everyone shapes the layout.
activities.How To Complete the Activity: Start from the user's task and block out where each piece goes on the screen. Use a tool like Figma or FigJam to lay out simple boxes, then share it for quick feedback.
activities.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

activities.Activity Description: Release scope definition is deciding what will and will not go into an upcoming release. It draws a clear line around the next chunk of work.
activities.Why Is This Activity Important?: A focused release actually ships, and clear scope sets honest expectations with everyone involved.
activities.How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It spans discovery through launch and produces epics, release-level scope, and the release plan. Teams often scope together so priorities are shared, and re-scope as they learn.
activities.How To Complete the Activity: List the possible work, then sort it into what is in and what waits. In Notion or FigJam, agree on the cut with the team and write down what the release will include.
activities.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

activities.Activity Description: Requirements gathering is collecting what a product needs to do by talking to stakeholders and users. It turns scattered wants into a clear list.
activities.Why Is This Activity Important?: Getting requirements right early is one of the biggest reasons projects succeed instead of drifting.
activities.How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It runs through discovery and requirements and feeds problem statements, acceptance criteria, and user stories. It is often a workshop so the whole room agrees.
activities.How To Complete the Activity: Ask lots of open questions and listen for the real need behind each request. Capture what you hear in Notion or Trello and play it back to confirm you got it right.
activities.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

activities.Activity Description: Requirements refinement is sharpening rough requirements into clear, buildable detail. It is the tidy-up that makes a to-do list ready to work from.
activities.Why Is This Activity Important?: Refined requirements mean the team stops guessing what an item really means, so building goes smoothly.
activities.How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens across discovery and requirements and produces acceptance criteria, user stories, and a refined backlog. Teams often refine together in a quick working session.
activities.How To Complete the Activity: Take each rough item and add detail, examples, and a clear definition of done. In Notion or Trello, resize and reword items with the team until they are clear.
activities.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

activities.Activity Description: Design component creation is building the reusable interface pieces, like buttons and cards, that a product is assembled from. It is making the parts once so they can be used everywhere.
activities.Why Is This Activity Important?: Reusable components speed up design and keep a product looking consistent instead of slightly different on every screen.
activities.How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in the Implement work and builds the component library that feeds the design system. It supports every screen the team designs.
activities.How To Complete the Activity: Identify the pieces used again and again, then build each one cleanly in Figma. Set them up as shared components so the whole team can reuse them.
activities.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

activities.Activity Description: Brand identity formation is shaping how a product looks, sounds, and feels so it is recognizable and consistent. It gives the product a personality.
activities.Why Is This Activity Important?: A clear identity builds trust and makes a product memorable, tying the whole experience together.
activities.How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in the Implement work and produces the editorial style guide, brand identity, archetypes, and brand assets. It is often shaped in a collaborative workshop.
activities.How To Complete the Activity: Explore words and visuals that capture the product's character, then agree on a direction. Use Figma and Notion to define the voice, colors, and rules others will follow.
activities.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

activities.Activity Description: Writing requirements is putting down clearly what needs to be built and how you will know it is done. It captures needs in a form the team can act on.
activities.Why Is This Activity Important?: Written, agreed requirements keep designers and developers building the same thing instead of different versions.
activities.How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It spans requirements and launch and produces acceptance criteria, user stories, task flows, and scope. Teams often draft these together to align quickly.
activities.How To Complete the Activity: Write each need as a short, testable statement with clear acceptance criteria. In Notion or Trello, review them with the team and adjust anything unclear.
activities.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

activities.Activity Description: Icon and logo creation is designing the small, recognizable marks that represent a brand or an action. These tiny visuals carry a lot of meaning.
activities.Why Is This Activity Important?: Clear, consistent icons and logos make a product easier to use and instantly recognizable.
activities.How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in the Implement work and produces logo and brand assets. It builds on the brand identity the team has set.
activities.How To Complete the Activity: Sketch several directions, then refine the strongest in Figma. Test them small to be sure they stay clear and simple at real size.
activities.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

activities.Activity Description: Feature vision definition is deciding what a specific feature should achieve and why it matters. It sets the point of a feature before the details.
activities.Why Is This Activity Important?: A clear feature vision keeps the team building toward a purpose instead of just adding functionality.
activities.How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in the Requirements work and shapes the acceptance criteria that define the feature. It is often set with the team so everyone shares the goal.
activities.How To Complete the Activity: Describe the problem the feature solves and what success looks like. In Notion or FigJam, agree on the vision with the team before detailing it.
activities.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

activities.Activity Description: Feature scope definition is deciding what is included in a single feature and what is left out. It draws the boundary around one piece of work.
activities.Why Is This Activity Important?: Clear boundaries keep a feature from ballooning and help the team estimate and finish it reliably.
activities.How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in the Requirements work and feeds the acceptance criteria for the feature. Teams often scope features together to keep priorities shared.
activities.How To Complete the Activity: List everything the feature could do, then agree on the must-haves for now. Capture the decision in Notion or Trello so it is clear later.
activities.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

activities.Activity Description: Generating problem statements is writing short, clear descriptions of the problems worth solving, from the user's point of view. It names the real issue plainly.
activities.Why Is This Activity Important?: Clear problems keep the team from building slick solutions to the wrong thing.
activities.How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It runs through discovery and requirements and produces problem statements, checklists, and how-might-we questions. It is often done as a group so problems are shared.
activities.How To Complete the Activity: Turn what you learned from users into simple 'who struggles with what and why' statements. In FigJam or Notion, refine them with the team until they ring true.
activities.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

activities.Activity Description: Analyzing research findings is making sense of what a study turned up to find what it really means. It is where raw notes become insight.
activities.Why Is This Activity Important?: Careful analysis keeps the team from jumping to conclusions, so decisions rest on what the data actually shows.
activities.How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in discovery and acceptance testing and produces research reports, rainbow tables, and analysis. Teams often analyze together to catch more patterns.
activities.How To Complete the Activity: Group your notes into themes and look for what repeats. Use FigJam, Dovetail, or a spreadsheet to cluster findings and write down the clear takeaways.
activities.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

activities.Activity Description: Strategy definition is deciding how a product or team will reach its goals. It sets the approach before the doing begins.
activities.Why Is This Activity Important?: A clear strategy focuses effort on what will actually move things forward instead of scattering energy.
activities.How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in discovery work and feeds the business plan and go-to-market plan. It is often shaped with the team in a working session.
activities.How To Complete the Activity: Clarify the goal, then map a few realistic paths to it and pick one. In Notion or FigJam, write the approach down so the whole team can follow it.
activities.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

activities.Activity Description: Sprint planning is the team agreeing on what they will complete in the next short work cycle. It picks a focused slice of the backlog.
activities.Why Is This Activity Important?: A clear, achievable target keeps agile work steady and lets the team make smart trade-offs.
activities.How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens at intake and repeats every sprint, producing the sprint plan and goals. It is a team workshop by design.
activities.How To Complete the Activity: Review the top of the backlog, estimate what fits, and agree on a goal. In Notion or Trello, commit to the sprint's work together.
activities.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

activities.Activity Description: Level of effort estimation is the team's best guess at how much work an item will take. It sizes the work so it can be planned.
activities.Why Is This Activity Important?: Estimates help the team plan realistically and avoid over-committing a sprint.
activities.How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It runs across discovery, requirements, and every sprint, refining the backlog and sprint goals. Teams estimate together so many views are heard.
activities.How To Complete the Activity: Compare each item to ones you have done before and agree on a rough size. Capture the estimates in Notion or Trello for planning.
activities.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

activities.Activity Description: Velocity calculation measures how much work a team actually completes per sprint. It turns past sprints into a planning guide.
activities.Why Is This Activity Important?: Knowing real velocity helps a team plan future sprints honestly instead of hopefully.
activities.How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens at intake and across sprints, informing the sprint plan and goals. It supports the scrum master's planning.
activities.How To Complete the Activity: Add up the work finished in recent sprints to find an average. Track it in Notion or a spreadsheet and use it to size the next sprint.
activities.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

activities.Activity Description: Identifying priorities is deciding which work matters most right now. It sorts a big pile into a clear order.
activities.Why Is This Activity Important?: A clear order means effort goes to what matters most instead of what is nearest or loudest.
activities.How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It runs through discovery and requirements and shapes the prioritized and refined backlog. Teams often prioritize together to align.
activities.How To Complete the Activity: Weigh each item by value and effort, then rank them. In FigJam, agree on the order with the team and record it.
activities.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

activities.Activity Description: Presenting research results is sharing what a study found with the team in a clear, usable way. It turns insight into shared understanding.
activities.Why Is This Activity Important?: Research only helps if the team acts on it, and a clear share makes that far more likely.
activities.How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in discovery and produces research reports and usability test reports. It is often a presentation or workshop for the team.
activities.How To Complete the Activity: Lead with the key findings and what they mean for the work. Use Notion or presentation tools to tell a simple, honest story.
activities.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

activities.Activity Description: Kickoff, or intake, is the first working session where the team and client get aligned before the work begins. It sets the tone for everything after.
activities.Why Is This Activity Important?: Projects that start fuzzy tend to stay fuzzy, so a clear kickoff prevents confusion down the road.
activities.How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It opens a project or phase and produces the statement of work, project plan, goals, and KPIs. It can recur when direction shifts, and it is a shared workshop.
activities.How To Complete the Activity: Talk through goals, scope, roles, and how you will work together. Capture agreements in Notion so everyone can refer back to them.
activities.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

activities.Roles: Scrum Master, Project Management, Product Operations
activities.Activity Description: Defining team working agreements is setting the ground rules for how a team will work together. The team writes its own social contract.
activities.Why Is This Activity Important?: Agreed norms head off friction, so the team spends energy on the work instead of avoidable conflict.
activities.How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens at intake and produces working agreements and a psychological safety plan. It is a group workshop by nature.
activities.How To Complete the Activity: Discuss how you want to communicate, meet, and handle disagreement, then agree on a few clear norms. Write them in Notion where everyone can see them.
activities.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

activities.Activity Description: This is clarifying who owns what on a team. It makes sure every important job has a clear owner.
activities.Why Is This Activity Important?: It prevents both the 'someone else has it' gap and two people redoing the same work.
activities.How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens at intake and produces the RACI chart. It is best done together so roles are truly agreed.
activities.How To Complete the Activity: Map each key responsibility to who is responsible, accountable, consulted, and informed. Capture it in a RACI chart in Notion or FigJam.
activities.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

activities.Activity Description: Moderating UX research is guiding a research session live, like an interview or usability test, keeping it on track. The moderator draws out honest, useful input.
