duties.Duty Description: The Agile Coaching duty helps teams work better together, not by managing them but by guiding how they collaborate. Coaches teach agile ways of working, run workshops, and help a team build trust, ownership, and steady improvement. Much of the job is noticing how people interact and gently helping them get unstuck.
duties.What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes strong coaching and facilitation skills, deep familiarity with agile methods, and the patience to guide rather than direct. The best coaches lead with empathy and read a team's dynamics well enough to know when to step in and when to hold back.
duties.Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: This duty raises the whole team's ceiling. By helping people collaborate, take risks, and keep improving, it turns a group of individuals into a real agile team, which is what makes everything else on a project work better.
You might enjoy this duty if you care about people's growth, like facilitating more than directing, and find satisfaction in watching a team come into its own.
duties.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

duties.Duty Description: The QA Analysis duty makes sure the product actually works before it reaches users. QA analysts write test plans and cases, put the product through its paces, and catch bugs and broken flows while they are still cheap to fix. In agile work they test continuously, checking each piece as it is built rather than waiting until the very end.
duties.What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes sharp attention to detail, logical thinking, and the discipline to test methodically, plus skills like writing BDD scenarios and QA test plans. The best analysts stay curious about how something might break and communicate the issues they find clearly.
duties.Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: This duty protects quality and trust. Shipping something broken costs far more than catching it early, so by finding problems before launch, QA keeps the product reliable and the team's reputation intact.
You might enjoy this duty if you like finding the flaw everyone else missed, enjoy methodical work, and take pride in making sure things really work.
duties.Where Can I Learn More?: MDN Web Docs, a trusted resource for building software: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn

duties.Duty Description: The Graphic Design duty creates the visual pieces that give a product its personality, logos, icons, illustrations, and brand assets. Designers turn ideas into clean, recognizable visuals that help a product look polished and feel like itself. It is craft-focused work where small details add up to a strong overall impression.
duties.What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes visual craft, an eye for hierarchy and detail, and skills like icon design and illustration. Add collaboration and openness to feedback, since visuals usually go through several rounds before they feel right.
duties.Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: This duty shapes how a product looks and feels at first glance. Strong visuals build trust and make a product memorable, tying the whole experience together so it feels professional and complete.
You might enjoy this duty if you love visual craft, enjoy making things look clean and clear, and get satisfaction from polishing details until they feel right.
duties.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

duties.Duty Description: The UX Strategy duty connects the day-to-day design work to the bigger picture of the user experience. Strategists map user journeys, storyboard experiences, and shape how the whole product should feel over time, so individual screens add up to a coherent journey. It is high-level thinking that keeps design pointed at real user and business goals.
duties.What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes strong strategic and systems thinking, an understanding of the full customer experience, and the ability to zoom out from single screens to the whole journey. Add advocacy and business sense to connect user needs with what the organization is trying to achieve.
duties.Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: This duty keeps design decisions aligned with a bigger goal instead of happening piece by piece. By mapping the journey and setting experience strategy, it makes sure the many parts of a product add up to something that genuinely works for users.
You might enjoy this duty if you like seeing the big picture, enjoy connecting the dots between user needs and business goals, and prefer shaping direction over polishing details.
duties.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

duties.Duty Description: The Product Operations duty sets up how a team actually works together. Ops people define working agreements, map team processes, choose the right agile method, and clarify who owns what, so the team runs smoothly instead of tripping over itself. It is the behind-the-scenes work that makes good collaboration possible.
duties.What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes process thinking, facilitation, and a good feel for team dynamics, plus skills like agile method selection and defining working agreements. The best ops people balance structure with flexibility, since a process should help a team, not box it in.
duties.Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: This duty is what lets a team scale and stay healthy. By defining clear processes and agreements, it reduces confusion and conflict, freeing everyone else to focus on the actual work rather than on how to work together.
You might enjoy this duty if you like building systems that help people work better, enjoy smoothing out friction, and get satisfaction from a team that runs well.
duties.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

duties.Duty Description: The Account Management duty owns the relationship with the client. Account managers keep communication clear, set expectations, and make sure the client feels heard while the team focuses on the work. Much of the job is trust-building, being the steady point of contact who keeps everyone aligned.
duties.What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes strong relationship-building, communication, and business sense, plus the diplomacy to balance client wishes with what the team can deliver. Skills like stakeholder management and clear expectation-setting sit at the center of the role.
duties.Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: This duty keeps the client relationship healthy, which protects the whole project. By managing expectations and communication, it prevents misunderstandings that could derail the work and builds the kind of trust that leads to lasting partnerships.
You might enjoy this duty if you like working with people, enjoy being the trusted point of contact, and are good at balancing what a client wants with what is realistic.
duties.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

duties.Duty Description: The Everyone duty covers the work that is not owned by one role but shared by the whole team. Things like giving sprint demos and writing AI prompts are part of everyone's job, whatever their specialty. It is a reminder that on an agile team, some responsibilities belong to all of us.
duties.What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes the shared basics of good teamwork: clear communication, presentation skills, and a willingness to pitch in beyond your own lane. Comfort with common tools and a habit of helping wherever needed go a long way.
duties.Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: This duty reflects how real agile teams work, with people stepping up for shared tasks rather than staying strictly in their roles. That shared ownership is part of what makes a team resilient and keeps work from falling through the cracks.
You might enjoy contributing here if you like pitching in wherever you are needed, enjoy presenting the team's work, and believe the best teams share the load.
duties.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

job-functions.Job Function Description: A UX Designer shapes how a product looks, feels, and works for the people who use it. Most days you take fuzzy ideas and turn them into screens and flows that feel simple and clear. You sketch, try layouts, and put your work in front of others to get feedback, always asking whether it makes sense for a real person. It is a blend of creative and practical work, and you do it shoulder to shoulder with researchers, writers, and engineers.
job-functions.Other Job Titles You May See in the Worl: Product Designer, Interaction Designer, UI/UX Designer, Experience Designer, Digital Product Designer
You may like this job function if you enjoy turning fuzzy ideas into clear, usable screens, like sketching and refining based on feedback, and care about how something works as much as how it looks. It suits people who are part creative and part practical, and who are happy collaborating with researchers, writers, and engineers.

job-functions.Job Function Description: A UI Designer focuses on the look and polish of a product, the part people actually see and touch. You choose colors, type, spacing, and the small details that make a screen feel clean and easy to use. A lot of the job is making things consistent, so every button and page feels like it belongs together. You care about craft, and you enjoy the moment a rough design turns into something that looks and feels finished.
job-functions.Other Job Titles You May See in the Worl: Visual Designer, User Interface Designer, Product Designer, Digital Designer
You may like this job function if you have an eye for detail and love making things look clean and polished. It fits people who care about color, type, and spacing, enjoy creating consistency across a product, and feel satisfied when a rough design turns into something that looks finished.

job-functions.Job Function Description: A UX Researcher is the team's connection to real users. Your job is to answer questions like what people actually need and whether something works for them. You talk to users, run tests, and look for patterns, then share what you learned so the team can make better choices. It suits people who are curious, like listening more than talking, and enjoy turning messy human behavior into clear insights.
job-functions.Other Job Titles You May See in the Worl: User Researcher, Design Researcher, User Experience Researcher, Insights Researcher
You may like this job function if you are endlessly curious about people and would rather ask a good question than assume the answer. It suits those who enjoy listening, digging into problems, and turning what real users say into insights the team can act on.

job-functions.Job Function Description: A Product Designer is a generalist who blends research, UX, and UI to solve whole problems, not just one slice. One day you might be talking to users, the next sketching flows or polishing a screen. You care about both how something works and how it feels, and you stay close to the goal of the product the whole way through. It is a good fit if you like variety and enjoy carrying an idea from first question to finished design.
job-functions.Other Job Titles You May See in the Worl: UX Designer, UX/UI Designer, Digital Product Designer, Product Design Lead
You may like this job function if you enjoy variety and dislike being boxed into one slice of the work. It fits people who like moving between research, design, and polish, and who want to carry an idea all the way from first question to finished product.

job-functions.Job Function Description: A UX Writer crafts the words inside a product: the buttons, labels, messages, and instructions that guide people along. It sounds small, but the right words can make something feel simple, and the wrong ones can leave people lost. You think hard about tone and clarity, and you cut anything that confuses. It fits people who love language and care about making things easy to understand.
job-functions.Other Job Titles You May See in the Worl: Content Designer, UX Content Strategist, Content Strategist, Product Writer
You may like this job function if you love language and believe the right handful of words can make something finally click. It suits people who care about clarity and tone, enjoy trimming the confusing bits, and like shaping how a product speaks to the people using it.

job-functions.Job Function Description: A Project Manager keeps the work organized and moving. You track what needs to happen, help the team stay on schedule, and clear roadblocks before they slow people down. A lot of the job is communication, making sure everyone knows the plan and nothing important falls through the cracks. It suits people who like structure, enjoy helping others do their best work, and stay calm when things get busy.
job-functions.Other Job Titles You May See in the Worl: Delivery Manager, Project Lead, Program Coordinator, Technical Project Manager
You may like this job function if you like structure, enjoy helping a team stay on track, and stay calm when a lot is happening at once. It fits organized communicators who get satisfaction from clearing the path so others can do their best work.

job-functions.Job Function Description: An Engineer builds the product, turning designs and ideas into working software. You write code, solve technical puzzles, and make sure things actually run the way they should. Much of the day is problem-solving: breaking a big challenge into small pieces and getting each one working. It fits people who like logic, enjoy building things, and feel real satisfaction when something they made finally works.
job-functions.Other Job Titles You May See in the Worl: Software Engineer, Developer, Software Developer, Full Stack Engineer, Front-End or Back-End Engineer
You may like this job function if you like logic, enjoy building things, and feel a real spark when a tricky problem finally clicks into place. It suits people who like breaking big challenges into small pieces and seeing their work run in the real world.

job-functions.Job Function Description: A Product Owner decides what the team should build next and in what order. You take a long list of possible work and turn it into a clear, prioritized plan the team can act on. A lot of the job is saying this first, that later, and explaining why. It suits people who like making decisions, can balance many voices, and enjoy owning the details of getting a product delivered.
job-functions.Other Job Titles You May See in the Worl: Backlog Owner, Technical Product Owner, Associate Product Manager, Product Lead
You may like this job function if you like making decisions and bringing order to a long list of possibilities. It fits people who can weigh many priorities, enjoy explaining the why behind the order of work, and like owning the details of getting things delivered.

job-functions.Job Function Description: A Product Manager sets the direction for a product, the what and the why behind the work. You spend time understanding users and the business, choosing which problems are worth solving, and rallying the team around a shared goal. You do not do all the work yourself; you help everyone pull in the same direction. It fits people who like strategy, enjoy connecting people, business, and technology, and are comfortable with a good deal of ambiguity.
job-functions.Other Job Titles You May See in the Worl: Associate Product Manager, Senior Product Manager, Group Product Manager, Growth Product Manager
You may like this job function if you enjoy strategy and connecting the dots between people, business, and technology. It suits those who are comfortable with ambiguity, like rallying a team around a shared goal, and care about building the right thing, not just building things.

job-functions.Job Function Description: A Business Analyst is the bridge between what people need and what the team builds. You dig into problems, ask a lot of questions, and turn vague requests into clear requirements everyone can understand. Much of the work is listening, mapping how things work today, and spelling out what should happen next. It fits people who like detail, enjoy untangling messy problems, and are good at translating between different groups.
job-functions.Other Job Titles You May See in the Worl: Systems Analyst, Requirements Analyst, Product Analyst, Business Systems Analyst
You may like this job function if you enjoy untangling messy problems and translating between what people want and what a team can build. It fits detail-oriented people who like asking questions, mapping how things work today, and writing down exactly what should happen next.

job-functions.Job Function Description: An Agile Coach helps a team work better together, not by managing them, but by guiding how they collaborate. You teach agile ways of working, run workshops, and help the team build trust, ownership, and steady improvement. A lot of the job is noticing how people interact and gently helping them get unstuck. It fits people who care about others' growth, like facilitating more than directing, and find satisfaction in watching a team come into its own.
job-functions.Other Job Titles You May See in the Worl: Scrum Master, Delivery Lead, Iteration Manager, Team Coach, Agile Delivery Manager
You may like this job function if you care more about how a team works together than about any single deliverable. It suits patient, people-focused folks who like facilitating over directing and who find real reward in watching a team grow stronger and more independent.

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A vision board is a simple, visual snapshot of where a product is headed and the future it is trying to create. Teams use it to capture the big idea in a form everyone can see and rally around before diving into the details.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It gives the team a shared thing to aim at, so day-to-day choices line up with the larger goal instead of drifting apart.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: It takes shape during the Vision milestone and sets the direction that later work like the roadmap, epics, and scope grows out of. Teams often revisit it as they learn more.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

Workshops.label: Scenario-Based Problem Statement Generation Workshop Template

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A problem statement is a short, clear description of the problem a team is solving, written from the user's point of view. It keeps everyone focused on the real issue instead of jumping straight to a solution.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Teams that skip this often build something polished that solves the wrong problem. A sharp problem statement keeps the effort aimed at something that genuinely matters.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: It emerges in Discovery and Requirements and feeds almost everything after it, from how-might-we statements to user stories and scope, and it gets sharper as the team learns.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Workshops.label: Scenario-Based Problem Statement Generation Workshop Template

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A problem checklist is a running list of the specific problems and needs a team has spotted and wants to address. It turns a vague sense that things are broken into concrete items the team can track.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It keeps real user problems from getting lost as the work speeds up, so the team can prioritize honestly instead of chasing whatever is loudest.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: It grows in Discovery and Requirements alongside problem statements and helps shape what makes it into scope. The list keeps changing as new problems surface.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

deliverables.Deliverable Description: Epics and features are the mid-sized chunks a big idea gets broken into. An epic is a large body of work, and features are the smaller, usable pieces inside it that a team can actually build and ship.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Breaking work this way lets an agile team deliver value in pieces instead of waiting to finish one giant thing, and it makes progress easy to see.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: They come out of the Requirements and Scope milestones and sit between the high-level roadmap and the detailed user stories the team builds from.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

deliverables.Deliverable Description: Release-level scope is the decision about what will and will not be included in a particular release. It draws a clear line around a chunk of work so the team knows what they are committing to next.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Without it, a release can balloon and never ship. Defining scope keeps a release focused and sets honest expectations with everyone involved.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: It is set during the Scope milestone, sits below the roadmap, and shapes the epics, features, and backlog the team pulls from. Teams re-scope as priorities shift.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

deliverables.Deliverable Description: Acceptance criteria are the plain, agreed conditions that tell everyone when a piece of work is truly done. They spell out what has to be true for a feature or story to be accepted.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: They stop the endless debate about whether something is finished, so designers, developers, and clients all share the same finish line.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: They attach to user stories in the Requirements milestone and guide the QA test plans and acceptance testing that check the work later on.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Workshops.label: Scenario-Based Problem Statement Generation Workshop Template

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A user story is a short description of a need from the user's point of view, usually in the form of who wants what and why. It keeps the focus on the person using the product, not just the feature.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Stories turn big requirements into small, buildable pieces the team can pick up one at a time, which is the heartbeat of agile delivery.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: They come from the Requirements milestone, carry acceptance criteria, and fill the backlog the team works through sprint by sprint.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

deliverables.Deliverable Description: BDD scenarios describe how a feature should behave in plain, structured language, usually as given-when-then steps. They turn a requirement into a concrete example of what should happen.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: They give developers and testers one shared, unambiguous description to build and check against, which cuts down on misread requirements.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: They grow out of requirements and acceptance criteria and feed directly into QA test cases and acceptance testing near launch.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A QA test plan lays out how a team will check that a product works before it ships: what will be tested, how, and what counts as passing. It is the roadmap for quality checking.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: A clear plan means testing is thorough and repeatable instead of a scramble at the end, which protects users from broken releases.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: It builds on requirements and acceptance criteria, spins off into detailed test cases, and drives the acceptance testing milestone.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: MDN Web Docs, a trusted resource for building software: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A system architecture diagram is a picture of how the major parts of a product fit and talk to each other, like the front end, back end, and databases. It gives everyone a shared map of the technical structure.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It helps the team spot problems and plan how things will scale before a single line of code is locked in, saving painful rework later.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: It is created in Requirements, guides the more detailed architecture specs and diagrams, and shapes how developers build in the Implement milestone.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: MDN Web Docs, a trusted resource for building software: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A task flow maps the steps a user takes to complete a single task, from start to finish. It shows the path through a product one goal at a time.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Laying out the steps reveals confusing detours and missing pieces early, so the team can smooth the path before building it.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Task flows come together in Requirements, lean on user stories and acceptance criteria, and guide the wireframes and prototypes designers create.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Workshops.label: Audience Segmentation, Goals, Motivations, and Use Cases Workshop Template

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A use case scenario walks through how someone uses a product to reach a goal, including the twists and turns along the way. It tells the story of the product in action.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It helps the team think through real situations, including the ones that are easy to forget, so fewer surprises show up during building.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Written in Requirements, use case scenarios build on user stories and inform use case diagrams, task flows, and acceptance criteria.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A use case diagram is a simple picture showing who uses a product and the main things they can do with it. It gives a quick, big-picture view of the product's functions.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It helps everyone see the full set of interactions at a glance, which makes gaps and overlaps easy to catch early.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: It comes from the Requirements milestone and summarizes the use case scenarios and user stories into one clear overview.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Workshops.label: Market Research and Competitive Analysis Workshop Template

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A competitive analysis is a study of what similar products do well and poorly. It gives the team an honest read on the landscape they are entering.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Knowing the competition helps a team find gaps to fill and avoid repeating others' mistakes, so their product can stand out.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: It is done during Discovery and feeds strategy work like positioning statements, the market research analysis, and the product vision.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

Workshops.label: Market Research and Competitive Analysis Workshop Template

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A market research analysis pulls together what a team learns about its market, customers, and trends. It turns scattered facts into a clear read on the opportunity.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It grounds big decisions in evidence rather than hunches, so a team invests where there is real demand.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Created in Discovery, it informs the business plan, go-to-market plan, and positioning work, and it pairs with the competitive analysis.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

Workshops.label: Brand Strategy and Identity Workshop Template

deliverables.Deliverable Description: An editorial style guide is the rulebook for how a product's words sound, covering tone, wording, and formatting. It keeps the writing consistent no matter who is writing it.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Consistent, clear language makes a product feel trustworthy and easy to use, and it saves writers from reinventing the rules each time.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: It is built in the Implement milestone alongside brand identity, and it guides the copywriting, microcopy, and content the team produces.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Workshops.label: Brand Strategy and Identity Workshop Template

deliverables.Deliverable Description: Brand identity is the personality of a product made visible and audible: its look, voice, and feel. It is what makes a product recognizable and distinct.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: A strong, consistent identity builds trust and makes a product memorable, tying the whole experience together.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: It comes together in Implement and shapes the logo and brand assets, editorial style guide, and archetypes that flow from it.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A user journey map traces a person's whole experience with a product over time, including what they do, think, and feel at each step. It shows the experience as a story, not a single screen.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It reveals the high and low points of an experience, so the team knows where to focus to make things better.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Built during Discovery from research, it connects to personas and empathy maps and guides design decisions across many milestones.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A user persona is a short, realistic profile of a typical user, based on research: their goals, needs, and frustrations. It puts a human face on the audience.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Personas keep the team designing for real people instead of a vague 'user,' which leads to choices that actually fit someone's life.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Made in Discovery from research, they pair with journey maps and empathy maps and steer design and product decisions throughout the project.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A proto persona is a quick, best-guess profile of a user made before deep research, based on what the team already believes. It is a starting point, not a final answer.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It gives a team something concrete to align around early, as long as everyone remembers it is a hypothesis to test.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Created early in Discovery, proto personas are the rough draft that real research later turns into full user personas.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

Workshops.label: Audience Segmentation, Goals, Motivations, and Use Cases Workshop Template

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A buyer persona is a profile of the person who decides to purchase a product, which is not always the person who uses it. It captures what drives a buying decision.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It helps the team and business speak to the people who actually pay, shaping pricing, messaging, and sales.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Built in Discovery, it complements user personas and feeds the marketing plan, positioning, and go-to-market work.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A business plan lays out how a product will create and sustain value: the market, the model, the costs, and the goals. It is the big-picture case for why the product should exist.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It forces a team to think past the idea to whether it can actually work and last, which protects everyone from building something unsustainable.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Shaped in Discovery, it draws on market research and strategy and sets the frame for the marketing, release, and go-to-market plans.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A marketing plan describes how a product will reach and win over its audience. It maps the channels, messages, and timing for getting the word out.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Even a great product needs people to find it. A clear plan makes sure the work actually reaches the audience it was built for.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: It runs across the whole project, builds on positioning and personas, and works hand in hand with the go-to-market and release plans.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A release plan lays out what will ship, when, and in what order across upcoming releases. It turns a roadmap into a concrete schedule of value going out the door.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It keeps the team and stakeholders aligned on what is coming next, and it supports shipping in steady pieces rather than one risky drop.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: It connects the roadmap and scope to the go-to-market plan, and in agile work it is expected to shift as the team learns.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A go-to-market plan is the strategy for launching a product to the world: who it is for, how it will be positioned, and how it will reach people. It ties product, marketing, and sales into one launch approach.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: A strong product can still flop with a weak launch. This plan gives the release the best shot at landing with its audience.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Built in Discovery and refined toward launch, it pulls together positioning, personas, pricing, and the release and marketing plans.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A project hand-off is the package of work, notes, and context passed on when a project or phase ends. It makes sure the next team or the client can pick things up cleanly.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Good hand-offs prevent knowledge from walking out the door, so momentum and understanding are not lost at the finish line.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Delivered around Launch, it gathers up the artifacts made across the whole project into one clear, usable summary.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A statement of work is the agreement that spells out what a project will deliver, on what timeline, and under what terms. It sets the shared expectations at the very start.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It prevents misunderstandings later by getting everyone to agree, in writing, on what success looks like before the work begins.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Created during Intake, it anchors the project plan, goals, and KPIs, and it is the reference point the team returns to when scope questions arise.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

deliverables.Deliverable Description: Prioritized backlog tasks are the to-do items for a product, sorted so the most valuable work sits on top. The backlog is the team's ordered pile of everything worth doing.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: A clear order means the team always knows what to pull next, so effort goes to what matters most instead of what is nearest.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Shaped in Requirements from user stories and priorities, the backlog feeds sprint planning and gets re-ordered constantly as things change.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A how-might-we statement reframes a problem as an open question that invites solutions, like 'how might we make sign-up feel effortless?' It turns a pain point into a springboard for ideas.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Framing problems this way opens up creative thinking instead of locking the team into the first fix that comes to mind.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: They come out of Discovery from problem statements and research, and they kick off ideation that leads toward scope and design.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Workshops.label: KPI Success Measurements Definition Workshop Template

deliverables.Deliverable Description: KPIs are the handful of numbers a team watches to know whether a product is succeeding, like sign-ups or retention. They are the scoreboard for the goals that matter.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Clear KPIs keep a team honest about progress and help everyone agree on what winning actually looks like.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Set during Intake alongside goals and OKRs, they guide decisions across the whole project and show up again in analytics and testing.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

deliverables.Deliverable Description: OKRs pair a clear objective with a few measurable results that show you are getting there. They connect a big goal to concrete signs of progress.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: They keep a team aligned on what matters and make it obvious whether the work is moving the needle or just staying busy.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Defined in Intake next to KPIs and project goals, they frame priorities that ripple into the roadmap and backlog.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A Gantt chart is a timeline view of a project's tasks, showing what happens when and what overlaps. It gives a bird's-eye view of the schedule.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It helps a team see how work fits together over time and spot crunches early, though in agile work it stays a living guide, not a fixed promise.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Created around Intake, it works with the project plan and roadmap and gets updated as milestones progress and plans shift.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A burn down chart shows how much work is left in a sprint as the days tick by. The line ideally drops toward zero by the sprint's end.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It gives the team a quick, honest read on whether they are on pace, so they can adjust before the sprint runs out.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Used across all milestones during sprints, it draws on the sprint plan and goals and feeds retrospective conversations.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A roadmap is a high-level view of where a product is going and roughly when. It shows the major themes and milestones without locking in every detail.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It keeps everyone pointed the same way and helps stakeholders see the plan, while leaving room to adjust as the team learns.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Shaped in the Vision milestone, it sits above scope, epics, and the release plan and gets revisited as priorities evolve.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A refined backlog is a backlog that has been cleaned up and clarified, with items sized, detailed, and re-ordered. Refinement keeps the to-do list ready to work from.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: A tidy backlog means sprint planning goes smoothly and the team is never left guessing what an item really means.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: It evolves through Discovery and Requirements, building on the prioritized backlog and feeding the sprint plan every cycle.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A sprint plan is the team's agreement on what they will tackle in the next short work cycle. It picks a focused slice of the backlog to complete.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It gives the team a clear, achievable target for the sprint, which keeps agile work steady and predictable.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Made from the refined backlog and sprint goals, it drives the burn down chart and the demo and retro that close the sprint.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

deliverables.Deliverable Description: Wireframes are simple, low-detail sketches of a screen's layout, showing where things go without color or polish. They focus on structure, not looks.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Starting rough lets a team test and change ideas cheaply, before anyone invests in a finished-looking design.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Created in the Implement milestone from task flows and requirements, they are the first step toward low- and high-fidelity prototypes.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A low-fidelity prototype is a rough, clickable version of a product used to test ideas quickly. It is more interactive than a wireframe but far from finished.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It lets a team put a rough experience in front of people early and learn from real reactions before building the real thing.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Built in Implement from wireframes, it feeds usability testing and grows into high-fidelity prototypes as ideas hold up.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A high-fidelity prototype looks and behaves close to the finished product, with real design and interactions. It is the most realistic preview before development.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It gives testers and stakeholders a true feel for the product, catching issues while they are still easy and cheap to fix.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: It builds on low-fidelity prototypes in Implement and hands developers a clear target, backed by UI specs and the design system.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

deliverables.Deliverable Description: UI development specifications are the detailed notes that tell developers exactly how a design should be built: sizes, spacing, colors, and behavior. They translate a design into build-ready instructions.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Clear specs prevent guesswork and mismatches between what was designed and what gets built, saving rounds of back-and-forth.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Created in Implement from high-fidelity prototypes, they pair with design annotations and the design system to guide developers.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

deliverables.Deliverable Description: Design annotations are notes added directly onto a design to explain how it should work and why. They fill in the details a picture alone cannot show.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: They make sure the intent behind a design survives the handoff to developers, so nothing important gets lost in translation.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Added in Implement to prototypes and UI specs, they support the developers building the design into working software.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A UX audit report is a review of an existing product against usability best practices, flagging what works and what gets in users' way. It is a health check for the experience.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It gives a team an evidence-based list of problems to fix, so improvements target real issues rather than guesses.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Produced in Requirements or Implement from heuristics analysis and analytics, it points toward design changes and research follow-ups.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

deliverables.Deliverable Description: An empathy map captures what a user says, thinks, does, and feels about a situation. It is a simple way to step into the user's shoes.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It helps a team build real understanding of users, which leads to designs that fit how people actually experience things.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Made in Discovery from research, it works alongside personas and journey maps to shape design decisions.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A storyboard tells the story of how someone experiences a product through a series of simple frames, like a comic strip. It shows the experience in context, moment by moment.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It helps a team imagine the real-world situation around a product, not just the screens, which sparks more human design ideas.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Created in Discovery, it builds on journey maps and personas and feeds early design and ideation work.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

deliverables.Deliverable Description: Sketches are quick, hand-drawn ideas for a design, made fast and cheap to explore lots of directions. They are thinking on paper.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Sketching lets a team generate and compare many ideas before committing, which keeps early design open and creative.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Done in Implement during rapid ideation, they are the loose starting point that firms up into wireframes and prototypes.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A task analysis breaks down exactly how a user accomplishes a task, step by step. It examines the how of a task in fine detail.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Understanding each step reveals where users struggle, so the team can simplify the hardest parts.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Created in Discovery from research planning, it informs task flows, journey maps, and the designs that follow.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A research report gathers what a study found and what it means into one clear document. It turns raw research into shareable insight.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It makes research usable by the whole team, so hard-won learning drives decisions instead of sitting in someone's notes.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Produced in Discovery from many research activities, it feeds personas, journey maps, and the priorities the team sets next.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A rainbow table (in research) is a color-coded grid that tracks which participants said or did what across a study. It makes patterns across people easy to see.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It helps a team spot which findings are common and which are one-offs, so they weigh evidence fairly.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Built in Discovery while analyzing findings, it supports the research report and the affinity mapping that surfaces themes.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

deliverables.Deliverable Description: An affinity map groups many individual notes or findings into clusters of related ideas. It is how a team makes sense of a pile of messy input.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Clustering turns scattered observations into clear themes, which is what makes a mountain of research actually useful.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Created in Discovery from research, it feeds the research report and helps shape priorities and problem statements.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A customer experience diagram maps the full relationship a customer has with a product or company, across every touchpoint. It zooms out beyond a single journey to the whole picture.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It helps a team see the experience as a connected whole, so improvements in one place do not create problems in another.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Made in Discovery or Implement, it builds on journey maps and personas and guides strategy across many milestones.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A research plan lays out what a team wants to learn, how they will study it, and who they will talk to. It is the blueprint for a piece of research.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Planning first keeps research focused and trustworthy, so the team gets clear answers instead of a muddle.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Created early in Discovery, it sets up the research activities that lead to reports, personas, and other findings.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Workshops.label: Tech Fleet Sprint Demo Slide Deck Template

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A sprint demo presentation is how a team shows the work they completed during a sprint. It is a chance to share progress and get feedback.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Demos make progress visible and invite input early, which keeps the team and stakeholders aligned and builds trust.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Given across all milestones at each sprint's end, it draws on the sprint plan and goals and feeds the next round of priorities.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A design system is a shared library of reusable design pieces, patterns, and rules for a product. It is the toolkit that keeps a product consistent.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It lets designers and developers build faster and more consistently, since they reuse trusted parts instead of remaking them.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Built in Implement from UI kit work, it underpins the component library, wireframes, and prototypes across the product.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A sitemap is a diagram of all the pages or screens in a product and how they connect. It shows the product's structure at a glance.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: A clear structure helps users find their way, and it helps the team see the whole product before building the pieces.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Created in Implement while developing information architecture, it guides navigation, taxonomy, and the designs that follow.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A copywriting document holds the written words that go into a product or its marketing, drafted and organized in one place. It is where the product's language lives before it ships.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Good copy guides and persuades users, and keeping it in one document keeps the voice consistent and easy to review.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Produced in Implement from the editorial style guide, it feeds the microcopy and content that appear throughout the product.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

deliverables.Deliverable Description: An analytics audit reviews the data a product collects to check that it is accurate and actually useful. It makes sure the team is measuring the right things well.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Trustworthy data is the basis for good decisions, so an audit keeps the team from acting on numbers that quietly mislead.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Done in Discovery or Acceptance Testing, it supports the research analysis and the KPIs the team tracks.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A taxonomy is the system of labels and categories a product uses to organize its content. It is the naming and grouping scheme behind the scenes.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Consistent, sensible categories help users and the product itself find and connect the right things.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Created in Implement alongside the sitemap while shaping information architecture, it supports search, navigation, and content.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Brand Strategy and Identity Workshop Template

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A positioning statement sums up what a product is, who it is for, and why it is different, in a sentence or two. It is the north star for how a product presents itself.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: A clear position helps everyone tell a consistent story and helps customers instantly grasp why the product is for them.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Shaped in Discovery from research and competitive analysis, it feeds the unique value proposition, marketing, and go-to-market work.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

Workshops.label: Market Research and Competitive Analysis Workshop Template

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A unique value proposition is a short, sharp statement of the main benefit a product offers that others do not. It answers 'why choose this?'
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It focuses the whole team and message on the one thing that matters most to customers, cutting through the noise.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Built in Discovery from positioning and market research, it anchors the marketing plan and go-to-market strategy.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

deliverables.Deliverable Description: Microcopy is the tiny bits of text scattered through a product: button labels, error messages, hints, and tips. Small as it is, it guides people at every step.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: The right microcopy can make a confusing moment feel simple, while the wrong words leave people stuck. It quietly shapes the whole experience.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Written in Implement from the copywriting document and style guide, it works alongside the designs and content it lives inside.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A usability test report captures what happened when real people tried to use a design, and what it means. It documents where users succeeded and where they struggled.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It gives the team hard evidence about what works, so design changes fix real problems instead of imagined ones.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Produced in Discovery from usability testing, it feeds design revisions and joins the broader research analysis.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A microservices architecture builds a product out of small, independent services that each do one job and talk to each other. It is an alternative to one big, tightly linked system.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Splitting a system this way lets teams build, update, and scale parts independently, which suits fast, parallel agile work.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Designed in Implement, it is a form of the system and technical architecture and shapes how developers build and deploy.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: MDN Web Docs, a trusted resource for building software: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn

deliverables.Deliverable Description: Network architecture is the design of how a system's servers, connections, and security fit together. It is the plumbing and walls behind a running product.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: A sound network design keeps a product fast, reliable, and secure, and it is where many security decisions are made.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Built in Implement by architecture and security work, it connects to the system architecture and security-related deliverables.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: MDN Web Docs, a trusted resource for building software: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn

deliverables.Deliverable Description: QA test cases are the specific checks a tester runs to confirm a feature works, each with steps and an expected result. They are the detailed to-do list of testing.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Written-out cases make testing thorough and repeatable, so the same checks catch problems every release.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Created near Launch from the QA test plan and acceptance criteria, they drive the acceptance testing milestone.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: MDN Web Docs, a trusted resource for building software: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A component library is a collection of ready-made, reusable interface pieces like buttons and cards. It is the shelf of parts designers and developers build from.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Reusing tested components speeds up building and keeps a product looking and behaving consistently.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Built in Implement from design component work, it is a core part of the design system and feeds every screen the team makes.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

deliverables.Deliverable Description: Research analysis is the work of making sense of research data to find what it really means. It is where raw input becomes insight.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Careful analysis keeps a team from jumping to conclusions, so decisions rest on what the data actually shows.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Done in Discovery and Acceptance Testing across many activities, it feeds research reports, personas, and the team's priorities.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

deliverables.Deliverable Description: Working agreements are the ground rules a team sets for how they will work together, from meeting norms to how they handle disagreement. The team writes their own social contract.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Agreed norms head off friction and confusion, so the team spends energy on the work instead of on avoidable conflict.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Created during Intake, they pair with the team charter and RACI chart to set up healthy collaboration from the start.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A RACI chart spells out who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed for each piece of work. It makes ownership crystal clear.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It prevents the twin problems of everyone assuming someone else has it and two people redoing the same work.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Built in Intake, it works with working agreements and the team process map to clarify roles across the project.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

Workshops.label: Market Research and Competitive Analysis Workshop Template

deliverables.Deliverable Description: A product-market fit analysis checks how well a product satisfies a real market need. It gauges whether the product truly resonates with its audience.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Finding fit is often the difference between a product that grows and one that stalls, so this analysis guides big strategic calls.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Done in Discovery from positioning and market research, it informs the business, marketing, and go-to-market plans.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

deliverables.Deliverable Description: Technical architecture specifications are the detailed rules for how a system will be built: the technologies, structures, and standards. They turn an architecture diagram into build-ready detail.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Clear specs keep developers building consistently and prevent shaky technical foundations that cause trouble later.
deliverables.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: Created in Requirements from the system architecture diagram, they guide the Implement milestone and the diagrams that support it.
deliverables.Where Can I Learn More?: MDN Web Docs, a trusted resource for building software: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn

deliverables.Deliverable Description: Architecture diagrams are pictures of how the technical parts of a system connect and interact. They make a complex structure easy to talk about.
deliverables.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: Shared diagrams help the whole team understand and improve the technical design without getting lost in words.

milestones.Milestone Description: Continuous Discovery is the practice of staying connected to the people a team is building for, instead of guessing what they need. Throughout a project the team keeps interviewing users, digging into problems, and testing its assumptions, and it turns what it hears into clear problem statements and a read on the competition. The name says it plainly: this is continuous. You learn a little at a time, all the way through, so the team is never designing in the dark.
milestones.Why Is This Milestone Important?: When teams stop listening, they start guessing, and guesses are expensive to build. Ongoing discovery helps the team rule out weak ideas early and lean into the strong ones, so the work stays pointed at problems that genuinely matter to the people using the product.
milestones.When Should You Do This Milestone In Pro: Discovery does not wait its turn and it never really ends. Teams run it while they are building and even after a launch, and they lean on it hardest whenever they hit a question only a user can answer. Like every milestone here, it is not a step in a line. It runs alongside the others and comes back around many times.
milestones.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

milestones.Milestone Description: Requirements is the work of turning a rough idea into a shared picture of what to build. The team writes what it has learned as user stories and acceptance criteria, plain statements of what needs to happen and how everyone will know it is finished. In agile work you write just enough to get moving and keep refining as you learn, rather than trying to spell out every detail before anyone starts.
milestones.Why Is This Milestone Important?: Vague requirements are one of the most common places projects quietly go wrong. When the team shares a picture of what 'done' looks like, designers, developers, and clients stop working from different assumptions, and a lot of expensive rework simply never happens.
milestones.When Should You Do This Milestone In Pro: Requirements tend to sharpen right before a piece of work gets built, but they are never a one-time step. The team keeps rewriting them as it learns, so one part of a product can be in requirements while another is already being built and a third is being tested.
milestones.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

milestones.Milestone Description: Scope is where a team decides what to take on now and what can wait. There are always more ideas than time, so the team chooses which pieces of work, the epics and features, to commit to and which to set aside for later. The goal is not to do everything, but to pick the right things to do first, and to keep adjusting that choice as the work teaches the team more.
milestones.Why Is This Milestone Important?: A project with no edges struggles to ship. Agreeing on scope keeps the team focused, sets honest expectations with clients, and protects everyone from the slow creep of 'just one more thing.'
milestones.When Should You Do This Milestone In Pro: Scope gets attention early, but in agile work it is rarely set once and left alone. The team defines scope as it goes, shifting what is in and out as it learns, so scoping happens again and again, often while other parts of the product are being built or tested.
milestones.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

milestones.Milestone Description: Implement is where the building happens and plans become real. Wireframes turn into working screens, and the product's components and brand come together. It is the hands-on, make-it-real work, and it usually takes the most time and energy, done in short repeating cycles rather than one long push.
milestones.Why Is This Milestone Important?: This is where the product's value actually gets made. Everything before it was preparation; this is the part users will see and touch, so the care the team puts in here shows up directly in the finished product.
milestones.When Should You Do This Milestone In Pro: Building does not wait for everything else to be figured out. One feature can be under construction while another is still being scoped and a third is already live. Expect implementation to run in parallel with almost every other milestone, in small cycles the team repeats as it learns.
milestones.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

milestones.Milestone Description: Launch is the point where the work reaches real users. The team ties up the final details, plans how the release will roll out, and gets everything ready for the people who will use it. It is part careful checklist and part milestone worth celebrating, the payoff for the work that came before.
milestones.Why Is This Milestone Important?: A strong product nobody can get to helps no one. A clear launch plan means the work actually reaches people, so the team ships with confidence instead of uncertainty.
milestones.When Should You Do This Milestone In Pro: Launch is often pictured as the finish line, but products rarely launch just once. A team might release a small version early, then keep discovering, testing, and building well after. It helps to see a launch as one of many moments a product meets its users, not the end of the road.
milestones.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

milestones.Project Phases: PILR Training Phase 2, Mindful Digits Phase 3, Baddies in Tech Phase 2
milestones.Milestone Description: Vision is where a team decides where it is headed and why the trip is worth taking. Before working through the details, the team steps back to describe the bigger picture: who it is serving, what success looks like, and a rough roadmap to get there. This becomes the reference point people line their work up against.
milestones.Why Is This Milestone Important?: Without a shared vision, teams drift and small decisions turn into debates. A clear vision gives people a standard to measure their choices against, which makes day-to-day decisions faster and more consistent.
milestones.When Should You Do This Milestone In Pro: Vision usually takes shape early, but it is worth returning to. As the team learns, the picture can change, so revisiting the vision partway through, even after a launch, is a healthy part of iterating rather than a sign that something went wrong.
milestones.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

milestones.Milestone Description: Acceptance Testing is the team's reality check on whether the work truly does what it should. The team puts the work in front of users and against its own quality standards, and this is where problems like a confusing screen or a broken flow show up while they are still cheap to fix.
milestones.Why Is This Milestone Important?: Shipping something flawed costs far more than catching the flaw early, in both money and user trust. Testing against real people and clear criteria is how a team earns the confidence that the work is genuinely ready.
milestones.When Should You Do This Milestone In Pro: Testing naturally follows building, but it is not a single gate at the end. Teams often test one piece while building another, and it is common to run acceptance testing after a launch, checking how real use goes and feeding what they learn straight back into the work.
milestones.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

milestones.Milestone Description: Intake is the first real handshake of a project, where the team and the client get on the same page before the work begins. Together they sort out what the project is, what success means, and how they will work together, and they capture it in things like a statement of work and a set of shared agreements. It is short, but it sets the tone for everything after.
milestones.Why Is This Milestone Important?: Projects that start fuzzy tend to stay fuzzy. A good intake means the team is not guessing about goals or stepping on each other later, because the important questions got asked right at the start.
milestones.When Should You Do This Milestone In Pro: Intake usually opens a project or a new phase, but it can come back around. A new client, a fresh goal, or a big change can call for another intake partway through, so it is less a one-time start and more a reset the team returns to whenever the direction shifts.
