milestones.Milestone Description: This is not a single stage but a catch-all for the work and habits that show up across the whole project. Some skills and ways of working are not tied to one moment; they run through everything a team does, from kickoff to launch. Think of it as the connective tissue of a project rather than a step along the way.
milestones.Why Is This Milestone Important?: It is a reminder that not everything fits neatly into a phase. Collaboration, learning, and steady improvement do not clock out after one milestone, and treating them as ongoing is part of what keeps a team healthy the whole way through.
milestones.When Should You Do This Milestone In Pro: There is no single time for this one. It applies at every milestone, start to finish, and that fits how these milestones really work: not as steps in a line, but as pieces of work that run in parallel, repeat, and overlap as the team learns and adjusts.
milestones.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

specializations.What Makes This Specialization Unique?: What makes this specialization unique is its focus on understanding people's emotions and experiences, rather than just numbers and data. Unlike other research roles that might focus on statistics, Qualitative UX Research is all about the stories and feelings behind user interactions. It's like being a storyteller who helps design better products by understanding what users truly need and want.

What makes Interaction Design special is its focus on how people interact with technology. Unlike other design fields that might focus more on how things look, Interaction Design is all about making sure things are easy and fun to use. It's like being a detective, figuring out what users need and how to make their experience as smooth as possible. You'll be the bridge between technology and people, ensuring that digital products are not just functional but also enjoyable.

What makes Information Architecture unique is its focus on making information easy to find and use, unlike other specializations that might focus more on how things look or function. It's like being the mastermind behind a treasure map, ensuring everyone can find the treasure (or information) they're looking for without getting lost.

What makes content strategy special is that it's not just about creating content; it's about making sure the content connects with the right people and serves a purpose. Unlike other roles that might focus only on writing or design, content strategists look at the big picture. They figure out what the audience needs and how to deliver it in the best way possible, making sure every piece of content has a clear goal and fits into a larger plan.

What makes Service Design unique is its focus on the big picture. Unlike other specializations that might focus on just one part of a service, Service Design looks at the entire journey a customer takes. It's like being a director of a movie, making sure every scene fits together to tell a great story. You'll work with different teams and use your imagination to create services that people love and find easy to use.

What makes Customer Experience Design special is that it's all about understanding people and making their experiences enjoyable and memorable. Unlike other specializations that might focus more on the technical side of things, this one is all about empathy and creativity. You'll be the one making sure that every interaction a customer has with a product or service is as smooth and delightful as possible!

What makes Quantitative UX Research unique is its focus on numbers and data to understand user behavior, unlike other UX specializations that might focus more on design or direct user interaction. You'll be like a scientist in the UX world, using data to uncover insights and improve user experiences. It's perfect for those who love puzzles and finding patterns in data!

What makes Product Operations unique is its focus on the big picture and the details. Unlike other roles that might focus solely on creating a product or marketing it, Product Operations ensures that every part of the process is efficient and effective. It's about making sure everyone is on the same page and working towards the same goals, which is crucial for the success of any project.

What makes Branding unique is its focus on storytelling and visual creativity. Unlike other specializations that might focus more on numbers or technical details, Branding is all about creating a memorable image and feeling. It's about making sure a brand stands out and connects with people on an emotional level. So, if you love mixing art with strategy and enjoy making things look and sound awesome, Branding could be your perfect fit!

What makes SEO unique is its focus on making websites stand out in search results, which is different from other digital marketing specializations that might focus more on social media or email marketing. SEO requires a mix of technical know-how and creativity to improve a website's ranking, making it a dynamic and ever-evolving field. You'll be constantly learning and adapting to new trends and technologies, which keeps the work exciting and challenging.

What makes UX Strategy unique is its focus on the big picture. Unlike other roles that might focus on just designing or coding, UX Strategy is all about understanding the whole user journey and making sure every part of a product fits together perfectly. It's like being the director of a movie, where you make sure every scene works together to tell a great story.

What makes UI Design unique is its focus on how things look and how users interact with them. Unlike other design fields that might focus more on the technical side or the overall user experience, UI Design is all about making sure the interface is visually appealing and easy to use. It's like being an artist and a problem-solver at the same time, ensuring that every button and icon is both beautiful and functional.

What makes an Accessibility Specialist unique is the focus on inclusivity. Unlike other roles in tech that might focus solely on design or functionality, this specialization is all about ensuring that digital spaces are welcoming and usable for everyone, regardless of their abilities. It's like being a digital architect who builds ramps and elevators in the online world, making sure no one is left out.

What makes being a Front-End Developer unique is that you get to combine creativity with technology. Unlike other tech roles that might focus more on the behind-the-scenes stuff, you'll be working on the parts of websites that people see and use every day. It's like being an artist and a problem-solver at the same time, making sure that websites are not only beautiful but also easy to use.

What makes back-end development unique is that, unlike front-end developers who focus on what users see and interact with, back-end developers ensure everything works perfectly behind the curtain. It's like being the wizard who makes sure the magic happens without anyone noticing the hard work involved.

What makes a Full Stack Developer unique is their ability to handle both the visual and technical sides of a project. Unlike specialists who focus only on front-end or back-end development, Full Stack Developers can switch between both, making them versatile and highly valuable in tech teams. They can see the big picture and understand how different parts of a project connect, which helps them create more cohesive and efficient solutions.

What makes a Web3 Developer unique is the focus on blockchain, which is like a digital ledger that keeps everything secure and transparent. Unlike other developers who might work on regular websites or apps, you'll be building the future of the internet, where everything is decentralized. This means no single company controls the data, making it a fairer and more open space for everyone. It's a bit like being a digital pioneer, exploring new frontiers in technology!

What makes Information Security unique is its focus on keeping data safe from hackers, unlike other tech roles that might focus on building or maintaining systems. You'll be on the front lines, ensuring that sensitive information stays protected, which is crucial in our digital world. It's like being a superhero for the internet, using your skills to keep everyone safe online!

What makes AI User Experience unique is its focus on blending technology with human needs. Unlike other tech roles that might focus solely on coding or data, this specialization is all about making sure the technology feels natural and intuitive for people to use. It's like being a bridge between the tech world and everyday users, ensuring that AI tools are not just smart but also user-friendly and enjoyable.

What makes Growth Product Management unique is its focus on growing a product's reach and success. Unlike other product management roles that might focus more on developing the product itself, this specialization is all about making sure the product finds its audience and thrives in the market. It's like being the coach of a sports team, where your job is to make sure the team wins by reaching more fans and playing the best game possible!

methodologies.When Is This Method Used?: Reach for a Design Sprint when you have one big, risky question and need a real answer fast, before pouring months into building. It shines when a team is unsure which direction to take and wants to test an idea with actual users in days rather than quarters. It is also a quick way to get a group aligned, since everyone works through the problem together in the same room.
methodologies.Who Created This Method?: The Design Sprint was created by Jake Knapp at Google in 2010, then refined with John Zeratsky and Braden Kowitz at Google Ventures (GV). The three shared the full process in their 2016 book, Sprint. Official source: gv.com/sprint.
methodologies.How Does This Method Compare to to Other: Unlike Scrum and Kanban, which run continuously, a Design Sprint is a short, one-week burst aimed at answering a single question. It shares the fast, test-driven spirit of Lean UX and Continuous Discovery but packs it into a fixed five-day structure. Teams often use a sprint to kick off an idea, then hand it to a Scrum or Kanban team for ongoing delivery.
methodologies.During While Kinds of Work Environments: A Design Sprint works best when a team faces one big question or opportunity and needs a tested answer fast, before committing months of work. It fits small, cross-functional teams that can clear a full week and get access to real users. It is a strong fit for startups and new product bets.
methodologies.Steps to Perform the Method:
The Design Sprint runs over five days:
1. Monday: map the problem and choose one target to focus on.
2. Tuesday: sketch competing solutions on your own.
3. Wednesday: decide on the strongest ideas and turn them into a storyboard.
4. Thursday: build a realistic prototype.
5. Friday: test the prototype with about five real users and learn what works.

methodologies.When Is This Method Used?: Scrum fits when you are building something complex that keeps changing, and the team needs a steady rhythm to stay on top of it. It helps most when regular feedback and quick course-correction matter, and when clear roles and a predictable cadence keep everyone moving in the same direction. If a team does better with routine than with a free-for-all, Scrum gives it that shape.
methodologies.Who Created This Method?: Scrum was created by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, who first presented it together at the OOPSLA conference in 1995. They keep its official definition in the Scrum Guide, maintained independently of any company, with the latest version released in 2020. Official source: scrumguides.org.
methodologies.How Does This Method Compare to to Other: Scrum gives more structure than Kanban, with fixed-length Sprints and set events, while Kanban focuses on continuous flow with fewer rules. It is broader than a Design Sprint, which is a single one-week event, and it provides the delivery cadence that discovery methods like Lean UX and Continuous Discovery feed into. For very large organizations, SAFe wraps Scrum-style teams into a bigger coordinated structure.
methodologies.During While Kinds of Work Environments: Scrum fits complex product work where requirements change and the team benefits from a steady rhythm. It works best with a stable, cross-functional team that can commit to the regular events and that values routine and clear roles.
methodologies.Steps to Perform the Method:
Scrum organizes work into short cycles called Sprints, usually one to four weeks:
1. Keep a Product Backlog of prioritized work.
2. Hold Sprint Planning to choose what to build this Sprint.
3. Meet for a 15-minute Daily Scrum to sync and adjust.
4. Do the work through the Sprint and produce a usable Increment.
5. Hold a Sprint Review to show the work and gather feedback.
6. Hold a Sprint Retrospective to improve how the team works, then start the next Sprint.
Three roles support this: the Product Owner, the Scrum Master, and the Developers.

methodologies.When Is This Method Used?: Kanban is the method to reach for when work arrives as a steady stream, like support, operations, or maintenance, and you want to improve how it flows without tearing up the way you already work. It suits teams whose priorities shift often and who value flexibility over fixed cycles. Because you can lay it on top of an existing process, it is often an easy first step into agile.
methodologies.Who Created This Method?: The Kanban Method for knowledge work was formalized by David J. Anderson around 2010, building on lean manufacturing ideas from Toyota's production system. Its official definition lives in the Kanban Guide from Kanban University. Official source: kanban.university.
methodologies.How Does This Method Compare to to Other: Kanban is lighter than Scrum. It has no fixed Sprints or required roles, so a team can adopt it on top of how they already work. Where Scrum plans in time-boxed batches, Kanban manages a continuous flow. It pairs well with discovery methods like Lean UX and Continuous Discovery, and unlike SAFe it is meant for a single team's flow rather than coordinating many teams.
methodologies.During While Kinds of Work Environments: Kanban fits teams with a steady stream of incoming work, like support, operations, or maintenance, and teams that want to improve without overhauling their current process. It suits work where priorities shift often and flexibility matters more than fixed cycles.
methodologies.Steps to Perform the Method:
Kanban improves how work flows through six core practices:
1. Visualize the work on a board so everyone can see it.
2. Limit work in progress (WIP) so the team focuses and finishes.
3. Manage flow to keep work moving smoothly.
4. Make policies explicit so everyone knows the rules.
5. Add feedback loops like regular reviews.
6. Improve collaboratively over time.
Teams pull new work only when they have capacity for it.

methodologies.When Is This Method Used?: Use Continuous Discovery when you want to stay close to your users and let what you learn shape the product as you go. It is most useful when user needs are unclear or keep changing, and when the team would rather adjust based on real evidence than commit to a fixed plan up front. It fits teams that treat learning as a constant habit, not a one-time phase.
methodologies.Who Created This Method?: Continuous Discovery was shaped and popularized by product coach Teresa Torres in her 2021 book, Continuous Discovery Habits. It builds on lean and agile ideas about learning from customers often. Official source: producttalk.org.
methodologies.How Does This Method Compare to to Other: Continuous Discovery is not a delivery method like Scrum or Kanban. It focuses on deciding what to build, while Scrum and Kanban focus on building it, so teams usually run it alongside one of them. It shares the test-and-learn mindset of Lean UX, but as an ongoing weekly habit rather than a project-by-project cycle.
methodologies.During While Kinds of Work Environments: It fits product teams that can reach customers regularly and that work toward an outcome rather than a fixed feature list. It is best where user needs change or are not fully understood, and where a cross-functional trio can share the discovery work.
methodologies.Steps to Perform the Method:
Continuous Discovery is a set of weekly habits:
1. Talk to at least one customer every week as a full product trio (product, design, and engineering).
2. Map what you learn on an opportunity solution tree that connects customer needs to a clear outcome.
3. Surface and test your assumptions before building anything.
4. Run small experiments to check ideas quickly.
5. Keep repeating so learning never stops.

methodologies.When Is This Method Used?: Lean UX is the right call when you are building something user-centered and are open to changing course based on what you learn. It helps most early on, when the real need is still fuzzy and the team wants to test ideas quickly instead of building a lot on a guess. It suits groups that value working closely together over producing polished documents.
methodologies.Who Created This Method?: Lean UX was created by Jeff Gothelf with Josh Seiden, who described it in their 2013 book, Lean UX. It blends the Lean Startup's build-measure-learn loop (from Eric Ries), Agile, and Design Thinking.
methodologies.How Does This Method Compare to to Other: Lean UX guides how a team designs and validates ideas, while Scrum and Kanban manage how the work gets delivered, so they are usually used together. It is close in spirit to Continuous Discovery, since both test assumptions with users, and it provides the fast, experiment-first thinking that a Design Sprint compresses into five days.
methodologies.During While Kinds of Work Environments: Lean UX fits early or uncertain products where the team needs to validate ideas quickly instead of building a lot up front. It works best with collaborative, cross-functional teams that care more about outcomes than polished documents.
methodologies.Steps to Perform the Method:
Lean UX works in a learning loop:
1. Declare your assumptions about the users and the problem.
2. Turn those assumptions into clear hypotheses you can test.
3. Design the smallest thing that can test a hypothesis, a minimum viable product (MVP).
4. Run an experiment and put it in front of users.
5. Measure the results and learn whether to keep, change, or drop the idea, then repeat.

methodologies.When Is This Method Used?: SAFe comes into play when the work is simply too big for one team, and many teams across an organization need to pull in the same direction. It helps when coordination, alignment, and planning at scale are the real challenge, and when leaders need everyone responding to change together rather than drifting apart. It is built for large, complex efforts, not small ones.
methodologies.Who Created This Method?: The Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe) was created by Dean Leffingwell and first released in 2011 through Scaled Agile, Inc. Its official source of truth is scaledagileframework.com.
methodologies.How Does This Method Compare to to Other: SAFe is the heaviest of these methods because it coordinates many teams at once, while Scrum and Kanban each run a single team. It uses Scrum-style and Kanban-style teams inside a larger structure. Smaller, faster methods like Design Sprints, Lean UX, and Continuous Discovery can still run inside a SAFe organization to shape what each team builds.
methodologies.During While Kinds of Work Environments: SAFe fits large organizations that need many agile teams working toward shared goals. It is best when the work is too big for one team and when coordination, alignment, and planning at scale really matter.
methodologies.Steps to Perform the Method:
SAFe scales agile across many teams. At a high level:
1. Organize teams around value into an Agile Release Train (ART), a team of teams of about 50 to 125 people.
2. Align the whole ART in PI Planning, a two-day event that sets shared goals for the next Planning Interval (about 8 to 12 weeks).
3. Deliver in short iterations within each team while coordinating dependencies across the train.
4. Integrate and demo the work regularly.
5. Hold an Inspect and Adapt session to review results and improve.
SAFe is guided by four core values: alignment, transparency, respect for people, and relentless improvement.

tools.Tool Description: Figma is a design tool where teams build the actual screens of a product, from rough wireframes to polished, clickable prototypes. Because it runs in the browser and lets people work together in real time, it is often where design and development meet, with designers laying out interfaces and handing off clear specs for engineers to build.
tools.Tool Features:
1. Build low fidelity interfaces
1. Build high fidelity interfaces
1. Create animations
1. Create design components
1. Define the UI styles
1. Define the specifications for development

tools.Tool Description: Notion is an all-in-one workspace for notes, documents, wikis, and simple databases. Teams use it to keep everything in one place, meeting notes, project plans, and shared knowledge that would otherwise get scattered, so anyone can find what they need without digging through a dozen tools.
tools.Tool Features:
1. Create docs and wikis
2. Build databases and boards
3. Organize a team knowledge base
4. Track tasks and backlogs
5. Collaborate in real time

tools.Tool Description: FigJam is an online whiteboard made by Figma, built for the messy, collaborative early stages of work. Teams use it to brainstorm, map ideas on sticky notes, run workshops, and sketch flows together, making it a natural home for group thinking before designs get polished.
tools.Tool Features:
1. Run sticky-note workshops
2. Draw diagrams and flows
3. Brainstorm as a group
4. Vote and react in real time
5. Start from templates

tools.Tool Description: Zoom is a video conferencing tool teams use to meet, run workshops, and talk face to face when they are not in the same room. For teams spread across places, it is often where daily standups, client calls, and working sessions happen.
tools.Tool Features:
1. Host video meetings
2. Record sessions
3. Share your screen
4. Use breakout rooms
5. Run remote interviews and workshops

tools.Tool Description: Dovetail is a research tool for storing and making sense of what users say. Researchers use it to keep interviews and notes in one place, tag patterns across them, and turn raw feedback into clear insights the whole team can search and revisit.
tools.Tool Features:
1. Store research data
2. Tag and code notes
3. Find themes across studies
4. Build insight repositories
5. Share findings with the team

tools.Tool Description: Trello is a simple visual board that tracks work as cards moving across columns like To Do, Doing, and Done. Teams use it to see at a glance who is working on what and what is coming next, which fits the steady, visible flow of agile work.
tools.Tool Features:
1. Create boards, lists, and cards
2. Track task status
3. Assign work to people
4. Add checklists and due dates
5. Automate simple workflows

tools.Category: User Experience, Product Management, Operations, Development
tools.Tool Description: ChatGPT is an AI assistant that can draft text, brainstorm ideas, summarize notes, and answer questions in plain language. Teams use it as a thinking partner to speed up early drafts and explore options, though the output always needs a human to check and refine it.
tools.Tool Features:
1. Draft and edit text
2. Brainstorm ideas
3. Summarize documents
4. Help with analysis and code
5. Answer questions conversationally

tools.Tool Description: Maze is a tool for running quick, remote tests on designs and prototypes. Teams use it to get fast feedback from real people, measuring how they move through a design so problems show up early and the team can keep improving.
tools.Tool Features:
1. Test prototypes with users
2. Run unmoderated usability tests
3. Create surveys
4. Measure task success
5. Generate reports automatically

tools.Tool Description: Optimal Workshop is a set of research tools for understanding how people organize and find information. Teams use it for things like card sorting and tree testing to shape a product's structure so it matches the way users actually think.
tools.Tool Features:
1. Card sorting
2. Tree testing
3. First-click testing
4. Surveys
5. Qualitative insights

tools.Tool Description: LettuceMeet is a lightweight scheduling tool that finds a time that works for a whole group. Teams use it to line up meetings and workshops without the endless back-and-forth of comparing calendars.
tools.Tool Features:
1. Share your availability
2. Find overlapping free times
3. Coordinate group meetings
4. Use it without an account
5. Simple grid interface

tools.Tool Description: Spreadsheet tools, like Google Sheets or Excel, are flexible grids for organizing data, running calculations, and tracking information. Teams reach for them constantly, from planning and budgeting to analyzing research numbers, because almost anything can start life in a spreadsheet.
tools.Tool Features:
1. Organize data in tables
2. Run formulas and calculations
3. Make charts
4. Sort and filter data
5. Share and collaborate

tools.Tool Description: Presentation tools, like Google Slides, PowerPoint, or Keynote, help teams turn ideas into clear slides for sharing. They show up whenever a team needs to walk others through their thinking, from sprint demos to client updates.
tools.Tool Features:
1. Build slide decks
2. Add visuals and charts
3. Present to stakeholders
4. Collaborate on slides
5. Export and share

tools.Tool Description: An IDE, short for integrated development environment, is the software developers write code in, with helpful features like error-checking and shortcuts built in. It is a developer's main workspace, the place where designs and requirements actually turn into working software.
tools.Tool Features:
1. Write and edit code
2. Debug programs
3. Run and test code
4. Manage version control
5. Extend with plugins

tools.Tool Description: GitHub is where developers store, share, and manage code together. It tracks every change, lets people review each other's work, and keeps a full history, which makes it possible for a whole team to build the same software without overwriting each other.
tools.Tool Features:
1. Host Git repositories
2. Review code with pull requests
3. Track issues
4. Automate with Actions
5. Collaborate on code

tools.Tool Description: UXtweak is a research platform for testing usability and studying how people interact with a product. Teams use it to run studies like usability tests and card sorts, gathering real evidence about what works and what confuses users.
tools.Tool Features:
1. Usability testing
2. Card sorting and tree testing
3. Session recordings
4. Surveys
5. Recruit participants

tools.Tool Description: Statistics tools help teams make sense of numbers, spotting patterns and checking whether a result is actually meaningful. Researchers and analysts use them to turn raw data into findings they can trust rather than guesses.
tools.Tool Features:
1. Analyze quantitative data
2. Run statistical tests
3. Summarize survey results
4. Measure significance
5. Visualize data

tools.Tool Description: An AI model is the engine behind smart tools that can generate text, images, or predictions from data. Teams use AI models to speed up tasks like drafting, summarizing, and analyzing, treating them as powerful assistants that still need human judgment to guide and check them.
tools.Tool Features:
1. Generate text or images
2. Summarize and analyze
3. Answer questions
4. Assist with drafts
5. Support decision-making

project-types.Project Type Description: A Website Project is a comprehensive initiative to design, develop, and optimize a digital platform that meets user needs and business goals. During this project, teams produce deliverables such as user personas, site maps, and accessibility analyses to inform design decisions, along with prototypes, content strategies, and analytics reports to ensure a user-centered and high-performing website.

A Web Application Project is a collaborative effort to design, develop, and optimize a user-centric web platform that meets business goals and user needs. During this project, teams produce detailed user experience strategies, wireframes, prototypes, and functional code, along with comprehensive research reports, branding assets, and accessibility guidelines to ensure a seamless and engaging user experience.

A Mobile App Project is a collaborative effort to design, develop, and optimize a mobile application that meets user needs and business goals. During this project, teams produce detailed user experience and interface designs, research insights, functional prototypes, and comprehensive documentation to guide development and ensure a seamless user experience.

A Service Design Project is a comprehensive initiative aimed at creating seamless and effective customer experiences by integrating various design and research disciplines. During this project, teams produce detailed service blueprints, customer journey maps, and user personas, along with prototypes, wireframes, and content strategies to ensure a cohesive and user-centered service delivery.

A Discovery Project is a collaborative effort to understand user needs, define problem spaces, and identify viable solutions to inform product development. During this project, teams produce insights through qualitative and quantitative UX research, user journey maps, and strategic documentation, culminating in a clear product vision and prioritized roadmap to guide subsequent design and development phases.

workshops.Workshop Summary: The team gets together at the start of a project to get to know each other as people, not just coworkers. Everyone shares things like their interests, how they like to work, what they are excited about, and what worries them. This helps the team feel safe with each other before the real work starts.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Help teammates get to know each other as people
Start building trust and psychological safety
Learn how each person likes to work
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Complete four activities with your team.
2. Follow the instructions in each activity section.
3. Run the intro activity: give time to fill out the template, then go around and share out loud.
4. Do the working style activity: place your name where you align on each scale.
5. Add hopes and fears to sticky notes, discuss briefly or invite people to review other’s sticky notes.
6. Run Crazy 6: draw six things about yourself. Invite people to explain their drawings and share anything they want to share.
7. Time-box each activity but leave space for natural banter and questions.
8. Have fun! It's okay if not everything gets done. The goal is team connection.
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?: People do better work when they feel comfortable with the people around them. Starting with a human connection makes it easier to speak up, ask for help, and share ideas later in the project.
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Run this once at the start of a new team or project phase. You can also do a short version any time new people join the team.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?: The Agile Coaching function owns this workshop and is responsible for running it with the team.
workshops.Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have a shared understanding of each other teammate, their background, their interest, and their working styles.
workshops.Additional Details: When to use: at kickoff, in the first week, before the team digs into project work.
workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: A casual first-day kickoff party where a new team gets to know each other as humans, laying the psychological safety and trust the next several weeks of work depend on.
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: This is the team's very first workshop, so no project prep is needed, just everyone present and willing to be a little playful. Set up the FigJam board with the four activity sections ready to copy, and bring a timer. An Agile Coach should be ready to facilitate and go first to set the tone.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. Who are my teammates as people?
2. How does each of us like to work, learn, decide, and get feedback?
3. What are our hopes and fears for this project?
4. What do we want to learn, and how can Tech Fleet support us?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave knowing each other as people, with a first layer of trust and openness in place. Done well, people laughed, shared a little of themselves, and feel safer speaking up. It is fine if not every activity finishes; connection is the goal.
workshops.Time Needed: About 45 to 60 minutes across the four activities
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: Do not over-formalize it; the point is fun and connection, not productivity. Time-box each activity but leave room for natural banter. Facilitators should go first and share openly to make it safe for everyone else.

# Agile vs. Waterfall Operations

  # Waterfall
    Agile vs. Waterfall
    There are two ways to build things through process:
Waterfall
Agile
Waterfall processes happen in sequential phases. Each phase must be complete before the next phase can begin.
Agile processes are flexible and handle work in parallel. There are no phases, there is only continuously delivering to users to gain feedback and determine next steps.
    The Waterfall Manifesto
    Waterfall Operations
    We’ve uncovered ancient ways of developing software and helping ourselves do it. Through this, we’ve come to value:
Processes and tools over interactions with individuals
Comprehensive documentation over working software
Contract negotiation over customer collaboration
Following a plan over responding to change

That is, we never value the things on the right. We’re rigidly following our principles. Forever.
    Waterfall is a process of building where:
Each team is “siloed”, working alone and handing off to the next when they are done
Everyone agrees to the scope of work in the beginning, and they never change the scope of work
Teams don’t collect feedback until they are finished with the project
No research work happens in the design phase; no design work happens in the requirements phase
There is no process built for adjusting previous work until the project is over
No one is validating their work with clients or users; they see it at the end of the delivery

    Client requests work
    Client
    Users
    BA gathers requirements
    Create a contract
(Weeks of work)
    Research happens
    Research Team
    Business Analyst
    Requirements (Months of work)
    Design happens
    Design Team
    Research Phase
(Months of work)
    Development happens
    Riding the waves of waterfall
    Development Team
    Design Phase
(Months of work)
    Product release
    Development Phase
(Months of work)
    Support Team
    Clients and users see the end-result
    Launch Phase
(Months of work)
    Client
    Users
    Hand-off to the Client
    Is there a change needed?
    Continue with life
    START OVER with  “Change Management”

  # Agile
    The Agile Manifesto
    Agile Operations
    We’ve uncovered better ways of developing software and helping others do it Through this, we’ve come to value:
Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
Working software over comprehensive documentation
Customer collaboration over contract negotiation
Responding to change over following a plan

That is, while we value the items on the right, we value the items on the left more
    Agile is a philosophy of building where:
Teams collaborate with each other across functions, and break down silos of work 
Teams work with customers and users to figure out their scope and vision as they proceed
Teams organize themselves and build the process of work that works for their context
Teams do work across functions in parallel, not in phases
Teams change their plan when the plan needs to change
Teams deliver their work early and often in order to collect feedback as they proceed

# Building Agile Teams that Perform
  The Basic Tenets of Agile Team Building
  Measuring the Agile Tenets
  Agile team strength is like a garden: you have to maintain agility and pick out the weeds to ensure health and growth of your team. How teams do this is open to the person owning the product, and the scrum master. 

Here are some key points to determine levels of self-organization, psychological safety, servant leadership, iterative value delivery, and continuous improvement.
  To measure Agility, teams must look at the components of what makes an Agile team agile: self-organization, psychological safety, servant leadership, iterative value, and continuous improvement. Here’s a set of checklists you can use to determine your team’s current state of agility.
  Self-organization: 

Allow the day-to-day people doing the work to make decisions themselves, instead of the people leading the team, and let the team carry out their own work in the way they want, or think is best
  Psychological Safety:

Build the sense of safety and belonging throughout the team:
Make every member of the team feel like they have room to speak their mind
Actively listen when others have things to say, and make team feel like their voice matters
Give the room for people to bring their own personalities and unique capabilities to the table in the way THEY want to do so
Allow room for team mates to challenge the status quo, and experiment with new ways of working
Encourage failing “fast”, i.e. failure and quick reflection and quick adjustment based on what the team thinks they should do
Let them take the risks that THEY decide to take, that could lead to failure or disaster, for the purposes of allowing them to build up decision making prowess
  Self-organization checklist
  Psychological Safety checklist
  Does your team wait for answers or initiate things on their own?
Does your team ask for clarity before starting or continuing work?
Does your team volunteer to work assignments?
Does your team contribute to conversations?
Does your team present new ideas for how to work, or idea for the product?
Does your team build consensus together and involve each other in decision making?
  Does your team speak up about concerns?
Does your team contribute to conversations freely?
Does your team voice dissent? 
Does your team celebrate each other for who they are and what they bring to the contributions?
Does your team experiment with new ways of working together? 
Does your team take risks together, and try new things?
  Servant Leadership:

All managers and all team mates should act as servant leaders to each other, those around them, those “above” them, or those “below” them in any organization’s hierarchy
  Servant Leadership checklist
  Iterative Value checklist
  Do your team members support each others’ growth instead of their own?
Does the person in charge tell everyone what to do, or do they transfer the power to the team?
Does your team show respect towards others? 
Does your team empathize with others and help each other?
Does your team seek to understand situations that arise, and communicate needs?
Does your team set expectations with each other in healthy ways?
  Does your team deliver work incrementally?
Does your team constantly involve clients,  stakeholders, and users in feedback sessions? 
Does your team collaborate with each other to determine the highest priorities to deliver in unison? 
Does your team work on the most important things at any given time, and deliver them quickly?
  Iterative value delivery: 

Teams should be empowered to deliver value early and often in order to gather feedback and decide themselves how they need to adjust. By doing so, and having self-organization, and psychological safety, the team can flag risks early or set better directions for them and for the organization.
  Continuous improvement:

Teams should be granted the opportunity to fail, and to build a process of quick adjustment when they fail. “Failure” is vague here: it could mean that the team’s plan didn’t work, or it could mean that something happened in the world requiring the team to change, or it could mean that someone made a mistake / didn’t do something.
  Continuous Improvement checklist
  Does your team have a “fail forward” attitude?
Does your team look at things in hindsight as opportunities?
Does your team look at problems as opportunities to improve? 
Does your team have a healthy amount of discussion in reflection of root causes?
Does your team avoid blaming others when looking at root causes in hindsight? 
Does your team work together to refine their working agreements as they fail forward?
Does your team manage the chaos of life, and client needs, together?
  The Pyramid of Agile Tenets
  This shows a hierarchical structure of Agile team success and what must be in place before teams can perform. At the foundational level, psychological safety must be in place.
  Iterative Value
  Continuous Improvement
  Self-Organization
  Servant Leadership
  Psychological Safety
  Continuous improvement
must be in place before

  Self-organization
must be in place before

  We are all in service to each others’ growth
  Servant leadership
must be in place before

# The Four Stages of Team Work
  The Four Stages of Teams: Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing
  Every single team in the world goes through four stages of team work. No one starts by working efficiently with each other. Teams must build and maintain their efficiency.

Reference: https://hr.mit.edu/learning-topics/teams/articles/stages-development
  Forming
  Storming
  Norming
  Performing
  Description: 
During the Forming stage, the team first gets together, and doesn’t have a common way of working established yet, but they meet each other
Tasks:
A team kickoff
Ice breakers
Expectation setting
Feelings: 
Excitement
Belonging
Cheer
Positivity
Confidence
Nervousness
Anxiety
Behaviors: 
Being polite with each other
Questions from team members
Acting excitedly
Uncertainty about the future
Anxiety about their place on the team
  Description:
During the Storming stage, the team starts figuring out how they should be working together, and this happens through talking out disagreements
Tasks:
Defining short-term action items based on goals
Starting work
Deciding how to work together
Feelings: 
Anxiety about whether the team can do what they are set out to do
Anger about the lack of progress
Frustration about the lack of progress
Behaviors:
Arguing about how to work together, and about decisions
Conflict and discussing differences of opinion
Discussing how to start in the work and the goals of the work
Criticizing team mates’ decisions
Questioning the future of the team
  Description:
During the Norming phase, team members resolve their differences, and align in how to work together. They start making agreements in how they should produce the work in collaboration and proceed in the work.
Tasks:
Agreeing to work process
Discussing and building consensus
Collective teamwork
Focusing on aligning goals
Feelings: 
Confidence
Inclusion
Comfort
Behaviors: 
Building Consensus with team mates
Constructive criticism 
Harmoniously working together
Being willing to hear people and work together 
Celebrating team mates for what they bring to the table
  Description:
During the Performing phase, members work efficiently together, and are satisfied in their work together. They work well, and are more aligned than ever in the work. 
Tasks:
Aligning on goals
Planning long-term work
Deepening knowledge
Increasing skills
Increasing accomplishments
Feelings: 
Satisfaction in the work
“Can Do” attitude
Increased confidence
Empowerment
Happiness
Behaviors: 
Getting more work done
More flexibility in the work

It grounds the team in agile itself: the Agile Manifesto's values (individuals and interactions, working results, customer collaboration, responding to change), the tenets of strong teams, and the four stages of team growth (forming, storming, norming, performing). It sets the shared mental model the rest of the workshops assume.

workshops.Workshop Summary:
In this workshop, cross-functional teams reflect together about how they can resolve conflict as a unified team while supporting each others' growth.

Conflict is a natural and even necessary part of doing great work in a cross-functional team. This workshop helps teams anticipate conflict and have a plan for what to do when it comes up.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Reflect in how to resolve conflict together as teammates.
Brainstorm contributing factors of conflict.
Hear perspectives from teammates about conflict resolution.
Learn about the relationship between conflict and service leadership.
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Set Context for the team
2. Write down things that have led you to be in conflict in past situations
3. Review the input from step #2 as a team, and reflect on what teammates have said together.
4. Everyone individually reads the Project-Specific Conflict Resolution Policy document.
5. Reflect as a team about how this approach to conflict resolution invokes service leadership.
6. Create breakouts together and discuss:
7. What will you do when you run into conflict?
8. What is your responsibility when you notice conflict on the team?
9. Hold a full group reflection together to discuss anything that surprised you or that you want to remember going forward from this conversation
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
Learning how to deal with conflict in a productive way is a huge superpower for any work situation
Conflict is a normal part of working on teams, and many of us feel like conflict is scary or something to be avoided. Learning the skills of conflict resolution and having it driven by teams themselves helps form stronger teammates.
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Run this early, in the first week or two of a project. Come back to it any time the team feels tension building or wants to reset how it handles disagreements.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?: Conflict is like Service Leadership. We are all responsible for our own behavior, and we are always looking to support others in their success and growth. The most important thing to remember is that unlike in a context of “work,” in Tech Fleet, no one person can fix or manage conflicts on the team. Our job is to figure out what we can do to make the situation better without blame or shame, even if it means we feel frustrated. We know it can be hard! Please join us for support office hours if you need to talk through a situation.
workshops.Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Working Agreements.
workshops.Additional Details:
When to use:
Every meeting can have a moment to identify or open the door to discussions of conflict. If conflicts are identified, then ASAP use the tools that are listed in our Conflict Resolution Policy.

Where to keep it:
The conflict resolution plan should be kept in the Notion space within the Team Hub.
We encourage everyone to revisit it when they feel there might be a possibility of conflict.

Have the Agile Handbook's conflict sections open (the four stages of team growth, resolving conflict as service leaders, the process for resolving conflict, and collective-agreement violations) and the two short conflict videos ready. # Conflict is Constructive
  Conflict is Constructive
  (10 minutes)

Conflict isn’t something to avoid if teams want to grow. 
Conflict can be good, creative, and generative when we are prepared and hold capacity for healthy conflict.
Through conflict we all must prioritize psychological safety and service leadership with each other. This is the only way for our team to move past instances of conflict: by respecting each other, and understanding each other. 
Anger and frustration are part of life. However, directing anger at another person isn’t healthy. Part of good conflict process is to recognize when we feel a sense of blame, judgment, or anger at someone else and to understand what in us needs attention. We should not suppress our feelings, and we need to own the feelings that we feel as our own feelings, not something someone else made them feel. 
No one can cause you to have a feeling. That doesn’t give us freedom to disregard other people and our impact we have on them, or for other people to disregard their impact on us as teammates.
Let’s watch two videos about conflict and the four stages of team growth.

  Agile Teams Prioritize Growth Over the Work
  Removing Conflict is Key to Team Success

workshops.Workshop Summary:
Teams who train on projects can use this to build a shared understanding and clarity when first working with clients.

The client intake workshop helps new teams onboard to new phases in Tech Fleet projects. Project representatives and the client enter basic details about the project, and thoughts about the work for the upcoming phase.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Meet the client and start building a working relationship
Learn the business goals and who the product is for
Agree on the top priorities for this phase of work
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Determine if the client has done a project before with the team
2. Go over "First time" flow if this is the first time working with the client
3. Go over "Returning" flow if this is not the first time working with the client
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?: This workshop allows your team to align with the client before each phase of work, and to ask them questions that are important to understand before teams start the work. It also gives the client and your team a chance to meet each other and develop a working relationship, and a shared understanding.
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Run this once at the start of each project phase, before the team starts the work. If the client or the goals change, hold it again.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?:
The project coordinators and Agile residents own this deliverable between project phases.
Product operations team functions own this deliverable during project phases
workshops.Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Statement of Work.
workshops.Additional Details:

The project coordinators and Agile residents perform this client intake workshop between project phases before the next phase starts recruiting for teammates. This allows new teams to have the intake information before they join the team.

workshops.Workshop Brief: This workshop produces the Statement of Work, the foundational agreement that defines a project's scope, objectives, deliverables, and terms. By aligning with the client on goals, audiences, and problems up front, it sets the shared expectations that keep the whole project from drifting.

workshops.Workshop Summary:
This is a workshop teams can run to help build awareness about how cross-functional agile teams operate each sprint. Teams get together and decide how they want to function individually as part of the shared outcomes for a team.

RACI charts are a key Agile team deliverable that breaks down activities and team functions. It shows who’s responsible, who’s accountable, who’s consulted, and who’s informed across the team. Agile teams use this to build shared knowledge and align in their understanding about how they should be working together. Teams create their own RACI charts every sprint. This document shows a template of typical responsibilities based on industry standards.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Educate teams about Agile cross-functional teamwork
Build a shared understanding about who's going to collaborate with whom on sprint teams
Help a team self-organize and build psychological safety by enabling them to make their own decisions about how they get involved


Background

Cross-functional Agile teams are like heist crews: people who get together work towards shared outcomes together and do not stick to only one isolated set of responsibilities. Every time the team plans work, they agree together about who owns what, and who wants to collaborate with whom. This happens every sprint. When you first get together as a new team, each person should identify the desires they are interested in participating and owning for teamwork. You as a self-organized team need to have the power to change this for each person. This allows people to explore new duties they have never done before. The team needs to support people doing work for the first time as Agile teams support each others’ growth together.
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Review the information provided about Agile teams in the user guide
2. Review the information about typical RACI chart responsibilities per team function
3. Get together as a team and each person will choose their “Hat”, or roles, they want to commit to for the project based on their desires.
4. Everyone builds an avatar character with their desired “Hats”, and voila, you have a cross-functional team outlined in a RACI!
5. Each sprint, you should plan your sprint and re-discuss the individual members’ commitments to the work
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?: RACI charts provide clarity on how team collaboration works on Agile teams. They help everyone on a team build expectations about what they should be doing and how they should be functioning.
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Build a new RACI every sprint during sprint planning. It is not a one time thing. Update it as people take on different work.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?:
The Scrum master function on teams owns this deliverable. They must:

Use the template RACI charts to build expectations about functions
Run a sprint planning every sprint where the team builds a new RACI every sprint based on their desired commitments
workshops.Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its RACI Charts.
workshops.Additional Details:
When to use:
Teams should be building a new RACI chart every sprint through the Sprint Planning activities. Your RACI chart should not just be drafted once. It needs to be adjusted every sprint based on the changing priorities and decisions on the team during the 8 weeks of work. The Scrum Master should make this a habit to keep adjusting the RACI as the weeks go by.

How to involve other teams:
The entire team should get together to review their RACI for the sprint and see whether everyone knows what to expect before the next sprint begins.
workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: A sprint-planning ritual where a cross-functional team decides together who wears which hats (owns which duties) this sprint, captured as a RACI chart of who is responsible, accountable, consulted, and informed.
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: Bring the whole team. Have the Agile Handbook material on cross-functional teams open, plus the template RACI charts showing typical responsibilities per function. Set up the FigJam board with the avatar hat-builder and the RACI tables. This is done fresh each sprint during sprint planning.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What does it mean to be a cross-functional team that shares duties rather than fixed titles?
2. What are the typical responsibilities per function?
3. Which hats (duties) does each person want to commit to this sprint?
4. Who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed for each activity?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with a RACI chart the whole team built for this sprint: each person's committed duties and clear R/A/C/I for every activity. Done well, people stretched into duties they wanted to grow into, and everyone knows what to expect from each other.
workshops.Time Needed: About 30 to 45 minutes within sprint planning
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: Every activity needs exactly one Accountable; shared accountability disappears. Rebuild the RACI every sprint, not once. And honor the self-organizing spirit: people choose the hats they want to grow into, and the team supports first-timers.
workshops.Where to Keep the Output: Keep it with the sprint plan; the Scrum Master updates it each sprint.

workshops.Workshop Brief: This workshop produces the team's RACI Charts, the responsibility-assignment matrix that clarifies who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed for each activity (with exactly one person Accountable). Tech Fleet frames it as 'hats' a self-organizing team chooses fresh each sprint.

workshops.Workshop Summary:
This template helps teams self-organize in their plan for fixed-timeline projects. Every team should get together and build a forecast based on the anticipated goals. This forecast, known as a Sprint Plan or Project Plan, changes every week, and the Product Owner roles on the team update and maintain this.

A Project Plan outlines each week of work that all team roles are doing, or planning on doing. A sprint team shouldn’t plan everything up front, but rather guess at what’s coming in the later weeks and adjust every week.

Every cross-functional Agile team gets together to decide how they deliver value every sprint. This workshop enables teams to break down their cross-functional work based on the shared outcomes that the project needs to achieve. The team takes the goals and deliverables for a project and determines the 11 week plan based on different functions on the team to make the project a success. In the industry, this deliverable is called a Sprint Plan. In this workshop we call it a Project Plan. It’s maintained every sprint and teams typically plan 2 to 3 sprints ahead so that they can forecast and plan ahead.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Build a forecast of work for the project
Align a full team in knowledge about the upcoming work
Help teams understand what's going on and what's coming up in sprint work
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Enter the project phase goals as determined by the team
2. Enter the project phase deliverables as determined by the team
3. Everyone get together for an hour: each individual reviews the 11 week breakdown of work that’s provided in the template and maps out additional anticipated activities across functions.
4. Everyone reviews and collaborates together on this activity, and it’s important to develop a consensus.
5. After this workshop, when a team plans a sprint, they will review the project roadmap to identify the planned activities and review them to determine a plan for a two-week chunk of work. During this time, they will commit themselves individually to different kinds of responsibilities they want to take on as people on the team. See the sprint planning workshop template here.
6. Outli
7. Review the pre-determined deliverables per project milestone in Agile product development lifecycles
8. Enter the goals you understand about the project
9. Enter the phase for the project (phase 1, 2, 3, 4, or other)
10. Choose the deliverables your team should work on in your project based on Agile product milestone deliverables provided in this template
11. Enter the project phase deliverables as determined by the team in the space for your project phase
12. The team chooses a pre-determined project plan for phase 1, 2, 3, or 4
13. Everyone reviews the project plan together and determines whether any deliverable outcomes need to change or shift in the project timeline
14. After the project plan is created, a team can run the workshop to outline the sprint goals together. They do this for each sprint and the outcomes of the sprint are based on the project plan.
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
A project plan(AKA Sprint Plan) is valuable because it:

Aligns teams in work plans across roles
Shows how a team can meet their outcomes
Identifies differences in priority
Helps identify when teams should start work
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Your project roadmap (AKA Sprint Plan) should not just be drafted once. It needs to be adjusted every week based on the changing priorities and decisions on the team during the 8 weeks of work. The product strategy team should make this a habit to keep adjusting this sprint plan as the weeks go by. They should have the sprint updated by the time they do sprint planning.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?: The Product Owner function owns the deliverables that come from this workshop, as they own the near-term roadmap orchestration and priorities.
workshops.Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Gantt Chart, Sprint Plan, Project Plan, and Project Goals Definition.
workshops.Additional Details:
How to involve other teams:
The product strategy team must constantly “own” this deliverable and ensure it’s accurate. They need to talk to the other team roles to ensure that they are bought in with the priorities for each role. This is a conversation and collaboration that takes place weekly. The product strategy team may need to keep this artifact up to date daily. This artifact is used for the basis of sprint planning.

When to Maintain This Deliverable:
A team will be using this deliverable every week to adjust forcast plans. The rest of the team should be using this as a viewable artifact to see what they need to be working on, or identify gaps in priorities that are not already planned.

What to Do After the Workshop:
Every cross-functional Agile team gets together to decide how they deliver value every sprint. This workshop enables teams to break down their cross-functional work based on the shared outcomes that the project needs to achieve. The team takes the goals and deliverables for a project and determines the 11 week plan based on different functions on the team to make the project a success. In the industry, this deliverable is called a Sprint Plan. It’s maintained every sprint and teams typically plan 2 to 3 sprints ahead so that they can forecast and plan ahead.
workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: A whole-team workshop that turns the project's goals into a forecast of work across sprints, so everyone can see what is coming and when, and adjust it weekly.
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: Bring the whole team and your project goals from the client intake. Know your project phase (1 to 4) and project type (web platform, discovery, or service design). Open the FigJam board with the deliverables-per-milestone reference and the pre-built phase plans. The Product Owner drafts it, but the whole team reviews and confirms.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What are our project goals?
2. What phase and project type are we in?
3. Which deliverables should we produce this phase?
4. Which pre-built phase plan fits us?
5. Do the planned sprint outcomes look right, or do we need to adjust the timeline?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with a phase project plan the whole team confirmed: goals, chosen deliverables, and planned outcomes per function across pre-kickoff, four sprints, and hand-off. Done well, everyone can see what is coming, and it is understood as a living forecast, not a fixed promise.
workshops.Time Needed: About 60 to 90 minutes to build, then updated weekly
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: Do not plan everything up front in detail; forecast the later weeks and adjust weekly. Remember the lifecycle is non-linear, so milestones repeat and overlap rather than run in a straight line. The Product Owner keeps it current and uses it to run sprint planning.
workshops.Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam; the Product Owner updates it weekly, before each sprint planning.

After the project plan is created, a team can run the workshop to outline the sprint goals together. They do this for each sprint and the outcomes of the sprint are based on the project plan.
  A Project Plan outlines each week of work that all team roles are doing, or planning on doing. A sprint team shouldn’t feel the pressure to plan everything up front, but rather guess at what’s coming in the later weeks and adjust every week.
  GOALS OF THE WORKSHOP
  Build a forecast of work for the project
Align a full team in knowledge about the upcoming work
Help teams understand what's going on and what's coming up in sprint work
  HOW TO INVOLVE OTHER TEAMS
  WHY IS IT VALUABLE?
  A Project Plan is valuable because it:
Aligns teams in work plans across roles
Shows how a team can meet their outcomes
Identifies differences in priority
Helps identify when teams should start work
  The product strategy team must constantly “own” this deliverable and ensure it’s accurate. They need to talk to the other team roles to ensure that they are bought in with the priorities for each role. This is a conversation and collaboration that takes place weekly. The product strategy team may need to keep this artifact up to date daily. This artifact is used for the basis of sprint planning.
  WHO OWNS THIS DELIVERABLE?
  The Product Owner role owns this deliverable. They must: 
Draft the first Project Plan
Collect other teams’ thoughts on what needs to be included
Change priorities weekly on this board
Use it to facilitate sprint planning sessions
  WHEN DO TEAMS USE THIS?
  A team will be using this deliverable every week to adjust forcast plans. The rest of the team should be using this as a viewable artifact to see what they need to be working on, or identify gaps in priorities that are not already planned.
  WHERE SHOULD THIS BE KEPT?
  The Project Plan should be kept and maintained in Figjam or some other place where it can be quickly edited.
  HOW OFTEN SHOULD IT BE UPDATED?
  Your Project Plan should not just be drafted once. It needs to be adjusted every week based on the changing priorities and decisions on the team during the 8 weeks of work. The product strategy team should make this a habit to keep adjusting this sprint plan as the weeks go by. They should have the sprint updated by the time they do sprint planning.

workshops.Workshop Brief: This workshop produces the Project Plan, along with a Gantt-style timeline, sprint plan, and project goals. A project plan lays out phases, milestones, and outcomes across the work, but in agile it is a living forecast that adjusts weekly, not a fixed waterfall schedule.

workshops.Workshop Summary: Products aren’t just made from ideas. They take a lot of coordination, research, decisions, and negotiations to make happen. Teams in the world who focus on their audience’s problems can transform their teamwork into a larger long-term map of success. Teams must maintain and update the deliverables that showcase the long-term outcomes over time as they learn new insights in research. This workshop helps a team to outline how to take a team’s current understanding of the problems in their audience’s current state, identify the goals, and create the maps for long-term release outcomes that they need to follow while performing UX, product, or development work.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Identify your known audiences
Identify problems you think your audiences experience today in current state of the world
Prioritize the problems you want to focus on now and later.
Communicate the problems you identify as goals, value, unique advantage, and outcomes in a vision for near-term and long-term releases.
Organize the work outcomes into themes and chunk the backlog work into feasible work items.
Develop a roadmap plan for the next year that you can maintain.
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Enter the components of product vision you want to focus on for yourself
2. Your target audiences
3. Your personal opportunities and problems
4. Your business goals
5. Your value you bring to the world when you solve the problems you want to solve
6. What makes you unique as a business compared to others in the market space, and how you differentiate the business
7. The barriers and risks that may get in your way to success in the product release, and how you will mitigate them
8. The “costs” of money, time, and energy involved
9. Your KPI’s and measures of success
10. Your scope of outcomes to achieve based on the problems you want to solve
11. Prioritize the problems in a priority matrix
12. Pick the most important 5 problems for you to work on near-term, and choose them for your “MVP #1 Release” for the vision
13. Create vision boards for your upcoming releases based on the problems you’ve prioritized:
14. “MVP #1”, also known as “Problems to solve and validate first”
15. “MMP”, also known as “Problems to solve at market”
16. Create your scope of outcomes to achieve based on the value and problems to solve for each release
17. Create epics, features, and tasks based on the scope of outcomes
18. Create your roadmap
19. Populate your backlog with the tasks related to features and epics
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
A vision, scope, and roadmap for products and services is valuable because:

It breaks down larger goals into smaller, more accomplishable results
It helps you communicate language around your goals, needs, value delivery, and action items.
It helps you determine what your team should focus on now and later, and organizes work for the entire team.
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: You should revisit the vision and roadmap on a regular basis. This will help you keep track of items you work on throughout the year and pivot when you need to.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?: The product owner and product manager own these deliverables for the purposes of release management and backlog management.
workshops.Expected Outcomes:
Problems and opportunities that audiences experience
KPI’s for your release
Release-Level vision for MVP and MMP
Release-Level scope of work for MVP and MMP
Epics, features, and tasks list for MVP and MMP
Release roadmap
Backlog with task tickets and appropriately categorized epics / features

workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: A workshop where the team turns its audiences' prioritized problems into release-level vision boards and a clear scope of outcomes for what to build now (MVP) and later (MMP).
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: Bring the product owner and product manager (they own it) and the whole team, plus your known audiences and the problems you assume they face. Set up FigJam with the vision components, the priority matrices, and the vision-board templates. Best once discovery is underway; revisit regularly.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What are our audiences, problems, goals, value, unique advantage, barriers, costs, and KPIs?
2. Which problems matter most now versus later?
3. What are our top few problems for the first release?
4. What is the release vision (MVP and MMP) per audience?
5. What scope of outcomes will each release achieve?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with a release-level vision board per audience for MVP and MMP, a prioritized problem set, and a scope of outcomes per release. Done well, everyone can see exactly what value each release delivers to each audience, and the vision is understood as living, not final.
workshops.Time Needed: A substantial session, then revisited regularly
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: These are assumptions, not truths yet; you validate them in research. Make one vision board per audience per release on purpose, so the value stays specific. And treat the vision as never final; revisit it as you learn.
workshops.Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam; the product owner and manager maintain it.

# For Each Audience: Prioritize the Problems
  For Each Audience: Prioritize the Problems
  Take your use cases you’ve identified on the first section and prioritize them for each audience
  How do you know which problems to solve first?
In short: you don't, and no one does. It's all just a guess and a judgment call based on what you know. You could get the guess wrong, and Agile is built for quick adjustments when you get it wrong. One needs to embrace this lifestyle in requirements work for Agile teams. You will constantly be guessing which is the correct way to go. "Continuous improvement" all the way. You can use tools like prioritization matrices to rank problems to solve and decide which ones to solve first. The rest is up to what the team decides to put into their release-level vision, and what they learn after they deliver iterations towards the release.

# Create your Release Vision and Scope

You’ve now identified the key problems, goals, value, barriers, and unique advantage about your product or service. You are ready to put together a release-level vision board! The release is made up of many problems to solve. In the sections below, write the components of the vision board based on the input you provided in part 1. Only worry about the first release (MVP #1) and the market-ready release (MMP).

You should make one vision board per audience, per release. 

For instance: if you have two target audiences, you will be making 4 vision boards: MVP for Audience 1, MMP for Audience 1, MVP for Audience 2, and MMP for Audience 2.

You may be asking yourself, "Why? This seems like more work..." Yes it is. It is very purposeful. This approach is helpful to specify what exact value you're delivering for each audience each time you release. Without this approach, you may not communicate the exact problems you're solving, or value you're delivering, for each audience. It's best to proceed one audience, one release at a time.

workshops.Workshop Brief: This workshop produces the release Vision Boards, Release-level Scope, Epics and Features, and Roadmap. A vision board (Roman Pichler's tool) captures the vision, target group, needs, key features, and business goals; scope draws the line around what a release will and will not include. Both stay living as the team learns.

workshops.Workshop Summary: You may think that someone dictates how a team should work in Agile. After all, we have all of the rules written in Scrum, right? Don't all Agile teams operate the same? They tell us what meetings to do, when to do them, and how to do them. This is a misconception. Agile teams govern themselves and own their own process together. Everyone on the team, even the interns, even the apprentices, should have a say in how they work together. This is a principle called self-organization, and it's crucial to build on Agile teams. In order for them to do their best work, they must be handed the keys to ownership of the process. A team process looks different on every team. At its core, it's a summarized agreement for how a team wants to work across functions to get work done. The process is visualized in a flow chart so that everyone can understand how work gets done. When the team takes retrospectives and discusses how to change their process with working agreements, they should update this team process flow chart to ensure it's accurately depicting how the team operates.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Learn about the Scrum method of Agile
Learn about how agile teams use a tool called a Kanban Board to manage a backlog of work and the statuses of work
Build your own team process in a flow chart
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Product strategy duties
2. Notion space and documentation of the product
3. Agile product development and milestones
4. Assumption forming and assumption testing
5. Building a process that works for your team
6. Implementing process in the kanban board on Notion
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?: Agile team process maps are valuable because they align a whole team in their understanding of how work happens together. When new team members join, they can be onboarded faster. When someone is uncertain what to do next, they can point to the team process and build clarity. It helps a team operate in a smooth fashion.
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Build the first version at the start of a project. Update it whenever the team changes how it works, usually after a sprint retro.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?: The Product Operations function maintains the team process. This is usually handled in Scrum teams by the Scrum Master role or the Product Owner role.
workshops.Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Prioritized Backlog Tasks, Refined Backlog, Kanban Board Statuses, and Team Process Map.
