# Problem Solving and Assumptions
  Assumption Forming and Testing
  This is what happens when you don’t document requirements, and run with assumptions that are not validated

  # Section 2
  Teams are making a lot of assumptions. In fact, every decision a team makes is an assumption. They assume they're making the right decision for the business or for the users. The assumptions could be justified with a lot of research, or backed by estimated guesses, but they are assumptions nonetheless.
Nothing will ever be verified to be true or false until your entire audience uses something and you get enough data that's representative of the population and statistically significant.
Agile teams release early and often, and they continuously improve by testing their assumptions and refining their vision. Over time, they deliver more value to users and validate more assumptions. This is cyclical in nature; every time something gets delivered, new assumptions form, and the team should keep validating every new assumption being made.

# Agile

# Milestones and the Development Lifecycle
  Requirements deliverables based on assumptions

Proto-personas
When first starting to gather requirements, teams can start with assumptions about their users with Proto-Personas. This is a common Agile UX deliverable and involves making personas based on your assumptions about users (no research necessary). Traditional personas are delivered after research, but proto-personas are only made with guesses. The purpose of this is to help a team align in the assumptions they are making about users, and to validate them early and refine. Over time, the proto-personas become more refined and less assumptive, turning into "personas".

Vision and Scope
The vision boards should NOT only be delivered once and forgotten about (like with Waterfall processes). Every time a team learns about the business or users, the vision must be reviewed and refined in order to adjust the assumptions being made. Sometimes this causes big changes in the vision and sometimes a team's assumptions were correct. This is to be expected when delivering things iteratively, and teams should adopt the mindset that the "vision is never final", only refined over time.

User stories and acceptance criteria
User stories and acceptance criteria operate on decisions that are made by teams, which are also, you guessed it, ASSUMPTIONS! Teams don't know for certain whether this will meet the audience's needs and need to deliver quickly or test before delivering to check the assumptions. It's important for user stories and acceptance criteria to be small chunks of work so that this process can happen quickly.

Release plans
Your release plan assumes you're going to deliver things when you think you are going to deliver. As the state of the world changes, and team or user needs change, so should the release plans. Teams who check their assumptions early and often must review and refine release plans constantly. This becomes a daily or weekly upkeep for product owners or product managers.

  # Kanban Process
    Kanban Process
    “To Do / Doing / Done”
    At its basic level, Kanban method helps teams track three statuses of work: To Do, Doing, and Done. Yes that’s it! A team simply gets work ready with requirements, starts the work when they are ready, and delivers the work when they are done. They do not plan when work will happen, they simply make judgments about the priorities of work based on the order of items in the backlog

Break down work into independent tasks
    Prioritize your Backlog
Have the backlog prioritized at any moment

    Do the work
Work items should be small and broken down so that they can be delivered in usable chunks (meeting the I.N.V.E.S.T. ACRONYM!)
Set a limit to the amount of tickets that can be in progress at a time (WIP limit), and don’t put any more in progress than the limit. Team sets the limit.

Once finished, the team delivers the work immediately to users or stakeholders
Team should gather feedback in case they need to adjust the work or plan new work. If they do, they add this work to the backlog.

WHAT IS THIS?
STEPS TO RUN THE WORKSHOP
You may think that someone dictates how a team should work in Agile. After all, we have all of the rules written in Scrum, right? Don't all Agile teams operate the same? They tell us what meetings to do, when to do them, and how to do them. This is a misconception. Agile teams govern themselves and own their own process together. Everyone on the team, even the interns, even the apprentices, should have a say in how they work together. This is a principle called self-organization, and it's crucial to build on Agile teams. In order for them to do their best work, they must be handed the keys to ownership of the process. A team process looks different on every team. At its core, it's a summarized agreement for how a team wants to work across functions to get work done. The process is visualized in a flow chart so that everyone can understand how work gets done. When the team takes retrospectives and discusses how to change their process with working agreements, they should update this team process flow chart to ensure it's accurately depicting how the team operates.
OUTCOMES OF THE WORKSHOP
Team process map to show how work gets done on the team that the team will maintain
HOW OFTEN SHOULD IT BE UPDATED?
Your team should be maintaining the team process whenever it needs to change. This will change with the working agreements and retrospectives.
WHY IS IT VALUABLE?
Agile team process maps are valuable because they align a whole team in their understanding of how work happens together. When new team members join, they can be onboarded faster. When someone is uncertain what to do next, they can point to the team process and build clarity. It helps a team operate in a smooth fashion.
GOALS OF THE WORKSHOP
Learn about the Scrum method of Agile
Learn about how agile teams use a tool called a Kanban Board to manage a backlog of work and the statuses of work
Build your own team process in a flow chart
WHO OWNS THIS DELIVERABLE?
The Product Operations function maintains the team process. This is usually handled in Scrum teams by the Scrum Master role or the Product Owner role.
WHERE SHOULD THIS BE KEPT?
Keep it in Figjam, or some other place where you can keep it over time
workshops.Workshop Brief: This workshop produces the Team Process Map and the Kanban Board Statuses. A Kanban board tracks work through statuses (To Do, Doing, Done) with work-in-progress limits to keep work flowing; the process map is the self-organizing team's own picture of how work moves from idea to done.

workshops.Workshop Summary: Sprint Goals are created every sprint before the sprint begins. Teams get together and review their plans to outline the outcomes they want to achieve. Then they break down the outcomes into steps to complete and considerations. The people on the team commit themselves to the work so that they can determine themselves how they want to be involved: responsible, accountable, consulted, or informed.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Create the plan of the shared outcomes for a sprint across a cross-functional teams
Assign people to work before the sprint begins
Set the sprint RACI chart
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Review the work that your team planned from the project plan above.
2. Copy the items from the planned sprint into the space where sprint outcomes go
3. Have everyone on the team who is committing to work add themselves to sticky notes to commit to the sprint
4. Team discusses the steps to complete each task
5. Team discusses any additional requirements or considerations that are needed to complete the work
6. The team assigns themselves either responsible, accountable, consulted, or informed for the work.
7. The team re-edits their RACI hats for the sprint and drops their new RACI hats on their character.
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
Sprint goals are valuable because they:
Set a plan for the sprint
Give clarity in who’s doing the work 
Give clarity in how the work will be done
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: You should create a new sprint goal set every sprint.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?: The Scrum Master duty on the team will own this deliverable alongside the product owner and the whole team who contributes to the input of the planned work.
workshops.Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Sprint Goals.
workshops.Additional Details:
When to use:
A team will be using this deliverable before every sprint begins. The rest of the team should be using this as a viewable artifact to see what they need to be working on, or identify gaps in priorities that are not already planned.
workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: A short, recurring session where the team turns the sprint's slice of the project plan into one clear goal, broken into steps with owners.
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: Bring the whole team and your project plan; it sets each sprint's planned outcomes. Do this at the start of each sprint, during sprint planning. Open the FigJam board with the sprint goal and steps template.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What outcomes does the project plan call for this sprint?
2. What is our single sprint goal?
3. What steps does it break into?
4. Who owns each step?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with one clear sprint goal, the outcomes it covers, and steps with owners the whole team agreed to. Done well, the goal is focused and attainable, and everyone knows their part.
workshops.Time Needed: About 30 to 60 minutes at the start of each sprint
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: Keep it to a single objective; a sprint goal is one focus, not a laundry list. Base it on the project plan's outcomes, and keep it visible so the team can check progress in the daily standup. The goal provides focus while leaving flexibility in exactly how you reach it.
workshops.Where to Keep the Output: Keep it with the sprint plan in FigJam, and revisit it in the daily standup.

  A Project Plan outlines each week of work that all team roles are doing, or planning on doing. A sprint team shouldn’t feel the pressure to plan everything up front, but rather guess at what’s coming in the later weeks and adjust every week.

  The product strategy team must constantly “own” this deliverable and ensure it’s accurate.   WHEN DO TEAMS USE THIS?

  WHERE SHOULD THIS BE KEPT?
  The Project Plan should be kept and maintained in Figjam or some other place where it can be quickly edited.
  HOW OFTEN SHOULD IT BE UPDATED?
  Your Project Plan should not just be drafted once. It needs to be adjusted every week based on the changing priorities and decisions on the team during the 8 weeks of work. workshops.Workshop Brief: This workshop produces Sprint Goals, the single objective for a sprint (per the Scrum Guide) that gives the team focus and a target to measure progress against, while leaving flexibility in exactly how the team gets there.

workshops.Workshop Summary: The team works with an Agile Coach to set up and organize its backlog. Together they turn ideas and requirements into user stories and task tickets, add acceptance criteria, and put the work in order in a tool like Notion, so the team always knows what to pick up next.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Turn requirements into clear user stories and tasks
Write acceptance criteria so everyone knows when work is done
Put the backlog in priority order
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?: A messy backlog slows a team down and causes confusion about what to build. A clear, ordered backlog lets the team focus on the most important work and move faster with less back and forth.
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Set up the backlog early, then keep it up to date. The team should refine and reorder it during every sprint.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?: The Product Operations function owns this workshop and is responsible for running it with the team.
workshops.Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Acceptance Criteria and Prioritized Backlog Tasks.
workshops.Additional Details: When to use: set it up at the start and keep it going through every sprint.
workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: A workshop where the team turns its release scope into an organized backlog of epics, features, and tasks, then builds a roadmap and populates the backlog to guide the build.
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: Bring the product owner and manager (they own release and backlog management) and your release-level vision and scope from the Vision and Scope workshop. Set up FigJam with the epic, feature, and task organizer and the roadmap. Revisit regularly as priorities shift.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What epics and features come out of our release scope?
2. What tasks make up each feature?
3. What does our release roadmap look like?
4. What goes into the backlog, and in what order?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with a backlog of epics, features, and tasks organized from the release scope, a roadmap, and a populated, prioritized backlog ready to write requirements against. Done well, the work ladders directly up to the release vision, and the team knows what to build next.
workshops.Time Needed: A substantial session, then maintained regularly
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: Organize work into themes (epics), then features, then small tasks that fit the INVEST idea. Keep the backlog prioritized at all times. And treat the roadmap as living; adjust it as you learn.
workshops.Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam and your backlog tool; the product team maintains it.

  Products aren’t just made from ideas. They take a lot of coordination, research, decisions, and negotiations to make happen. Teams in the world who focus on their audience’s problems can transform their teamwork into a larger long-term map of success. Teams must maintain and update the deliverables that showcase the long-term outcomes over time as they learn new insights in research. This workshop helps a team to outline how to take a team’s current understanding of the problems in their audience’s current state, identify the goals, and create the maps for long-term release outcomes that they need to follow while performing UX, product, or development work.
  GOALS OF THE WORKSHOP
  Identify your known audiences
Identify problems you think your audiences experience today in current state of the world
Prioritize the problems you want to focus on now and later. 
Communicate the problems you identify as goals, value, unique advantage, and outcomes in a vision for near-term and long-term releases.
Organize the work outcomes into themes and chunk the backlog work into feasible work items.
Develop a roadmap plan for the next year that you can maintain.

It breaks down larger goals into smaller, more accomplishable results
It helps you communicate language around your goals, needs, value delivery, and action items.
It helps you determine what your team should focus on now and later, and organizes work for the entire team.

# For Each Audience: Prioritize the Problems
  For Each Audience: Prioritize the Problems
  Take your use cases you’ve identified on the first section and prioritize them for each audience
  How do you know which problems to solve first?
In short: you don't, and no one does. It's all just a guess and a judgment call based on what you know. You could get the guess wrong, and Agile is built for quick adjustments when you get it wrong. One needs to embrace this lifestyle in requirements work for Agile teams. You will constantly be guessing which is the correct way to go. "Continuous improvement" all the way. You can use tools like prioritization matrices to rank problems to solve and decide which ones to solve first. The rest is up to what the team decides to put into their release-level vision, and what they learn after they deliver iterations towards the release.

You’ve now identified the key problems, goals, value, barriers, and unique advantage about your product or service. You are ready to put together a release-level vision board! The release is made up of many problems to solve. In the sections below, write the components of the vision board based on the input you provided in part 1. Only worry about the first release (MVP #1) and the market-ready release (MMP).

You should make one vision board per audience, per release. 

For instance: if you have two target audiences, you will be making 4 vision boards: MVP for Audience 1, MMP for Audience 1, MVP for Audience 2, and MMP for Audience 2.

You may be asking yourself, "Why? This seems like more work..." Yes it is. It is very purposeful. This approach is helpful to specify what exact value you're delivering for each audience each time you release. Without this approach, you may not communicate the exact problems you're solving, or value you're delivering, for each audience. It's best to proceed one audience, one release at a time.

workshops.Workshop Brief: This workshop produces a refined, Prioritized Backlog and its Acceptance Criteria. Backlog refinement keeps the to-do list clear, sized, and ordered; acceptance criteria are the agreed conditions (often given-when-then) that define when each item is done.

workshops.Workshop Summary:
This is a sprint retrospective template for Agile cross-functional teams to reflect in their previous sprint, measure their agility, and take action on the process changes they want to make as a team.

A sprint retrospective is the most important meeting for a sprint team. The full team, all apprentices and co-leads, get together after every sprint and hold a safe space to reflect on their last sprint.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Every sprint, Agile teams should get together to reflect in their work:

Celebrate what went well
Measure how far they have progressed
Discuss what they want to improve about their own process together
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Do the 4 L's: what did the team like, learn, lack, and long for? 
2. Who gave great service leadership? 
3. What deliverables did you complete? 
4. Rank your agile maturity scores
5. Identify action items and make plans for improvement
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
A sprint retrospective is valuable because:

It allows room for people to speak freely about what process changes they want to make.
It holds space for teams to continuously improve after reflection and collective agreement.
It reinforces self-organization, putting the success of the team in the hands of the team itself, and no one outside the team.
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Hold a retro at the end of every sprint. It is one of the most important team meetings, so do not skip it.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?:
People playing the Scrum Master role own this deliverable. They must:

Facilitate this meeting as Scrum Master role
Document action items
Send out the summary after
Update working agreements
workshops.Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Sprint Retro Action Items and Agile Maturity Measurements.
workshops.Additional Details:
When to use:
After every sprint, the team should get together to hold a sprint retrospective.

How to involve other teams:
Get together after every sprint
Part 1: what did you like, what did you learn, what did you lack, and what did you long for?
Part 2: Identify action items for how to change process on the team, and brainstorm together about how to change it, and assign the person who’s going to own the outcomes of the changes (it could be anyone on the team)
Part 3: Measure your team’s levels of agility by answering the questions on the workshop

Everyone on the team, including apprentices and co-leads, needs to participate in retrospectives. The team owns their own process and they must participate to feel the full stake of ownership in it.
workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: The team's most important recurring meeting: a safe space after every sprint to reflect, celebrate wins, and agree concrete changes to how the team works.
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: Bring the whole team, including apprentices and co-leads; everyone participates. Set up the FigJam board with the 4 Ls retro and the action-items table. The product strategy team facilitates it as Scrum Master. Do it after every sprint.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What did we like, learn, lack, and long for this sprint?
2. Who showed great service leadership, and why?
3. What should we change about our process?
4. Who owns each change, and does it update our working agreements?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with honest reflections, service-leadership recognition, and a set of owned action items for improving your process, with working agreements updated. Done well, everyone spoke freely, and the team, not anyone outside it, owns the changes.
workshops.Time Needed: About 60 minutes after each sprint
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: Keep it a safe space; this reinforces self-organization, so no one outside the team drives the changes. Turn reflections into owned action items, or nothing actually changes. Send the summary and update the working agreements afterward.
workshops.Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam; update the working agreements and send a summary afterward.

workshops.Workshop Brief: This workshop produces Sprint Retro Action Items. A retrospective is the recurring meeting where a team reflects and commits to concrete improvements; Tech Fleet uses the 4 Ls format (liked, learned, lacked, longed for) and turns reflections into owned action items, the engine of continuous improvement.

workshops.Workshop Summary:
This is a workshop template to help cross-functional Agile teams develop their own principles of self-organization known as a working agreement. There are multiple working agreements across different areas on teams. These change whenever the team takes a retrospective on work and agrees to change the way they work.

Working agreements are an Agile deliverable that act as a set of guidelines and expectations established by a team or group to govern how they will work together effectively. The team changes them as their team matures over time. Working agreements are commonly used in various contexts, including Agile and Scrum development teams, but they can be applied to any group or project where people need to work together cohesively.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Define team expectations in how a whole team approaches work together
Collect perspectives and desires from the team in how they want to work together across functions
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Review the information provided about Agile teams in the user guide
2. Answer the questions as a team for how you will abide by the Agile tenets together:
3. How will your team build psychological safety?
4. How will your team build service leadership?
5. How will your team build self-organization?
6. How will your team build continuous improvement?
7. How will your team deal with and resolve conflict?
8. How will your team handle pivoting?
9. How will your team handle communication?
10. What else do you want to agree to?
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?: Working agreements provide expectations and guidelines for teams who need to work together across functions. These agreements help create a shared understanding of how team members will interact, communicate, and collaborate to achieve their goals.
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Working agreements should be updated as teams go through sprint retros and learn how they want to change their process together.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?: The Scrum Master role owns this deliverable and facilitates it with the team. They get the team together to build a collective consensus and take action on listing out agreements that the team wants to note. The Scrum Master maintains these working agreements as they change after every retro.
workshops.Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Psychological Safety Plan.
workshops.Additional Details:
When to use:
The collective team, led by the Scrum Master role, should build a consensus about working agreements before the project begins. This should happen during the first two weeks of a project phase, and they adjust after each sprint retro.

How to involve other teams:
The entire team should get together to build their working agreements together so that they commit to them collectively. Each time the agreements change, the full team should review and approve them before enacting new working agreements.
workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: A session where a new team writes its own ground rules, deciding together how it will build psychological safety, share leadership, self-organize, improve, and handle conflict and change.
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: Bring the whole team, with the Scrum Master to facilitate. Have the Agile Handbook's material on strong agile teams open (the tenets and the agility checklists), and set up the FigJam board with an agreement section for each agile tenet. This works best in the first two weeks of a phase.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering: How will our team build: 1. psychological safety, 2. service leadership, 3. self-organization, 4. continuous improvement? And how will we: 5. resolve conflict, 6. handle pivoting, 7. communicate, 8. collaborate across functions, and 9. move past storming?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with a set of written agreements the whole team shaped and committed to, covering each agile tenet plus conflict, pivoting, and communication. Done well, they are the team's own words, not a template, and everyone genuinely buys in.
workshops.Time Needed: About 60 to 90 minutes
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: These are living; revisit and update them after every sprint retro as the team matures. Build them together so people commit collectively, and re-approve as a full team when they change. Ground each agreement in the agile tenet it supports.
workshops.Where to Keep the Output: Keep them in the team's shared space; the Scrum Master maintains them and the team revisits after each retro.

# WORKING AGREEMENT INSTRUCTIONS
  WORKING AGREEMENT INSTRUCTIONS
  WHAT IS THIS?
  HOW TO RUN THE WORKSHOP
  Working agreements, also known as team agreements or ground rules, are a set of guidelines and expectations established by a team or group to govern how they will work together effectively.The team changes them as their team matures over time. Working agreements are commonly used in various contexts, including Agile and Scrum development teams, but they can be applied to any group or project where people need to work together cohesively.
  Review the information provided about Agile teams in the user guide
Answer the questions as a team for how you will abide by the Agile tenets together: 
How will your team build psychological safety? 
How will your team build service leadership? 
How will your team build self-organization? 
How will your team build continuous improvement? 
How will your team deal with and resolve conflict?
How will your team handle pivoting?
How will your team handle communication?
What else do you want to agree to?
  WHY IS IT VALUABLE?
  Working agreements provide expectations and guidelines for teams who need to work together across functions. These agreements help create a shared understanding of how team members will interact, communicate, and collaborate to achieve their goals.
  HOW TO INVOLVE OTHER TEAMS
  The entire team should get together to build their working agreements together so that they commit to them collectively. Each time the agreements change, the full team should review and approve them before enacting new working agreements.
  WHO OWNS THIS DELIVERABLE?
  The Scrum Master role owns this deliverable and facilitates it with the team. They get the team together to build a collective consensus and take action on listing out agreements that the team wants to note. The Scrum Master maintains these working agreements as they change after every retro.
  WHEN DO TEAMS USE THIS?
  The collective team, led by the Scrum Master role, should build a consensus about working agreements before the project begins. This should happen during the first two weeks of a project phase, and they adjust after each sprint retro.
  HOW OFTEN SHOULD IT BE UPDATED?
  Working agreements should be updated as teams go through sprint retros and learn how they want to change their process together.

# Building Agile Teams that Perform
  The Basic Tenets of Agile Team Building
  Measuring the Agile Tenets
  Agile team strength is like a garden: you have to maintain agility and pick out the weeds to ensure health and growth of your team. How teams do this is open to the person owning the product, and the scrum master. 

Here are some key points to determine levels of self-organization, psychological safety, servant leadership, iterative value delivery, and continuous improvement.
  To measure Agility, teams must look at the components of what makes an Agile team agile: self-organization, psychological safety, servant leadership, iterative value, and continuous improvement. Here’s a set of checklists you can use to determine your team’s current state of agility.
  Self-organization: 

Allow the day-to-day people doing the work to make decisions themselves, instead of the people leading the team, and let the team carry out their own work in the way they want, or think is best
  Psychological Safety:

Build the sense of safety and belonging throughout the team:
Make every member of the team feel like they have room to speak their mind
Actively listen when others have things to say, and make team feel like their voice matters
Give the room for people to bring their own personalities and unique capabilities to the table in the way THEY want to do so
Allow room for team mates to challenge the status quo, and experiment with new ways of working
Encourage failing “fast”, i.e. failure and quick reflection and quick adjustment based on what the team thinks they should do
Let them take the risks that THEY decide to take, that could lead to failure or disaster, for the purposes of allowing them to build up decision making prowess
  Self-organization checklist
  Psychological Safety checklist
  Does your team wait for answers or initiate things on their own?
Does your team ask for clarity before starting or continuing work?
Does your team volunteer to work assignments?
Does your team contribute to conversations?
Does your team present new ideas for how to work, or idea for the product?
Does your team build consensus together and involve each other in decision making?
  Does your team speak up about concerns?
Does your team contribute to conversations freely?
Does your team voice dissent? 
Does your team celebrate each other for who they are and what they bring to the contributions?
Does your team experiment with new ways of working together? 
Does your team take risks together, and try new things?
  Servant Leadership:

All managers and all team mates should act as servant leaders to each other, those around them, those “above” them, or those “below” them in any organization’s hierarchy
  Servant Leadership checklist
  Iterative Value checklist
  Do your team members support each others’ growth instead of their own?
Does the person in charge tell everyone what to do, or do they transfer the power to the team?
Does your team show respect towards others? 
Does your team empathize with others and help each other?
Does your team seek to understand situations that arise, and communicate needs?
Does your team set expectations with each other in healthy ways?
  Does your team deliver work incrementally?
Does your team constantly involve clients,  stakeholders, and users in feedback sessions? 
Does your team collaborate with each other to determine the highest priorities to deliver in unison? 
Does your team work on the most important things at any given time, and deliver them quickly?
  Iterative value delivery: 

Teams should be empowered to deliver value early and often in order to gather feedback and decide themselves how they need to adjust. By doing so, and having self-organization, and psychological safety, the team can flag risks early or set better directions for them and for the organization.
  Continuous improvement:

Teams should be granted the opportunity to fail, and to build a process of quick adjustment when they fail. “Failure” is vague here: it could mean that the team’s plan didn’t work, or it could mean that something happened in the world requiring the team to change, or it could mean that someone made a mistake / didn’t do something.
  Continuous Improvement checklist
  Does your team have a “fail forward” attitude?
Does your team look at things in hindsight as opportunities?
Does your team look at problems as opportunities to improve? 
Does your team have a healthy amount of discussion in reflection of root causes?
Does your team avoid blaming others when looking at root causes in hindsight? 
Does your team work together to refine their working agreements as they fail forward?
Does your team manage the chaos of life, and client needs, together?

Working agreements are team-authored norms for how to collaborate; Tech Fleet frames them around the agile tenets, starting with psychological safety (Edmondson, Timothy Clark) as the foundation.

workshops.Workshop Name: Scenario-Based Problem Statement Generation Workshop Template
workshops.Workshop Summary: The team learns how to write clear problem statements based on real situations users face today. Starting from what is happening in the world right now, the team describes the problem, the user's needs and goals, and turns those into user stories the team can act on.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Learn how to write problem statements from real user situations
Describe user needs and goals in plain language
Turn problems into user stories the team can build from
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Dump the unrefined problems
2. Break into aspects
3. Refine the aspects
4. Break the aspects into Formal Problem Statements (why, what, who, when)
5. Create Problem Checklist (user goal, user need, consequences, user story) for each Formal Problem Statement
6. Prioritize the problems to put back into the Vision and Scope
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?: Teams waste time when they jump to solutions before they understand the problem. Writing clear problem statements keeps the team focused on what users actually need, so the work solves a real problem.
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Do this during discovery whenever the team is trying to understand a new problem. Come back to it as you learn more from research.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?: The Product Management function owns this workshop and is responsible for running it with the team.
workshops.Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Problem Statements, Problem Checklists, and User Story Statements.
workshops.Additional Details: When to use: during discovery, after sprints begin, when the team is deciding what to solve.
workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: A workshop that turns a pile of assumed problems into sharp, root-cause problem statements, problem checklists, and user stories the team can build against.
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: Bring the team and every problem you assume about the current state, per audience (from discovery or your own hunches). Set up the FigJam board with the problem-dump space and the breakdown tables. Best during discovery and requirements.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What problems do we assume, for each audience?
2. What are the raw aspects (situations) behind each?
3. What is the root of each, found with the 5 Whys?
4. Who faces it, when, and why does it matter, and what user goal, need, and consequences follow?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with formal problem statements (root + aspect + who + when + why), a problem checklist for each (goal, need, consequences to avoid), and a user story for each. Done well, they describe real problems, never solutions, and give the team something concrete to prioritize.
workshops.Time Needed: A substantial amount of working sessions over the course of a sprint
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: Describe problems, not solutions; the board warns of this trap repeatedly (a goal and a need are not a solution). Use the 5 Whys to reach the real root. And write one audience per checklist, so problems can be prioritized cleanly later.
workshops.Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam and refine the problem statements constantly as you learn.

# Section 6
  Assumption Forming and Testing
  This is what happens when you don’t document requirements, and run with assumptions that are not validated
  Assumptions and Requirements
  Teams are making a lot of assumptions. In fact, every decision a team makes is an assumption. They assume they're making the right decision for the business or for the users. The assumptions could be justified with a lot of research, or backed by estimated guesses, but they are assumptions nonetheless.
Nothing will ever be verified to be true or false until your entire audience uses something and you get enough data that's representative of the population and statistically significant.
Agile teams release early and often, and they continuously improve by testing their assumptions and refining their vision. Over time, they deliver more value to users and validate more assumptions. This is cyclical in nature; every time something gets delivered, new assumptions form, and the team should keep validating every new assumption being made.
  Credit: Google Ventures (Google Design Sprint)
  Requirements deliverables based on assumptions

Proto-personas
When first starting to gather requirements, teams can start with assumptions about their users with Proto-Personas. This is a common Agile UX deliverable and involves making personas based on your assumptions about users (no research necessary). Traditional personas are delivered after research, but proto-personas are only made with guesses. The purpose of this is to help a team align in the assumptions they are making about users, and to validate them early and refine. Over time, the proto-personas become more refined and less assumptive, turning into "personas".

Vision and Scope
The vision boards should NOT only be delivered once and forgotten about (like with Waterfall processes). Every time a team learns about the business or users, the vision must be reviewed and refined in order to adjust the assumptions being made. Sometimes this causes big changes in the vision and sometimes a team's assumptions were correct. This is to be expected when delivering things iteratively, and teams should adopt the mindset that the "vision is never final", only refined over time.

User stories and acceptance criteria
User stories and acceptance criteria operate on decisions that are made by teams, which are also, you guessed it, ASSUMPTIONS! Teams don't know for certain whether this will meet the audience's needs and need to deliver quickly or test before delivering to check the assumptions. It's important for user stories and acceptance criteria to be small chunks of work so that this process can happen quickly.

Release plans
Your release plan assumes you're going to deliver things when you think you are going to deliver. As the state of the world changes, and team or user needs change, so should the release plans. Teams who check their assumptions early and often must review and refine release plans constantly. This becomes a daily or weekly upkeep for product owners or product managers.

# Section 8
  Solution vs. Problem vs. Need vs. Goal
  “We want you to draw 7 red lines, 4 with blue ink, 3 with transparent ink. Can you do it?”
  How do you know the solution that a stakeholder brings you will meet user needs? How do you know it's solving the right problem to begin with?
You don't!
  A solution is something that is assumed HOW to solve a problem.

A problem describes a SITUATIONAL USE CASE that’s happening in the current state of the world, describing something lacking or missing in the state of the world. Users experience problems because of how they interact with the world.   A user goal describes THE OUTCOME a user is trying to achieve.  A business goal describes THE OUTCOME a business is trying to achieve.

A user need describes basic human-level expectation and desire based on the problem to be solved.   A business need describes expectation and desires for a business based on the problem to be solved.  A technical need describes requirement from a technical standpoint based on the problem to be solved.

# RESEARCHING THE CURRENT STATE OF THE WORLD
  Researching the Current State of the World
  Teams must understand: 
How something works today
How users behave
How users expect 
How users think
How they experience the problems 
The ecosystem in which the problems live

UX research Methods
Contextual inquiries - Walk alongside a user as they go through activities in "a day in the life", ask them questions
Ethnography - Observe things in the world and take note
Interviews - Ask people questions in conversation
Card sorts - Understand how people would rank or categorize things
Surveys - Ask people questions asynchronously
Web analytics audits - Look at web analytics to see how audiences are behaving online
Usability tests - Measure how successfully people do or understand something
Concept tests - Test a concept idea with potential audiences

Teams must also understand the market: 

Market size
Teams should understand the state of the market and the opportunities for growth within the market. This comes with analyzing the total market cap of products that are similar to the product being built. Tools online offer abilities to look at market research and understand the market they're trying to enter. This is important in order to understand how "saturated" the market is before moving too far ahead with their work. If the market has too many other competitors that try to solve the same problems, then the team needs to strategize on how their product is going to uniquely provide value.

Market segmentation
Within markets there may be sub-categories of products that specifically solve problems. Teams should understand where exactly their product fits into the market in order to form good assumptions about where their product fits in.

Direct and indirect competitors
There may be other products on the market that try to solve the same or similar problems. Vetting them is key to deciding how to differentiate your product from others. There could be products that have similar features and similar customers as yours, or products that indirectly solve the problems you are trying to solve. Teams should document and analyze all of this before moving ahead with their vision.

Unique selling proposition / competitive advantage
If a product doesn't bring something uniquely valuable to the table, there's a low likelihood that users will abandon existing products and convert to the one your team's building. Refining a unique selling proposition takes analysis of the market and its competitors to understand what none of them do well.

  Finding the Root of Problems
  When a problem is defined, it may not be the root of the problem. Keep asking “Why is this a problem” to find the most meaningful root problem.
  People don’t have enough resources and it causes them to get sick
  Enter the problem
  Not having enough food impairs your brain activity
  Keep digging: Why is this a problem?
  People may not be able to function in society
  Keep digging: Why is this a problem?
  People may be more likely to resort to stealing 
People may not be able to have as much choice in their own lives
  Keep digging: Why is this a problem?
  So: What is the root problem?
  Anatomy of a problem statement

Problem statements have several parts:

What is the root problem?
The root of the problem can be tricky to describe, or uncover. It takes research and understanding your audiences to be able to do so. Once you have a good understanding, the root problem should be described in one sentence. See the other lessons in this section for details about how to uncover the root problems, and aspects of the problem.

Which audience experiences the problem?
This describes your target audiences that experience the problem. You must have a good understanding about the audiences you are building for first, but this can be a guess (an assumption) before you validate with further work.
When and where is it a problem for users?
Describe the situations and scenarios where this comes up for users. Doing this helps others understand how to empathize with the user and understand the context in which they experience the problem.

Why is it important to solve?
There's a quote from a movie: "ABC: Always Be Closing". Always be closing when describing your problem statements. Provide justifications why the problem is worth solving, or else. In team discussions, if you do not have a good reason why it's important to solve this problem for users, no one on your team, and especially no one outside your team, will be bought in to building it. Why spend time and money on solutions if it's is not worth solving? ABC!
  Formal Problem Statement
  Create one problem statement per problem to solve in your product. There may be hundreds of problem statements in scope of your product.
  Describe the problem in the state of the world:

  Why is this problem important to solve for users?

# Section 10
  Problem Checklists
  Problem Checklist
  Create one problem statement per problem to solve in your product. There may be hundreds of problem statements in scope of your product.
  FOR: 
PROBLEM STATEMENT: 
USER GOALS:
USER NEEDS:
THE CONSEQUENCES THEY ARE TRYING TO AVOID:
  FOR: Drop your target audience here
  PROBLEM: Drop your problem statement here
  USER GOALS: enter the outcomes that the user is trying to achieve
  USER NEEDS: describe the basic human need behind the problem. There could be multiple.
  THE CONSEQUENCES THE USER IS TRYING TO AVOID: What are the consequences of the problem that the user is trying to avoid? There could be multiple.
  The problem checklist has five parts:
The audience involved
The problem statement (see previous section)
The user goal
The user needs behind the goal
The consequences that the user is trying to avoid

Each problem statement has a corresponding problem checklist. Each problem statement / problem checklist has a corresponding user story statement.

Audience
Only write one audience per problem checklist. If two or more audiences face the same problem, then write different problem checklists for each audience. You should do this so that they can properly be prioritized in your vision and scope (see the next week's lessons for more). You will use this section later when you generate your user story statements.

Problem statement
Take your problem statement that you formed and drop it here. Only write one problem statement per problem checklist.

User goal
Only write one goal per problem checklist. Write the outcome that the audience is trying to achieve when experiencing the problem. THIS IS NOT THE SOLUTION! Be careful here. It's very common for people to write out the solution when trying to describe the goal. Seek to describe the end-result, the outcome, not the solution. You will use this section later when you generate your user story statements.  
User needs You may write one or many user needs per problem checklist. Describe the human expectation that they want to be in place in order to solve the problem. THIS IS NOT THE SOLUTION! THIS IS NOT THE GOAL! Be careful here. It's very common for people to write a solution (i.e. "They need a button..." or "they need to know where their cat is...") when trying to describe the user need. Refer back to the earlier sections in this week's lesson for reminders about needs vs. solutions. This is where the "rubber meets the road," and your knowledge about needs vs. solutions is put to the test.

Consequences to avoid
Make a list of all of the bad things that the user is trying to avoid (successfully or not) when experiencing the problem, and add them here. This provides helpful context for teams when trying to ABC (always be closing) and convincing teams (through their requirements) that the problem is worth solving. You will use this section later when you generate your user story statements.

workshops.Workshop Brief: This workshop produces Problem Statements, Problem Checklists, and User Story Statements. A problem statement is a clear, user-focused description of a problem, never a solution; the team finds each root with the 5 Whys, then turns it into a checklist (goal, need, consequences) and a user story.

workshops.Workshop Summary:
UX is a scientific field! We UX’ers follow the Scientific Method in our work. We pose hypotheses and build tests to test the hypothesis. They are either true or false. Sometimes, the results are undetermined.

In the context of Agile UX, UX’ers finish one single round of research in a short period of time known as “an iteration”. This could be one week, or two weeks, based on the Agile Method you are following.

This training framework provides a way to follow a repeated cycle of mapping questions and hypotheses to assumptions and points of measurement for the purposes of building a research test.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Pick your top research topics
Identify your assumptions about research topics
Prioritize your assumptions about the topics
Create details about your assumption:
Implications
Questions to users
Points of measurement to collect from tasks and observations
Problem statements related to the assumptions

9. Choose your research methods to answer the questions
10. Build your resulting research test plan

workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
This research test framework is valuable because it allows teams to always work on the most important assumptions to validate in research at any given time.
This helps teams always map their research to an assumption or a research question for better organization.
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Make a new research plan for each round of research, usually once a sprint. Update it as your questions and priorities change.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?: The UX Research function and UX Strategy function owns this deliverable. Whomever is working in this function should collaborate with other functions to collect necessary input about assumptions or priorities before deciding how to proceed with the test plan creation.

Where to keep it:
Keep it in Figjam, or some other place where you can keep it over time
workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: A workshop that turns research topics into a rigorous, repeatable test plan, treating UX as a science: prioritize topics, form assumptions, map them to questions and measurements, choose methods, and document the test.
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: Bring the team (UX Research and UX Strategy lead, but collaborate with all functions) and the topics or problems you want to learn about. Set up the FigJam board with the topic list, assumption table, method-selection guide, and test-plan template. This runs each research iteration of a week or two.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What do we want to learn (research topics)?
2. Which are most important to do now?
3. What assumptions do we hold, and what problem, implications, and measurements attach to each?
4. Which research method fits each question?
5. What is our full test plan?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with prioritized research topics, an assumption table mapping each to a problem, implications, and ways to test it, chosen methods, and a complete test plan (background, goals, questions, assumptions, methodology, limitations). Done well, it is rigorous enough to repeat and aims at the highest-value assumptions.
workshops.Time Needed: One research iteration (about one to two weeks of planning and testing)
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: Treat UX as a science: everything starts as a hypothesis you test to true, false, or undetermined. You cannot test everything in one iteration, so prioritize the riskiest, least-certain assumptions. Choose the method from the type of question (generative vs evaluative, what vs why, short vs long). And name the research's limitations honestly.

workshops.Workshop Brief: This workshop produces the UX Research Plan (and supports analytics and accessibility analyses). A research plan documents a study's goals, questions, methods, and participants; Tech Fleet frames UX as a science, mapping assumptions to hypotheses and measurements so tests can be prioritized and repeated.

workshops.Workshop Summary: How does a team know what they will decide after doing all of the research or gathering all of the information? THEY DON’T! They all may have ideas, but they could be totally wrong. It’s best to quickly get to a shippable idea that gets tested than to keep talking about the possibilities of the direction a team could make. Rapid Ideation is just that: Quick (so many ideas get generated from this!) and generative (creative ideas get generated from thin air!), getting teams to the other side of delivery after thinking about all of the possibilities that could occur.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Problem-solve in creative ways

Rapidly generate a lot of ideas to work with

Move ahead with a testable concept
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Compile a list of your problem statements
2. Translate your problem statements into How Might We statements
3. Prioritize the How Might We statements
4. Vote on the top HMW statements
5. Perform Rapid Ideation (with Crazy 8’s Method)
6. Present the Rapid Ideation
7. Vote on the top choices
8. Write requirements for the decisions you’ve made that will go to design
9. Design and implement and test the solutions you propose
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
A Rapid Ideation workshop is valuable because it:

Provides room for creative problem-solving that’s collaborative in nature

Provides ways for more than just one perspective to be heard in decision making and ideation

Provides ways for teams to combine ideas quickly, and form cohesive solutions that can be complex
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Teams can perform this as often as they want for continuous rounds of delivery work that turns into designs and concepts to test and ship.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?: The UX Strategy hat owns this deliverable. The strategy side of UX is purposeful decision making. Rapid Ideation is where the Research meets the Design. Together, with formed knowledge about current state problems, the strategy hats in the room can come together to ideate on how to solve the problems.
workshops.Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its How Might We (HMW) Statements and Sketches.
workshops.Additional Details:
When to use:
Teams should do this whenever they feel it fits their needs and outcomes! This is not just something that should happen “after research”. If everything is an assumption, then we can ideate on assumptions without research, and use the ideation as the grounding to validate the ideas with research. This is how the Lean UX and Google Design Sprint methods operate!

How to involve other teams:
Do NOT just include the UX designers in this kind of session. Everyone should get involved in rapid ideation, no matter who you are on the team or what roles you want to play! Everyone has an important perspective to share and ideas that UX Designers may have never even thought of.
workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: A fast, everyone-in session that turns a pile of assumed problems into fresh ideas and narrows them to the ideas worth testing.
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: Come in with your research findings or assumed problems (ideally as problem statements) and the audiences you serve. Get the whole team in the room, not just designers, and set up the FigJam board with the How Might We table, the risk/certainty priority matrix, and the Crazy 8's grids. A timer is essential. You do not need finished research; you can ideate on assumptions and validate them afterward.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What problems do we assume about the current state, for each audience?
2. How might we solve each one, as a How Might We statement?
3. Which HMWs are the riskiest and least certain, so most worth our ideation time?
4. What are all the ways we might solve them?
5. Which ideas are worth turning into requirements and testing?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with prioritized How Might We statements and a set of voted, sketched ideas for the top ones, clear enough to write into requirements and test. Done well, everyone sketched, the group converged without endless debate, and the risky, uncertain problems got the most creative attention.
workshops.Time Needed: About 90 minutes (two 8-minute Crazy 8's rounds plus discussion and voting)
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: Do not make this designers-only; the best ideas often come from outside UX. Do not skip the risk-and-certainty prioritization, or you will waste time ideating on safe, low-risk problems. Honor the Crazy 8's timing (eight ideas in eight minutes) so speed pushes people past their safe first idea. And do not wait for perfect research; ideate on assumptions and validate after, the way Lean UX and Design Sprints do.
workshops.Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam or another quickly editable space, so the HMWs, priorities, and ideas stay easy to revisit and turn into requirements.

workshops.Workshop Brief: This workshop moves a team from problems to testable ideas, and it produces two things: How Might We statements and quick sketches. A How Might We statement is a design-thinking tool (popularized by IDEO) that reframes a research insight as an open question, like "how might we make sign-up feel effortless?" The wording matters: "how" assumes there is an answer to find, and "might" keeps the door open to many paths, so the question sparks ideas without locking in one. The sketches come from Crazy 8's, a Design Sprint method where each person draws eight rough ideas in eight minutes, one per box. The whole point is quantity over polish; the tight timer pushes people past their safe first idea and surfaces options they would never have reached by talking. Nothing here is meant to be pretty or final. It is raw fuel for deciding what to test.

workshops.Workshop Summary: Storyboards are visual representations of significant points in a storyline, incorporating illustrations and images to support your main idea. It is a powerful tool for structuring a story or adding a narrative element to technical linear sequences, including workflows, operational processes, and user pathways, whether for a customer journey or the hero’s journey. In our case, the storyboard will depict a potential member’s experience with skills and practices measurements.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Tell a story of the current state of the experience for people
Envision what the world could look like in the future
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Add your audience segments you want to focus on
2. Add your use case scenarios for audiences that you want to storyboard for current and future state
3. Choose the use cases you want to storyboard
4. Everyone break out and create both a CURRENT and FUTURE state storyboard for each use case you choose
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?: Storyboards are valuable because they help everyone visualize what life is like today in different situations for audiences, and what life could be like into the future. It’s a great way to brainstorm and strategize before you make decisions of change.
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Use this whenever the team wants to picture a user's experience, now or in the future. Revisit it as you learn more from research.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?: Everyone in all functions on cross-functional teams should be using storyboard to strategize before they decide and build alignment with people who have a stake in the results.
workshops.Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Storyboard.
workshops.Additional Details:
When to use:
This technique helps your team visualize the real-life activities of your users, empathize with them, find important moments along their journey, and uncover gaps and problems you can address.

Specific use case examples for using a storyboard template also include:
Mapping out a business plan to present to a stakeholder.
Visualizing an upcoming marketing campaign. Include important details and resources needed to launch.
Understanding how users interact with a product or service, especially by mapping out key scenes or touch points within the customer journey.
workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: A workshop where the team draws a user's current and future experience as an eight-panel storyboard, so everyone can see what life is like today and imagine what it could be.
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: Bring the team and your audience segments and use case scenarios (from segmentation and discovery). Set up FigJam with the storyboard panels and sticker tools. Everyone participates, and drawing skill is not required.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. Which audiences and use cases do we want to storyboard?
2. What does the user's experience look like today, step by step?
3. How do they struggle and feel?
4. What could the experience look like in the future once their problems are solved?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with current and future storyboards for each chosen use case, drawn as simple eight-panel stories. Done well, the current one honestly shows today's struggles, and the future one is a creative, specific vision of what could be.
workshops.Time Needed: About 10 minutes per storyboard, plus discussion
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: Keep it low-fidelity; doodles and emojis are fine as long as the story reads. Always do both current and future. For the future, go wild; it is your blue-sky wish list, so be specific about how each problem gets solved.
workshops.Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam with your discovery work.

  Storyboards are visual representations of significant points in a storyline, incorporating illustrations and images to support your main idea. It is a powerful tool for structuring a story or adding a narrative element to technical linear sequences, including workflows, operational processes, and user pathways, whether for a customer journey or the hero’s journey. In our case, the storyboard will depict a potential member’s experience with skills and practices measurements.
  GOALS OF THE WORKSHOP
  Tell a story of the current state of the experience for people
Envision what the world could look like in the future
  WHY IS IT VALUABLE?
  Storyboards are valuable because they help everyone visualize what life is like today in different situations for audiences, and what life could be like into the future. It’s a great way to brainstorm and strategize before you make decisions of change.
  WHO OWNS THIS DELIVERABLE?
  Everyone in all functions on cross-functional teams should be using storyboard to strategize before they decide and build alignment with people who have a stake in the results.
  WHEN SHOULD YOU DO STORYBOARDS?
  This technique helps your team visualize the real-life activities of your users, empathize with them, find important moments along their journey, and uncover gaps and problems you can address. 

Specific use case examples for using a storyboard template also include:

Mapping out a business plan to present to a stakeholder.
Visualizing an upcoming marketing campaign. Include important details and resources needed to launch.
Understanding how users interact with a product or service, especially by mapping out key scenes or touch points within the customer journey.

# How to
  How do you make a storyboard

As a group, draw out a specific user scenario or story in sequential panels (like a comic book). This is commonly done in eight panels and participants are usually given ten minutes to complete the story. 

Make sure to include two versions:

Current Experience 
How does the user experience the product/service in the moment? What do they struggle with? How does it impact their life? How do they feel? What do they wish they had?

Future Experience 
How does the user experience the product/service now that all their problems have gone away? In the future state storyboards, you should be specifically ideating what could be possible to solve the current state problems.  Be specific. Instead of saying "People are confused", say what exactly should be happening, in order to solve the problem of confusion. 

What to include:

The imagery can be very low fidelity (and even use things like emojis, doodling, or pictures) so long as the narrative is communicated.

What to include:

Once the storyboard is complete, come together and analyze it with the whole team, and then you can fill in smaller details that connect the main story points.
  Tip: Future Experience is your wish list, your "blue sky" ideation time. The future storyboards should be creative and depicting what would be and could be! 

This is where you can GO WILD. Remember some of the greatest ideas came through seemingly impossible solutions!

workshops.Workshop Brief: This workshop produces a Storyboard, a comic-strip-style visualization of a user's experience in context. Its four elements (character, scene, plot, narrative) help the team imagine the real situation around a product, not just its screens, sparking more human design ideas.

workshops.Workshop Name: Audience Segmentation, Goals, Motivations, and Use Cases Workshop Template
workshops.Workshop Summary: To properly understand how you should be solving problems for your audiences, teams need to work to understand the day in the life of users. This happens in a variety of ways. It involves a lot of brainstorming, assumption mapping, and research to understand how to communicate goals and motivations of your audiences. Understanding how you want to describe your audience is up to you and the team and the clients involved. You can use Segmentation to describe your audiences from different perspectives: where they live, how they behave, their background, or their socioeconomic status. From there, you can work together to identify the motivations and goals that audiences have, and what kinds of segments are the most valuable to focus on for the business. This workshop helps teams brainstorm about the segmented traits of potential audiences, and communicate what they care about to gain a common understanding.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Build semantic labels around audience segments.
Agree to the audience segment descriptions your team wants to align on.
Brainstorm motivations, goals, and scenarios to support that will be important to audience segments.
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Identify potential traits of segments based on:
2. Geography
3. Behavior
4. Demographics
5. Socioeconomic status
6. Pick the most impactful traits and describe your audiences you want to focus on.
7. Identify the motivations of the audience segment.
8. Identify the situational goals and life goals that audience segment has in the end-to-end experience.
9. Identify the use case scenarios that are the most impactful to support for each audience segment.
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
The team can align with clients, stakeholders, and each other about the areas of focus that will bring the most value to audiences based on how they describe the audiences.
The team can base the user research, market research, and implementation of designs based on what they define for segmentation.
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Do this during discovery, then update it as research teaches you more about your audiences.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?: The Product Manager hat owns the audience segmentation that should be focused on. As teams do more research over time, the segmentation of audiences changes and evolves. The product manager hat maintains the definitions of target audience segments over time.
workshops.Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Buyer Personas and Customer Segmentation.
workshops.Additional Details: When to use: during discovery, after sprints begin, when the team is deciding who to build for.
workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: A workshop where the team labels and describes its target audiences by segment, then digs into each one's motivations, goals, and the use cases worth supporting.
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: Bring the team and whatever you know about your audiences. Set up the FigJam board with the segmentation fields (geographic, behavioral, demographic, socioeconomic) and the per-audience motivation, goals, and use-case sections. Best early in discovery; owned by the Product Manager hat.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What segment traits (geographic, behavioral, demographic, socioeconomic) describe our audiences?
2. Which traits matter most, and how do we label our focus audiences?
3. What motivates each audience, and what are their situational and life goals?
4. Which use case scenarios are most impactful to support?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with labeled audience segments, each with its motivations, situational and life goals, and a prioritized set of use cases to support. Done well, the team, clients, and stakeholders share one language for who you serve and why.
workshops.Time Needed: A focused session, then refined through research
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: Segments are often guesses at first; document them and refine with research. Pick the most impactful traits rather than trying to capture everything. And prioritize the use cases so you focus on what brings the most value.
workshops.Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam; the Product Manager maintains it as segments evolve.

  How does anyone know which work to decide, or which features to include, or which research to do first? YOU DON’T! You make the best judgment you have at the time and build consensus with the team to decide. Using tools like a prioritization matrix helps you decide quickly based on categories that matter to you. This workshop builds a templated process for a team to prioritize work based on risk and certainty, or effort and value, using what’s called a “MOSCOW” Matrix (which stands for Must, Should, Could, Won’t)

workshops.Workshop Summary: All great case studies have great stories to tell. People in the fields of product management, project management, UX, or other related fields always need to describe the story of humans that are affected by changes that get made. This workshop helps teams concretely tie project deliverables to case study components based on empowered teamwork and self-organized thinking principles.

2. Map project deliverables to case study outcomes
3. Learn about story arcs
4. Learn about the attributes of a great case study

workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?: This is valuable because it helps individuals who are a part of teamwork see how other kinds of work affects their own success story and case study. It sets expectations for teams about how to be cross-functional in order to share your success at the end in concrete ways.
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Use this at any point in a project, and again near the end when people are ready to write up their work. It helps to start collecting the story early.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?: The whole team owns this outcome together! You all work together across different kinds of work to share the outcomes of a case study.
workshops.Additional Details: When to use: any time, and especially near the end of a phase when people build their portfolios.
workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: A reflection workshop that prepares each teammate to build a strong case study, the story of their growth and work on the project, by planning for it from the start rather than scrambling at the end.
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: Bring the team and your understanding of the project's deliverables and milestones. Set up FigJam with the reflection prompts and the story-driven outline. Best done early, so the team sets the project up to produce good case studies.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What makes a good case study, and what makes a bad one?
2. What must the team do, and what events must happen, to produce a great one?
3. How will we work with other teams to produce it?
4. What is the story-driven outline of our case study?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with a shared understanding of what a strong case study is and a story-driven outline, plus a plan for the events and collaboration that produce one. Done well, the team sets itself up to tell the story of its growth, not just list deliverables.
workshops.Time Needed: A focused reflection session
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: A great case study tells the story of your growth and process, not just the artifacts you made. Plan for it during the project (capture events, collaboration, and decisions), not after. And it takes cross-team collaboration to produce, so set that up early.

# How to Create a Great Case Study from Any Work!
  How to Create a Great Case Study from Any Work!
  Case studies are crucial for telling your story about how your team collaborated together. Case studies are so challenging because it’s hard to know what information to share, and how to condense it in a compelling manner. You have to tell the story in such a way that keeps the audiences’ attention. This is where you can put on your User Experience hat! They should showcase meaningful problem-solving and concrete outcomes. Really great case studies don’t have a “perfect ending”, just like really great stories may not have a “perfect ending”.  The work will never stop,  you are possibly presenting a small piece of work on a short timeline that will continue after. It probably started before you joined the team too. You still need to showcase impact and progress in your team’s work.
  You Can Tell the Story from Your Timeline
  Although there was work before you started, and there will be work after you stopped, you can still tell a meaningful story. You’ve contributed to a better holistic outcome of progress. You’ve contributed toward solving problems with teams. Your perspective was valuable and should be showcased. You can speak about how you would measure impact or value once the problem is solved even if that’s years from now.
  The previous team’s work
  Your work
  The next team’s work
  Good Case Studies Have...
  A Story Arc
  Everyone loves a great story. There are different ways to tell it, but it should start with some kind of problem and show how it progressed. Try to avoid describing “multiple events” like if you were describing how it all happened. Take the readers there. Envelop them into the story itself, relive the story through the case study with them. There are way to structure a story called “Arcs”, and this template focuses on the arc that depicts three parts: problem, journey, progress.
  Measurable Concrete Outcomes
  You may have heard the phrase “Do the work with the end in mind”. While visuals can be key to showing how the work happened, it’s not enough to add a lot of pictures of your interface designs or produced results. Showing how you measured success, or how you would measure success, is the most important part of showing the work. You can do this in a lot of ways. If you were not in the position to actually measure change, you should show how you would measure change so that readers can see your thought process. Doing this will highlight the potential impact of your decisions as a team.
  A Focus on The “Why”
  Focusing on the reasoning and “why” behind your design decisions in a UX case study is crucial because it reveals your problem-solving mindset and critical thinking skills. Employers and stakeholders aren't just interested in what you designed. They want to understand the logic, research, and trade-offs that guided each choice. By articulating the “why,” you demonstrate that your design isn’t arbitrary or based on trends, but grounded in user needs, business goals, and usability principles. This level of insight differentiates you from others who simply showcase visuals, highlighting your ability to think strategically and collaborate effectively within cross-functional teams.
  User Audience Perspective
  This will ground your work in real human needs and context. UX is not a creative field. UX is an applied science field. We follow the scientific method to test hypotheses. Our product decisions are hypotheses, and we need to show how we tested them. We need to show the data that helped us form the hypotheses. All adjacent roles should follow this structure too. Product owners, business analysts, product designers, UX designers, UX researchers: you also need to showcase user perspective about the problems you are solving. Whatever title you are after, your case study should tell the story about the current state, and how you strategized to make the current state different.
  Conflict to Resolve
  The conflict you resolve could be the user pain points, conflict within the team, or both. Your audiences don’t want to see that you did this work alone. They want to see how your team pulled together to tackle the conflict. They want to see how you progressed through adversity and changing winds. This is an understated strength of teamwork when people face conflict and resolve it to grow together. Discuss in your case study how you grew through the conflict, and how your team and outcomes grew through the conflict.
  Cross-Functional Collaboration
  UX and product work often happens in a team, and sometimes teams isolate themselves based on a department. Employers value designers who can collaborate effectively and contribute to a shared vision, not just produce individual work in a vacuum. Employers who run agile teams want to see your cross-functional collaboration skills meaning how you worked together as a unified team across all kinds of work functions to accomplish an outcome. This is easier said than done. It relies on you to understand the overarching project plan and the work that others did. It relies on you as a teammate getting involved in other work functions so you can tell the story of the context. Showcasing how you worked within a team highlights your communication skills, adaptability, and ability to integrate diverse perspectives into your design process
