# A Focus on The “Why”
  A Focus on The “Why”
  Focusing on the reasoning and “why” behind your design decisions in a UX case study is crucial because it reveals your problem-solving mindset and critical thinking skills. Employers and stakeholders aren't just interested in what you designed. They want to understand the logic, research, and trade-offs that guided each choice. By articulating the “why,” you demonstrate that your design isn’t arbitrary or based on trends, but grounded in user needs, business goals, and usability principles. This level of insight differentiates you from others who simply showcase visuals, highlighting your ability to think strategically and collaborate effectively within cross-functional teams.
  What problems did you assume, and explore?
  What did you learn about the problems in the current state?
  What use cases and common tasks are very important to users you’re designing for?

# User Audience Perspective
  User Audience Perspective
  This will ground your work in real human needs and context. UX is not a creative field. UX is an applied science field. We follow the scientific method to test hypotheses. Our product decisions are hypotheses, and we need to show how we tested them. We need to show the data that helped us form the hypotheses. All adjacent roles should follow this structure too. Product owners, business analysts, product designers, UX designers, UX researchers: you also need to showcase user perspective about the problems you are solving. Whatever title you are after, your case study should tell the story about the current state, and how you strategized to make the current state different.

This is an understated strength of teamwork when people face conflict and resolve it to grow together. workshops.Workshop Brief: This workshop does not produce a project deliverable; it prepares each teammate's case study, the story of the growth and work they did on the project. It grounds a strong portfolio piece in the real outcomes, collaboration, and process of the work.

workshops.Workshop Summary:
This is a continuation of the UX Research Test Plan Workshop.

UX is a scientific field! We UX’ers follow the Scientific Method in our work. We pose hypotheses and build tests to test the hypothesis. They are either true or false. Sometimes, the results are undetermined.

In the context of Agile UX, UX’ers finish one single round of research in a short period of time known as “an iteration”. This could be one week, or two weeks, based on the Agile Method you are following.

This training framework provides a way to follow a repeated cycle of mapping questions and hypotheses to assumptions and points of measurement for the purposes of building a research test. In this workshop, results from research are analyzed based on assumptions.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Analyze research results based on theme.
Form conclusions from research data.
Determine whether assumptions were true, false, or undetermined.
Identify the next priorities for research based on latest test results.
Present summarized results to other kinds of stakeholders.
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Run the research through the UX Research Test Plan Workshop.
2. Create an affinity map of the results
3. Create the conclusions table
4. Form summarized results to present to stakeholders
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
This research analysis framework is valuable because it allows teams to analyze their assumptions and present key takeaways.
This helps teams always map their research to an assumption or a research question for better organization.
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Do this after each round of research, usually once a sprint, so findings turn into decisions while they are fresh.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?: The UX Research function and UX Strategy function owns this deliverable. Whomever is working in this function should collaborate with other functions to collect necessary input about assumptions or priorities before deciding how to proceed with the research analysis.
workshops.Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its UX Audit Report, Research Report, Rainbow Table, Affinity Map, and Research Analysis.
workshops.Additional Details:
Where to keep it:
Keep it in Figjam, or some other place where you can keep it over time

How to involve other teams:
Researchers should collaborate with all other team functions including product people, UX designers, and even developers in their research analysis. This provides space for all cross-functional teammates to get involved directly in the results of research before it’s presented to them, and provides ways for other perspectives to be heard.
workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: The after-the-test workshop where a team turns raw research results into clear themes, conclusions about each assumption, and the next research questions, run every sprint.
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: Bring the UX Research and UX Strategy leads (with the whole team's input) and your completed test results from the Research Plan workshop. Set up FigJam with the results tables, an affinity-map space, and the assumption-conclusion table. Do this every sprint after testing.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What were the raw results of each question, task, and observation?
2. What themes emerge across them?
3. For each assumption, was it true, false, or undetermined?
4. What new research questions has this raised?
5. What do we research next?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with documented results, an affinity map of themes, a conclusion for every assumption, and a prioritized set of new research questions. Done well, the analysis clearly says what you learned and what to explore next, and the cycle continues.
workshops.Time Needed: A focused session each sprint after testing
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: Separate what people said from what they did; observations often matter more than statements. Conclude honestly, including 'undetermined.' And always form new assumptions and questions, since research never stops in agile.
workshops.Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam; it feeds the next Research Plan iteration.

# ABOUT MARKET RESEARCH
  ABOUT MARKET RESEARCH
  Market research is when you collect information about people who might use your product like what they want, what they buy, and what problems they have. This helps teams build something they actually care about. 

Product managers do market research early in discovery so they don’t waste time or money making something no one wants. It helps them understand the market, define a clear vision, and make smarter decisions from day one.

Market research includes:
Market segments: These are the different groups of people in the market, like teenagers who game, college students who love coffee, or parents who need help with homework apps. Segmenting helps you figure out exactly who you’re building for.
Market size: This tells you how many people are in each segment and how much money they might spend. A big market size means more potential customers and more money to be made.
Market opportunity: This is where you spot a gap, something people want but aren’t getting. If your research shows that gamers want a social app with fewer ads and there’s nothing like that, that’s a clear opportunity.

How it affects the product vision:
Market research shapes the product’s purpose and direction. For example, if you find that students want a fast, ad-free study app, the product vision might be: “The most focused and ad-free homework helper for high school students.” Every decision going forward is based on that vision.

How to perform market research:
Identify the possible market segments in the same space as your product or service.
Identify the size of each market segment in market cap.
Identify the opportunities that exist in the markets so that you can build the best opportunity for the market and your business.

# ABOUT COMPETITOR ANALYSIS
  ABOUT COMPETITOR ANALYSIS
  Direct and indirect competitor analysis is when you study businesses or products that are either exactly like yours (direct competitors) or similar but not the same (indirect competitors). This analysis helps define what makes your product unique and how it can stand out.

For product managers, doing this analysis early in the discovery phase is important because it helps them understand the competition, know what features customers are used to, and identify any gaps in the market. This analysis affects the product vision by showing where there’s room to stand out. 

To do a direct and indirect competitor analysis:
Identify the questions you want to answer about competitors unique to your project
Identify the direct competitors in the market segment
Analyze their strengths and weaknesses: What do they do well? What are they missing?
Identify opportunities: Look for features or needs that are unmet, and think about how your product can fill that gap.

# ABOUT DESIGN PATTERN ANALYSIS
  ABOUT DESIGN PATTERN ANALYSIS
  Design pattern analysis is when product designers study how other apps or websites are built—like how buttons look, how menus open, or how people sign up—to see what works well and what users are already used to. It’s kind of like looking at how popular games design their controls so yours feels familiar and easy to use.

Doing this early in discovery is important because it helps designers make smarter choices before they start building. It saves time, avoids confusing users, and keeps the product feeling modern and simple. It also helps shape the product vision—if the vision is to be “the easiest budgeting app for teens,” then the design patterns should support simplicity, clarity, and fun. This helps create a product that looks good, works well, and feels just right for the people using it.

How to do a design pattern analysis:
Choose similar products: Look at apps or websites that solve the same problem.
Study their design patterns: Notice how they handle navigation, buttons, forms, layouts, and colors.
Compare the patterns: What’s common across all of them? What feels easy or hard?
Decide what to use or improve: Keep the helpful patterns and change or improve anything that seems confusing or outdated.

# ABOUT FEATURE ANALYSIS
  ABOUT FEATURE ANALYSIS
  Feature comparison analysis is when you look at your product and compare its features to other similar products on the market. 

Product managers do this early in discovery to understand what competitors offer, what customers like or don’t like, and what’s missing. It helps them avoid building something that’s already out there and instead focus on features that are better, different, or more valuable.

This analysis shapes the product vision by showing where the biggest opportunities are—like if all music apps have ads, maybe the vision becomes “the best free, ad-free music experience.” It helps define what makes the product special and worth building.

To do a feature comparison analysis:
Pick your direct and indirect competitors (see competitor analysis)
List their features. What does each one offer?
Compare them side by side. Use a table or chart to see what's common, what's unique, and what's missing.
Describe the feature-related gaps or opportunities. Look for features people want but no one offers well.

# ABOUT PRODUCT POSITIONING
  ABOUT PRODUCT POSITIONING
  Product positioning is a way to describe how you will approach describing your product. This includes how you make people see and understand what your product is, who it’s for, and why it’s better or different from others. Think of it like giving your product a “personality” and a spot in the customer’s mind—like “the fastest sports drink for teen athletes” or “the easiest music app for beginners.”

Product managers figure this out early during discovery so they can build a product that connects with the right audience. If you don’t know how to position your product, people might not understand why it matters, or it might seem just like everything else. It affects the product vision by helping define what the product will be known for and why it exists. 

To perform product positioning analysis:
Identify your target audience: Who is the product for?
Understand what your target audiences care about: What problems do they have? What do they value?
Compare with competitors: What are other products known for?
Find your unique spot: What makes your product different or better from competitors?
Write a product positioning statement.

# ABOUT COMPETITOR ANALYSIS
  ABOUT COMPETITOR ANALYSIS
  Direct and indirect competitor analysis is when you study businesses or products that are either exactly like yours (direct competitors) or similar but not the same (indirect competitors). This analysis helps define what makes your product unique and how it can stand out.

For product managers, doing this analysis early in the discovery phase is important because it helps them understand the competition, know what features customers are used to, and identify any gaps in the market. This analysis affects the product vision by showing where there’s room to stand out. 

To do a direct and indirect competitor analysis:
Identify the questions you want to answer about competitors unique to your project
Identify the direct competitors in the market segment
Analyze their strengths and weaknesses: What do they do well? What are they missing?
Identify opportunities: Look for features or needs that are unmet, and think about how your product can fill that gap.

# ABOUT FEATURE ANALYSIS
  ABOUT FEATURE ANALYSIS
  Feature comparison analysis is when you look at your product and compare its features to other similar products on the market. 

Product managers do this early in discovery to understand what competitors offer, what customers like or don’t like, and what’s missing. It helps them avoid building something that’s already out there and instead focus on features that are better, different, or more valuable.

This analysis shapes the product vision by showing where the biggest opportunities are—like if all music apps have ads, maybe the vision becomes “the best free, ad-free music experience.” It helps define what makes the product special and worth building.

To do a feature comparison analysis:
Pick your direct and indirect competitors (see competitor analysis)
List their features. What does each one offer?
Compare them side by side. Use a table or chart to see what's common, what's unique, and what's missing.
Describe the feature-related gaps or opportunities. Look for features people want but no one offers well.

# ABOUT DESIGN PATTERN ANALYSIS
  ABOUT DESIGN PATTERN ANALYSIS
  Design pattern analysis is when product designers study how other apps or websites are built—like how buttons look, how menus open, or how people sign up—to see what works well and what users are already used to. It’s kind of like looking at how popular games design their controls so yours feels familiar and easy to use.

Doing this early in discovery is important because it helps designers make smarter choices before they start building. It saves time, avoids confusing users, and keeps the product feeling modern and simple. It also helps shape the product vision—if the vision is to be “the easiest budgeting app for teens,” then the design patterns should support simplicity, clarity, and fun. This helps create a product that looks good, works well, and feels just right for the people using it.

How to do a design pattern analysis:
Choose similar products: Look at apps or websites that solve the same problem.
Study their design patterns: Notice how they handle navigation, buttons, forms, layouts, and colors.
Compare the patterns: What’s common across all of them? What feels easy or hard?
Decide what to use or improve: Keep the helpful patterns and change or improve anything that seems confusing or outdated.

# ABOUT PRODUCT POSITIONING
  ABOUT PRODUCT POSITIONING
  Product positioning is a way to describe how you will approach describing your product. This includes how you make people see and understand what your product is, who it’s for, and why it’s better or different from others. Think of it like giving your product a “personality” and a spot in the customer’s mind—like “the fastest sports drink for teen athletes” or “the easiest music app for beginners.”

Product managers figure this out early during discovery so they can build a product that connects with the right audience. If you don’t know how to position your product, people might not understand why it matters, or it might seem just like everything else. It affects the product vision by helping define what the product will be known for and why it exists. 

To perform product positioning analysis:
Identify your target audience: Who is the product for?
Understand what your target audiences care about: What problems do they have? What do they value?
Compare with competitors: What are other products known for?
Find your unique spot: What makes your product different or better from competitors?
Write a product positioning statement.

workshops.Workshop Brief: This workshop grounds a team in its market and turns that understanding into a sharp story, producing five connected outputs. A competitive analysis studies a handful of direct competitors (and a couple of indirect ones) across usability, features, and value to find gaps worth filling. A market research analysis pulls together data on market size, customers, and trends so big bets rest on evidence, not hunches. From that, the team writes a positioning statement, an internal compass of how the product is different and for whom (For [target], [product] is the [difference] among [category] because [reason]), and a unique value proposition, the sharper, customer-facing sentence of the single main benefit. Finally, product-market fit gets judged; it is less a single number and more a set of signals, like whether people are using the product as fast as you can ship it and whether word of mouth is spreading (a common check is Sean Ellis's rule that 40 percent of users would be "very disappointed" to lose it). Together these move a team from "we think there's a market" to a clear, defensible story about who the product is for and why it wins.

workshops.Workshop Summary: A customer experience map is an essential piece of documenting the current and future customer experience for different audiences. It’s a great communication tool for teams to help others build empathy and understand how things work today for user audiences. This workshop helps teams create customer experience maps. It explains the difference between user journey maps and Customer Experience Maps, which are similar but different deliverables for different purposes. Both work together to help teams communicate the current experience and the future experience.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Map each step in the experience for each audience
Identify pain points in each step of the experience for each audience
Strategize around how to change the current experience based on pain points and business goals.
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Map the current customer experience in a flow chart for each audience
2. Identify pain points, ideas, and questions in the flow charts
3. Map the future customer experience in a flow chart for each audience
4. Outline how the experience will work through the customer lifecycle funnel: awareness, engagement, consideration, conversion, retention, and loyalty.
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
A customer experience map is valuable because it:

Aligns teams in understanding the current steps in the experience for each audience today
Helps teams see where pain points are introduced in the experience
Helps teams build empathy with users about the current experience and user audiences
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Your team doesn’t just produce a customer experience map once. As they proceed through continuous discovery, they should come back to the customer experience maps and update them as they learn new things about the experience today and plan the experience for the future.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?:
The UX functions on the team own the customer experience maps (UX research, UX design, UX strategy, UX writing). They must:

Draft the first customer experience map iteration
Collect other teams’ thoughts on what needs to be included
Collect stakeholder thoughts on what needs to be included
Collect user thoughts on what needs to be included
Iterate on the customer experience maps as they learn from continuous discovery
workshops.Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Customer Experience Diagram.
workshops.Additional Details:
When to use:
Teams should produce the initial customer experience map during discovery, and they should never stop updating the customer experience maps after each round of research. They should utilize continuous discovery to keep learning about the customer experience map and keep documenting it over time.

Where to keep it:
The customer experience maps should be kept and maintained in Figjam or some other place where it can be quickly edited.

How to involve other teams:
All teammates across all functions should collaborate together to produce the customer experience maps. All perspectives should be heard and collaborate together.
workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: A cross-functional workshop that maps each audience's current and future experience as a flow chart through the customer lifecycle funnel, surfacing pain points and the strategies to fix them.
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: Bring the whole team and your discovery work: personas, empathy maps, and research. Set up the FigJam board with the funnel stages (awareness, engagement, consideration, conversion, retention, loyalty) and the color legend. This works best after personas and empathy maps.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What are the steps in each audience's current experience, funnel stage by funnel stage?
2. Where are the pain points, ideas, and open questions?
3. What should the future experience look like?
4. What strategies would solve the current pain points?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with current and future experience flow charts for each audience, pain points and strategies marked, mapped across the whole customer lifecycle funnel. Done well, the team shares a clear picture of how things work today and a plan for how they should work.
workshops.Time Needed: A substantial session, then updated through discovery
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: Do not confuse this with a user journey map. A CX map is a flow chart across the whole funnel for all audiences; a journey map is a table for a single audience. Use the color legend (red = pain, yellow = idea, blue = question, green = strategy). And never call it done; update it through continuous discovery.
workshops.Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam and update it after each round of research.

# Current User Journey Map
  Current User Journeys
  We will document the current customer experience for each audience to define the current sentiments and opportunities. In the table below, write as many details as you know about the current experience. Complete the table to outline all of the steps, actions, and details involved in the current experience today. Be sure you cover all of the parts of the “customer lifecycle funnel”: Awareness, Consideration, Engagement, Conversion, Retention, and Loyalty.

  # Section 3
    Awareness
The awareness stage is the most vital stage, as it’s the start of the customer journey. In the awareness stage, prospects and leads will be made aware of your brand. 
The idea here is simple. The customer has an issue, want, or need, and your brand is presented as a solution — nothing more, nothing less. You want to get them thinking about your brand, product, or service. This is usually done through some strategically placed ads or organic campaigns that bring top-of-the-funnel traffic.
    Credit: https://encharge.io/customer-lifecycle-marketing/
    Engagement
Let’s assume you run a real estate agency. Whenever someone makes a big purchase, they tend to reach out and voluntarily engage with the brand before following through with a conversion. Maybe the lead will follow you on social media, schedule a consultation, or even send an email asking some questions. 

You can see how making this effort beforehand is necessary for a larger purchase. However, it’s not always considered a part of the customer lifecycle with everyday purchases like an in-store product or a subscription to a company like Netflix. 

Put in other words, if you run a B2B business, you most likely will need to include this stage as a part of your customer lifecycle, but that might not be the case if you are in the B2C space.
    Consideration
Now it’s time to really show the lead what you’re made of. The consideration stage is where they will take everything they’ve learned and evaluate which brand best suits their needs. The goal here is to nurture your leads and constantly but subtly remind them that you’re the best option. Typically, this is considered the middle of the funnel.

There are a few ways to go about this, but leads in this stage must be handled with care. One wrong move on your part, missed opening, or even poorly worded message can send the lead marching in the opposite direction.
To avoid that, here are some questions that your messaging should be answering for leads in this stage:
What is unique about your product?
What specific features set you apart from the rest?
What can you add to sweeten the deal and outshine your competition?

Here, it’s all about pushing the lead to pull the trigger. For a lot of brands, that means bringing out the big guns and doing whatever it takes. But, at this point in the funnel, your advertising strategy can either make or break you. This goes back to what we were saying before and understanding your customers through-and-through. Knowing precisely what leads need to see at this stage can end up saving you some big bucks in ad spend.
    Conversion
Congratulations! You’ve just made another sale and gained a new customer. Your job is done. Or is it? 
In truth, the battle is only half-won at this point. Sure, you made a sale, and (hopefully!) your profit margins have gone up, but it’s not exactly over.
You still have to prove that what you’ve provided for the customer is valuable for them. After all, your customers are not just another dollar sign in the company’s bank account. You’ve started a relationship with this customer, and you need to make sure it stays strong.
How’s that done? 
Well, for a lot of companies, the end goal is always conversion. Although that’s not entirely wrong, you still have to think about a few things to knock off the customers’ socks. 
Things like:
How can you make the onboarding process as quick, easy, and enjoyable as possible?
How can you structure this relationship so that the customer can potentially make another purchase?
How can you improve the relationship and the customer’s experience with your product/service by upselling? (Keep in mind, this is not as simple as suggesting a more expensive option).
    Retention
The journey doesn’t end with a conversion. Conversion simply opens up the door to more possibilities. 

This all narrows down to retention, how you treat the customer after the sale, and what you plan on doing to maintain that relationship.

Car salespeople do a great job at this, and it’s worth taking a chapter or two from their book. If you’ve ever bought a car from a car lot, think about your experience there. Sure, there will be some horror stories, but the vast majority of people always mention the high level of service. Using the 3 points above, let’s think about how a good car salesman executes them.

They always show you all odds and ends of the car, showcasing all the cool gadgets and features that you’ll get to enjoy.
The salesman always makes sure you know their name, gives you their card and becomes your best friend on that lot. This ensures that you’ll think of them next time you want to buy a car or suggest where to buy a car to friends or family.
A large majority of a car salesman’s job is making calls to previous customers and telling them about the new offers, trade-in deals, and end-of-the-year sales they have so that they can get more money out of you. If the experience is good the first time, why wouldn’t you want to buy a better car from a great salesman?

That might be a lot of information for a single point, but it’s all to prove that the funnel stages don’t necessarily stop with a conversion.
    Loyalty
We’ve all heard it before. Companies thank their “loyal customers” and offer them the best of what they have to offer. Why?
 
The simple answer is that a loyal customer, one that has stuck with your brand, made several purchases, and gotten to know you as much as you have gotten to know them, is not just a customer anymore. They are brand advocates.

It means that you have someone that bleeds your brand colors, someone who would readily recommend you to friends and family, and someone that brings your company value in more ways than just money.

Customer lifecycle marketing is tricky at this point because you have to put in a ton of effort to get a customer to this stage. Few people will reach this point of the funnel, but that’s nothing to be upset about. They made it here because they’re fans of your brand. That means that their contributions need to be recognized, and they need to be treated like royalty.

workshops.Workshop Brief: This workshop produces the Customer Experience Diagram, a flow chart of an audience's end-to-end experience across the lifecycle funnel (awareness through loyalty). It is distinct from a user journey map (a single-audience table); the CX map is broader, showing all audiences and touchpoints.

workshops.Workshop Summary: A user journey map is an essential piece of documenting the current experience for different audiences. It’s a great communication tool for teams to help others build empathy and understand how things work today for user audiences. This workshop helps teams create user journey maps. It explains the difference between user journey maps and Customer Experience Maps, which are similar but different deliverables for different purposes. Both work together to help teams communicate the current experience.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Map each step in the experience for each audience
Identify pain points in each step of the experience for each audience
Identify sentiments about each step for each audience
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Produce one journey map per audience
2. Identify the steps involved in the current experience for each audience
3. Identify the common tasks and common audiences involved per step
4. Identify the sentiment at each step
5. Identify the KPI’s for each step
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
A journey map is valuable because it:

Aligns teams in understanding the current steps in the experience for each audience today
Helps teams see where pain points are introduced in the experience
Helps teams build empathy with users about the current experience and user audiences
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Your team doesn’t just produce a user journey map once. As they proceed through continuous discovery, they should come back to the user journey maps and update them as they learn new things about the experience today.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?:
The UX functions on the team own the user journey maps (UX research, UX design, UX strategy, UX writing). They must:

Draft the first journey map iteration
Collect other teams’ thoughts on what needs to be included
Collect stakeholder thoughts on what needs to be included
Collect user thoughts on what needs to be included
Iterate on the user journey maps as they learn from continuous discovery
workshops.Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its User Journey Map.
workshops.Additional Details:
When to use:
Teams should produce the initial journey map during discovery, and they should never stop updating the journey map after each round of research. They should utilize continuous discovery to keep learning about the journey and keep documenting it over time.

Where to keep it:
The user journey map should be kept and maintained in Figjam or some other place where it can be quickly edited.

How to involve other teams:
All teammates across all functions should collaborate together to produce the user journey maps. All perspectives should be heard and collaborate together.
workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: A workshop that lays out a single audience's journey as a table, step by step through the customer lifecycle funnel, capturing their tasks, feelings, pain points, and success measures.
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: Bring the team and your discovery work: personas, empathy maps, use case scenarios, and research. Set up the FigJam board with the journey table and the funnel stages. This works best during discovery, after personas and empathy maps.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering:
For a single audience:
1. What steps do they go through, and which funnel stage does each belong to?
2. What tasks and pain points happen at each step?
3. How do they feel at each step?
4. What KPIs would measure success, and what ideas could improve it?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with a journey table for the audience: each step tagged to a funnel stage, with description, tasks, pain points, sentiment, KPIs, and improvement ideas. Done well, it reads like a narrative of one real person's experience.
workshops.Time Needed: A focused session per audience, then updated through discovery
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: A journey map is for a single audience in a table, unlike the CX map's all-audience flow chart. Base the steps on real use case scenarios, and capture honest sentiment (the emoji scale) at each step. Update it as research evolves.
workshops.Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam and update it after research.

# Current User Journey Map
  Current User Journeys
  We will document the current customer experience for each audience to define the current sentiments and opportunities. In the table below, write as many details as you know about the current experience. Complete the table to outline all of the steps, actions, and details involved in the current experience today. Be sure you cover all of the parts of the “customer lifecycle funnel”: Awareness, Consideration, Engagement, Conversion, Retention, and Loyalty.

  # Section 3
    Awareness
The awareness stage is the most vital stage, as it’s the start of the customer journey. In the awareness stage, prospects and leads will be made aware of your brand. 
The idea here is simple. The customer has an issue, want, or need, and your brand is presented as a solution — nothing more, nothing less. You want to get them thinking about your brand, product, or service. This is usually done through some strategically placed ads or organic campaigns that bring top-of-the-funnel traffic.
    Credit: https://encharge.io/customer-lifecycle-marketing/
    Engagement
Let’s assume you run a real estate agency. Whenever someone makes a big purchase, they tend to reach out and voluntarily engage with the brand before following through with a conversion. Maybe the lead will follow you on social media, schedule a consultation, or even send an email asking some questions. 

You can see how making this effort beforehand is necessary for a larger purchase. However, it’s not always considered a part of the customer lifecycle with everyday purchases like an in-store product or a subscription to a company like Netflix. 

Put in other words, if you run a B2B business, you most likely will need to include this stage as a part of your customer lifecycle, but that might not be the case if you are in the B2C space.
    Consideration
Now it’s time to really show the lead what you’re made of. The consideration stage is where they will take everything they’ve learned and evaluate which brand best suits their needs. The goal here is to nurture your leads and constantly but subtly remind them that you’re the best option. Typically, this is considered the middle of the funnel.

There are a few ways to go about this, but leads in this stage must be handled with care. One wrong move on your part, missed opening, or even poorly worded message can send the lead marching in the opposite direction.
To avoid that, here are some questions that your messaging should be answering for leads in this stage:
What is unique about your product?
What specific features set you apart from the rest?
What can you add to sweeten the deal and outshine your competition?

Here, it’s all about pushing the lead to pull the trigger. For a lot of brands, that means bringing out the big guns and doing whatever it takes. But, at this point in the funnel, your advertising strategy can either make or break you. This goes back to what we were saying before and understanding your customers through-and-through. Knowing precisely what leads need to see at this stage can end up saving you some big bucks in ad spend.
    Conversion
Congratulations! You’ve just made another sale and gained a new customer. Your job is done. Or is it? 
In truth, the battle is only half-won at this point. Sure, you made a sale, and (hopefully!) your profit margins have gone up, but it’s not exactly over.
You still have to prove that what you’ve provided for the customer is valuable for them. After all, your customers are not just another dollar sign in the company’s bank account. You’ve started a relationship with this customer, and you need to make sure it stays strong.
How’s that done? 
Well, for a lot of companies, the end goal is always conversion. Although that’s not entirely wrong, you still have to think about a few things to knock off the customers’ socks. 
Things like:
How can you make the onboarding process as quick, easy, and enjoyable as possible?
How can you structure this relationship so that the customer can potentially make another purchase?
How can you improve the relationship and the customer’s experience with your product/service by upselling? (Keep in mind, this is not as simple as suggesting a more expensive option).
    Retention
The journey doesn’t end with a conversion. Conversion simply opens up the door to more possibilities. 

This all narrows down to retention, how you treat the customer after the sale, and what you plan on doing to maintain that relationship.

Car salespeople do a great job at this, and it’s worth taking a chapter or two from their book. If you’ve ever bought a car from a car lot, think about your experience there. Sure, there will be some horror stories, but the vast majority of people always mention the high level of service. Using the 3 points above, let’s think about how a good car salesman executes them.

They always show you all odds and ends of the car, showcasing all the cool gadgets and features that you’ll get to enjoy.
The salesman always makes sure you know their name, gives you their card and becomes your best friend on that lot. This ensures that you’ll think of them next time you want to buy a car or suggest where to buy a car to friends or family.
A large majority of a car salesman’s job is making calls to previous customers and telling them about the new offers, trade-in deals, and end-of-the-year sales they have so that they can get more money out of you. If the experience is good the first time, why wouldn’t you want to buy a better car from a great salesman?

That might be a lot of information for a single point, but it’s all to prove that the funnel stages don’t necessarily stop with a conversion.
    Loyalty
We’ve all heard it before. Companies thank their “loyal customers” and offer them the best of what they have to offer. Why?
 
The simple answer is that a loyal customer, one that has stuck with your brand, made several purchases, and gotten to know you as much as you have gotten to know them, is not just a customer anymore. They are brand advocates.

It means that you have someone that bleeds your brand colors, someone who would readily recommend you to friends and family, and someone that brings your company value in more ways than just money.

Customer lifecycle marketing is tricky at this point because you have to put in a ton of effort to get a customer to this stage. Few people will reach this point of the funnel, but that’s nothing to be upset about. They made it here because they’re fans of your brand. That means that their contributions need to be recognized, and they need to be treated like royalty.

workshops.Workshop Summary: How does anyone know which work to decide, or which features to include, or which research to do first? YOU DON’T! You make the best judgment you have at the time and build consensus with the team to decide. Using tools like a prioritization matrix helps you decide quickly based on categories that matter to you. This workshop builds a templated process for a team to prioritize work based on risk and certainty, or effort and value, using what’s called a “MOSCOW” Matrix (which stands for Must, Should, Could, Won’t)

Prioritize your work based on risk and certainty, or effort and value
Choose the top items to work on now vs. later

1. Add your work items in a common space together as a team
2. Choose whether you will prioritize based on:

4. Effort and value

workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?: A priority matrix is valuable because it helps teams quickly categorize work and choose the things they want to work on first.
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Use this whenever the team has more to do than it can handle and needs to decide what comes first. Revisit it as priorities change.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?: Everyone in all functions on cross-functional teams should be using prioritization matrices to decide their work items when they are uncertain about the path ahead.
workshops.Expected Outcomes:
A list of “backlogged” work
A list of the top priorities of work
workshops.Additional Details: When to use: during discovery, after sprints begin, any time the team needs to pick what to work on next.
workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: A team session that turns a messy pile of possible work into a clear, voted list of what to do next, using a simple priority matrix when the path ahead is uncertain.
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: Bring the whole cross-functional team and the work items or problems you're weighing (from discovery, requirements, or team ideas). Decide nothing yet; just gather them. Set up the FigJam board with the two priority matrices and the voting stars ready.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What work and future tasks can we identify as a team?
2. Will we prioritize by risk and certainty, or by effort and value?
3. Where does each item fall on the matrix?
4. Which items rise to the top once we vote?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with a backlog of identified work and a clear, voted set of top priorities for the next iteration. Done well, the team built the ranking together, so people trust and support the order even knowing it is a judgment call that may change.
workshops.Time Needed: About 45 to 60 minutes
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: Hold the board's honest point: no one truly knows the right order; it is a judgment call, and agile is built to adjust. Pick one lens (risk/certainty or effort/value), not both at once. Use more than one voting round if the top is not clear.
workshops.Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam or your backlog tool, and re-prioritize as you learn.

  How do you know which work to do first?

# Team Onboarding
  Team Onboarding
  Although this is not a milestone of product development, it’s a crucial first step to collaboration together. Teams need to get to know each other and build trust before they can produce actual work results. There should be a period of introducing each other before teams start doing work so that they know who they are working with and can understand difference in learning styles. It’s also important to map out the end goal in mind for an individual who’s on a team. The team onboarding period helps each person outline the end goals for themselves.

  One to two weeks

# Intake Milestone
  Intake Milestone
  During the intake milestone, teams compile the high level goals and anticipated deliverables for the project. They do not, however, create a contract that never changes. They work towards validating the assumptions and ideas that clients or teammates have after intake. Intake simply starts the organization of the work and collects information about the business needs from stakeholders’ perspectives.

Discovery findings help refine vision for products.

# Vision Milestone
  Vision Milestone
  Vision describes where a product is going, and is broken down by release. When forming an MVP vision, product teams seek to solve the most important problems in their problem space. They should define MVP's in such a way that they are able to learn from them and vet high risk items in their product plans early and often. The vision helps the team stay aligned or decide how to adjust where their product is going.

workshops.Workshop Brief: This is the master board that indexes all of Tech Fleet's agile workshop templates. It is a navigation hub rather than a single workshop with its own deliverable.

workshops.Workshop Summary: An audience persona represents traits about your audience. They help you team build for the needs of your audiences instead of building based on guess work. Personas don’t represent one person, but rather an entire audience, and should be generic to fit traits across all people within an audience. You do not need to know everything about your audience to create a persona! You can create a “proto-persona” full of guesses, and use it as a basis for assumption forming and assumption testing in UX work. The persona needs to be updated over time as you learn more about your audience.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Build empathy with the user base
Communicate your audiences’ perspectives
Communicate your audiences’ main goals
Communicate your audiences’ user-centered considerations like demographics and accessibility
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Identify your target audiences
2. Fill out the information for each audience:
3. Demographics
4. Where they go for information
5. Common tools
6. Accessibility needs
7. User goals
8. Motivations
9. Values
10. Pain points
11. Create a visual result of each audience persona based on the template provided
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
Audience personas are valuable because they:

Help teams understand the perspective and mental models of their audiences
Communicate the user-centered nature of user needs by way of appealing to the user perspective and user behavior
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Teams should revisit the personas whenever they do research so that they can document the changes in their understanding about user behavior and user perspective.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?: The UX function owns this deliverable. This could be created by the UX research function, UX design function, UX writing function, or UX strategy function.
workshops.Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its User Personas, Proto Personas, and Buyer Personas.
workshops.Additional Details:
When to use:
Teams should first create audience personas during discovery, and continue iterating on them as they progress in continuous discovery efforts.

Where to keep it:
Keep this in Figma and Notion for project repository hand off.

How to involve other teams:
Every team function should be involved in this workshop. You need all of the cross-functional perspectives to weigh in on what they think about the user audience you are designing for.
workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: A workshop where the team builds a rich profile of each key audience, capturing who they are, what they need, and what gets in their way, so design decisions rest on real people.
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: Bring the whole cross-functional team and whatever you know or have researched about your audiences. Set up the FigJam board with a persona section to copy per audience. If research is thin, start with proto-personas (best guesses) and refine as you learn.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering:
For each audience:
1. Who are they (demographics)?
2. Where do they go for information?
3. What accessibility and social considerations apply?
4. What tools do they use today?
5. What are their life and situational goals?
6. What motivates them?
7. What are their common tasks?
8. What are their pain points?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with a filled persona for each key audience, built from every function's input, with assumptions flagged for research. Done well, the personas feel like real people the team can design for, not vague labels.
workshops.Time Needed: About 15 to 20 minutes per audience
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: If you lack research, these are proto-personas (educated guesses); label them as such and validate later. Build them cross-functionally, and revisit as research changes your understanding. Where it matters, distinguish user personas (who uses it) from buyer personas (who decides to buy).
workshops.Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in Figma and Notion for the project repository hand-off.

workshops.Workshop Brief: This workshop builds shared understanding of a user, producing an empathy map and, alongside it, audience personas. An empathy map is a simple visualization of what a user says, thinks, does, and feels; the classic version (Dave Gray, refined by Nielsen Norman Group) uses those four quadrants. One thing to honor here: Tech Fleet's board uses a richer six-prompt, first-person version (I Think, I Act, I Feel, I Say, I Value, I'm Motivated By), so follow the board's six, not the classic four. The goal is the same either way: get everything the team knows or assumes about a user into one place so decisions rest on a shared picture instead of scattered opinions. A persona is a semi-fictional character standing in for a segment of users, and a buyer persona specifically represents the person who decides to purchase, who is not always the person who uses the product. Built from research, or as quick proto-personas when research is thin, these keep the team designing for real people rather than a vague "user."

workshops.Workshop Summary: This is a template slide deck built in Figma that cross-functional teams can use to provide results presentations for research as they continue doing discovery in their work.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Share research results in a clear, simple way
Help others understand what the team learned
Show what the team recommends doing next
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Copy the slide template
2. Make it your own content
3. Publish to the client
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?: Research only helps if people understand it. A clear presentation turns findings into decisions the whole team and stakeholders can act on.
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Use it after each round of research, when the team is ready to share results, usually once a sprint.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?: The UX Research function owns this workshop and is responsible for running it with the team.
workshops.Expected Outcomes:
Introduction
Background
Working assumptions
Research Goals
Research Questions
Top Conclusions
Full Results
Strategy Recommendations
Future Work Recommendations
workshops.Additional Details: When to use: after a round of research, when it is time to share results with the team or stakeholders.
workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: A workshop for turning analyzed research into a clear, honest presentation that helps the team and stakeholders understand what users need and decide what to do next.
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: Bring your completed research analysis (findings and conclusions) and the presentation slide template. Know your audience for the presentation (team, stakeholders, or client). Set up the slides with room for findings, conclusions, and recommendations.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What are the key findings, and what do they mean?
2. Who does the data represent, and what are its limits?
3. What should the team do about it?
4. What are the next steps?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with a presentation that conveys the key findings, their meaning, the data's limits, and clear, actionable recommendations. Done well, it builds empathy for users and aligns everyone on what to do next.
workshops.Time Needed: A focused session to build and present
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: Present truthfully and responsibly: say who the data represents and name its limitations. Lead with the findings and what they mean, not a dump of raw data. And translate findings into recommendations stakeholders can act on.
workshops.Where to Keep the Output: Keep the slides with your research deliverables.

workshops.Workshop Name: KPI Success Measurements Definition Workshop Template
workshops.Workshop Summary: It’s not enough to just perform agile product development work. How will a team know they have hit their mark? How will they know they have progressed in solving problems? The answer to this lies in Success measurements. Success measurements (otherwise known as Key Performance Indicators) are measurements that can be can be defined in a lot of ways. They relate to the problems that businesses focus on solving in a given release, and outline the steps for teams to measure their progress when they change and deliver results. This workshop outlines a framework for defining key performance indicators and measurements of success based on business goals and user audience pain points today.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Define measurements of success for the business based on business goals
Define ideas about how to collect measurements of success for users and the business
Define the measurements of success for each audience based on:
Key steps in their process today
Key goals and motivations for the audience
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Define the success measurements for the business:
2. Define business purpose
3. Define business goals
4. Define the success measurements related to the business goals
5. Define how your team will propose to collect success measurements that you define
6. Define the success measurements for each audience you consider to be target segments, and produce the following for each audience:
7. Relevant user goals
8. User motivations
9. User pain points
10. Steps in the process for the user today
11. Common user tasks today
12. Success measurements based on the steps in their process
13. Success measurements based on the goals that the user wants to achieve
14. Ways to collect the measurements of success
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
Defined KPI’s allows teams to focus on key strategic decisions in their product and service development that are always based on the problems and value to deliver.
Defined KPI’s help the business clearly state how they will know they have succeeded in their efforts.
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Teams must revisit this set of deliverables any time they have learned new information from previous discovery work or design work. Every phase in Tech Fleet, the “Intake” milestone produces the need to review a new set of KPI’s and success measurements.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?: The product manager owns the definitions of KPI’s and strategy for releases on a cross-functional agile team. They are the function who understands user and market needs, defines strategic releases, and plans their product or service to go to market through MVP and MMP lifecycles.
workshops.Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Key Performance Indicators (KPI's).
workshops.Additional Details:
Where to keep it:
House it with your vision and product strategy deliverables.
workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: A workshop that defines how the team will know it is succeeding, translating business goals and each audience's journey into concrete success measurements (KPIs) and ways to collect them.
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: Bring the team and your business goals from the client intake, plus any problem statements and customer-experience work. Set up the FigJam board with the business-measures section and a per-audience measures section. Owned by the Product Manager hat; revisited every phase at intake.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What is the business's purpose and goals?
2. How will we measure the business's success, and how will we collect it?
3. For each audience: what are their goals, pain points, motivations, common tasks, and steps today?
4. What success measurements fit each step and each outcome, and how will we collect them?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with success measurements for the business and for each audience, tied to real goals and steps, plus a plan to collect each one. Done well, the team can state clearly how it will know it has made progress.
workshops.Time Needed: A focused session, plus more time per audience
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: Good KPIs are specific, measurable, and tied to a goal, not vanity metrics. Base user measures on the actual steps and outcomes audiences care about. And revisit them every phase at intake, since goals shift.
workshops.Where to Keep the Output: House it with your vision and product-strategy deliverables.

workshops.Workshop Name: Product and Service Development Milestones for Different Types of Projects Workshop Template
workshops.Workshop Summary:
Product and Service Development Milestones for Different Types of Projects

Products aren’t just made from ideas. They take a lot of coordination, research, decisions, and negotiations to make happen. Teams must go through cycles to organize work and decide how to focus their efforts. There are specific deliverables that are involved in different types of projects across research, design, product, and development functions. This training shows the typical cross-functional deliverables set that exist, and how it translates to project phases in Tech Fleet.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Learn about the product development lifecycle
Understand how Agile work happens in parallel across different functions
Learn how work gets developed and designed for different project phases in Tech Fleet.
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Learn about the lifecycle to make products and services called the Agile Product and Service Development Lifecycle
2. Review the definitions of each milestone, or marker of progress, and learn about the deliverables involved in each milestone.
3. Review the typical types of projects that Tech Fleet takes on as an organization and what milestone deliverables will look like when we take on those kinds of projects.
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
The Agile product development lifecycle helps teams understand what they should be focusing on to enable releases.
Agile product development lifecycles help teams plan work over long-term.
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Use it at the start when planning a project, and as a reference any time the team needs to understand what comes next.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?:
The product manager owns the vision and scope of the release for a cross-functional agile team. They are the function who understands user and market needs, defines strategic releases, and plans their product or service to go to market through MVP and MMP lifecycles.



The product owner function owns the delivery of the product work on a cross-functional agile team. They are the function who owns product decisions, priorities, and backlog work towards MVP and MMP releases.
workshops.Additional Details: When to use: before sprints begin, when planning the shape of a project.
workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: A learning session that maps out the whole agile product and service development lifecycle, its milestones and deliverables, and how the work differs across Tech Fleet's project types.
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: Bring the whole team and the lifecycle diagram plus the deliverable and workshop references on the board. This is a training session, so come ready to read and discuss rather than produce a deliverable. Product managers and owners lead, since they own vision, scope, and delivery.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What is the agile product and service development lifecycle?
2. What does each milestone mean, and what deliverables belong to it?
3. Which workshops produce those deliverables?
4. How do the deliverables differ across project types (business strategy, website, service design)?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with a shared understanding of the lifecycle, its milestones and deliverables, the workshops that produce them, and how different project types shape the work. Done well, the team can see how their work ladders up to releases.
workshops.Time Needed: A learning session
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: The lifecycle is non-linear: milestones repeat and run in parallel, not in a straight line. Not every project does every milestone; discovery-only, discovery-plus-design, and full build differ. And teams reach MMP by shipping many MVPs along the way.

# Team Onboarding
  Team Onboarding
  Although this is not a milestone of product development, it’s a crucial first step to collaboration together. Teams need to get to know each other and build trust before they can produce actual work results. There should be a period of introducing each other before teams start doing work so that they know who they are working with and can understand difference in learning styles. It’s also important to map out the end goal in mind for an individual who’s on a team. The team onboarding period helps each person outline the end goals for themselves.

workshops.Workshop Name: Personal Growth Vision, Scope, and Roadmap Workshop Template
workshops.Workshop Summary:
Tech Fleet Personal Growth Roadmap

We all go through our own journey of growth and learning throughout our lives. Whether you are newly graduating from an education program or changing careers, we will never stop working on ourselves, our skills, our mindsets, and our growth. This is an individualized workshop for a person to run in order to build and maintain their own “vision” and “roadmap” for their own personal growth as a professional and a human.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Identify personal growth items you want to focus on related to:
Service leadership
Teamwork
Hard skills
Communication
Collaboration
Other soft skills
Prioritize the opportunities you want to focus on now and later.
Communicate the opportunities you identify as goals, value, unique advantage, and outcomes.
Develop a personal growth plan for the next year that you can maintain.
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Enter the components of personal growth you want to focus on for yourself
2. Your target audiences for personal growth
3. Your personal opportunities and problems for personal growth
4. Your goals for personal growth
5. Your value you bring to the world when you solve the problems you want to solve for personal growth
6. What makes you unique as an individual in the world compared to others and how you differentiate yourself
7. The barriers and risks that may get in your way to success in personal growth, and how you will mitigate them
8. The “costs” of money, time, and energy involved
9. Your KPI’s and measures of success for personal growth
10. Enter your scope of outcomes to achieve based on the problems you want to solve
11. Prioritize the problems in a priority matrix for yourself
12. Pick the most important 5 problems for you to work on near-term, and choose them for your “MVP #1 Release” for personal growth
13. Create vision boards for your own personal growth:
14. “MVP #1”, also known as “opportunities to work on right now”
15. “MMP”, also known as “opportunities to work on down the road”
16. Create epics and features for your roadmap
17. Compile your roadmap
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
A vision, scope, and roadmap for your own personal growth is valuable because:

It breaks down larger goals into smaller, more accomplishable results
It helps you communicate language around your goals, needs, value delivery, and action items.
It helps you determine what you should focus on now and later.
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: You should revisit the personal growth vision and roadmap on a regular basis. This will help you keep track of items you work on throughout the year and pivot when you need to.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?: You! This is for you to be able to keep track of goals and communicate them to others.
workshops.Expected Outcomes:
Personal growth problems and opportunities
Personal growth KPI’s
Personal growth vision
Personal growth scope of work
Personal growth epics
Personal growth roadmap
workshops.Additional Details:
Where to keep it:
Keep it in Figjam, or some other place where you can keep it over time
workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: An individual workshop where you build your own vision, scope, and roadmap for growing as a professional and a person, applying the product-development pattern to yourself.
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: This one is for you. Bring honest reflection and some quiet time. Set up FigJam with the vision components, priority matrix, vision boards, and roadmap. Revisit it regularly as you grow.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What is my 'why,' and what growth do I want (in leadership, teamwork, skills, communication)?
2. Which growth opportunities matter most now?
3. What is my near-term (MVP) and longer-term (MMP) growth vision?
4. What is my roadmap of epics, features, and tasks?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with a personal growth vision, a prioritized set of opportunities, and a roadmap you can maintain. Done well, it turns vague self-improvement into concrete, owned goals with a path.
workshops.Time Needed: A focused solo session, revisited regularly
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: Be honest about your growth areas; this is for you, so there is no reason to posture. Treat it as living; revisit and adjust it regularly. And prioritize a few things rather than trying to grow everything at once.
workshops.Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam; you own it and can share it with others.

It helps you determine what you should focus on now and later.

workshops.Workshop Name: Agile Team Maturity Measurements Workshop Template
workshops.Workshop Summary:
This helps self-organized Agile teams measure their own maturity in Agility, and how close they are to working efficiently together.

Agile maturity measurements help a self-organized team measure how agile their operations are. These are based on the different facets of the Agile Manifesto and the steps to create self-actualized agile teams.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Measure how Agile the team really is
Spot habits that are slowing the team down
Find areas to improve as a team
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Get together after every sprint
2. Hold a retrospective workshop
3. Hold the Agile Maturity measurements workshop to Measure how often a team:
4. Interacted with individuals to figure out work over making a perfect plan before starting work
5. Delivered working UX results to clients and to users to figure out their priorities through feedback
6. Collaborated with each other, with users, and with clients to define requirements over making contracted agreements.
7. Created a psychologically safe space for voices on the team
8. Acted as service leaders to each other (apprentices and co-leads)
9. Organized themselves and made their own governing decisions through consensus
10. Failed fast and continuously improved
11. Iterated on their value delivery
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
Measuring agile maturity is valuable because:

It helps a team self-heal when they are performing waterfall practices instead of agile practices.
It helps identify potential areas of improvement for team operations.
It creates a safe space for the team to hold psychological safety and be vulnerable with their potential issues as a team.
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Measure after every sprint, right after the retro, so the team can track how it is growing over time.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?: The Scrum Master function on a team owns this deliverable throughout a project.
workshops.Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Agile Maturity Measurements.
workshops.Additional Details:
When to use:
After every sprint, the team should get together to measure their agility.

Where to keep it:
This should be kept and maintained in Figjam or some other place where it can be quickly edited.

How to involve other teams:
Everyone on the team, including apprentices and co-leads, needs to participate in this activity because teams need voices from people doing day-to-day work. The team owns their own process and they must participate to feel the full stake of ownership in it.
workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: A quick, recurring self-check where the whole team rates how agile it really is across the tenets of strong agile teams, so it can self-correct and keep improving.
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: Bring the whole team, including apprentices and co-leads; every voice matters. Do it right after the sprint retrospective, every sprint. Set up the FigJam board with the 0-to-10 rating scales and space for reasons. The Scrum Master owns it.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering:
In the past sprint, how strongly did we show:
1. clarity,
2. psychological safety,
3. service leadership,
4. cross-functional teamwork,
5. teammate ownership, and
6. self-organization?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with the team's honest ratings across the agility dimensions, plus the reasons behind each score, feeding into retro action items. Done well, it surfaces where the team is slipping into waterfall habits so it can self-heal.
workshops.Time Needed: About 20 to 30 minutes after the retro
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: It only works if people are honest, so protect psychological safety; this is a safe space to be vulnerable. Treat maturity as a continuum, not pass or fail. And connect the scores to action items so the reflection changes something.
workshops.Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam alongside the retro.

# SPRINT RETROSPECTIVE INSTRUCTIONS
  SPRINT RETROSPECTIVE INSTRUCTIONS
  WHAT IS THIS?
  HOW TO GET STARTED
  A sprint retrospective is the most important meeting for a sprint team. The full team, all apprentices and co-leads, get together after every sprint and hold a safe space to reflect on their last sprint. They celebrate what went well and discuss what they want to improve about their own process together.
  Get together after every sprint
Part 1: what did you like, what did you learn, what did you lack, and what did you long for? 
Part 2: Identify action items for how to change process on the team, and brainstorm together about how to change it, and assign the person who’s going to own the outcomes of the changes (it could be anyone on the team)

It allows room for people to speak freely about what process changes they want to make

# AGILE MATURITY MEASUREMENT INSTRUCTIONS
  AGILE MATURITY MEASUREMENT INSTRUCTIONS
  WHAT IS THIS?
  HOW TO RUN THE WORKSHOP
  Agile maturity measurements help a self-organized team measure how agile their operations are. These are based on the different facets of the Agile Manifesto and the steps to create self-actualized agile teams.
  Get together after every sprint
Hold a retrospective workshop 
Hold the Agile Maturity measurements workshop to Measure how often a team:
Followed the Agile Manifesto
Interacted with individuals to figure out work over making a perfect plan before starting work
Delivered working UX results to clients and to users to figure out their priorities through feedback
Collaborated with each other, with users, and with clients to define requirements over making contracted agreements.
Followed the Agile tenets of strong Agile teams
Created a psychologically safe space for voices on the team
Acted as service leaders to each other (apprentices and co-leads)
Organized themselves and made their own governing decisions through consensus
Failed fast and continuously improved
Iterated on their value delivery
  WHY IS IT VALUABLE?
  Measuring agile maturity is valuable because:
It helps a team self-heal when they are performing waterfall practices instead of agile practices.
It helps identify potential areas of improvement for team operations.
It creates a safe space for the team to hold psychological safety and be vulnerable with their potential issues as a team.
  WHO OWNS THIS DELIVERABLE?
  The Scrum Master function on a team owns this deliverable throughout a project.
  HOW TO INVOLVE OTHER TEAMS
  Everyone on the team, including apprentices and co-leads, needs to participate in this activity because teams need voices from people doing day-to-day work. The team owns their own process and they must participate to feel the full stake of ownership in it.
  WHEN DO TEAMS USE THIS?
  After every sprint, the team should get together to measure their agility.
  WHERE SHOULD THIS BE KEPT?
  This should be kept and maintained in Figjam or some other place where it can be quickly edited.

workshops.Workshop Brief: This workshop produces Agile Maturity Measurements. It gauges how agile a team really is across the tenets of strong agile teams (grounded in the Agile Manifesto and self-actualized-team models like Agile Fluency), treating maturity as a continuum so the team can self-correct.

workshops.Workshop Name: Tech Fleet Sprint Demo Slide Deck Template
workshops.Workshop Summary: This is a slide template the team uses to show its work at the end of a sprint. The team walks stakeholders through what it built, gathers feedback, and shows progress toward the goals. It keeps demos clear and consistent from sprint to sprint.
workshops.Workshop Goals:
Show stakeholders what the team built this sprint
Gather feedback the team can act on
Show progress toward the goals
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Copy the slide template
2. Make it your own content
3. Publish to the client
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?: Demos are how the team shows its work and stays connected to stakeholders. A simple, consistent format makes demos easier to run and easier to follow.
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Use it at the end of every sprint for the sprint demo.
workshops.Who Owns the Workshop?: The Agile Coaching function owns this workshop and is responsible for running it with the team.
workshops.Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Sprint Demo Presentation and Stakeholder Feedback.
workshops.Additional Details: When to use: at the end of each sprint, when the team shows its work.
workshops.Workshop Pitch Statement: The sprint's show-and-collaborate session, where the team presents the work it completed and gathers stakeholder feedback to shape what comes next.
workshops.What You Need Before You Start: Bring the completed sprint work and the sprint demo slide deck template. Invite anyone with a stake, including the client. Grounded in Scrum's Sprint Review, this happens at the end of each sprint.
workshops.The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What did we complete this sprint, and what did we not?
2. What went well, and what problems did we solve?
3. What do stakeholders think?
4. What should we do next?
workshops.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave having shown the increment, surfaced honest progress, and gathered stakeholder feedback that shapes the next priorities. Done well, it is a collaboration on value and direction, not just a show-and-tell.
workshops.Time Needed: Timeboxed; up to about 4 hours for a one-month sprint, shorter for shorter sprints
workshops.Common Pitfalls & Tips: A sprint review is more than a demo; the point is to collaborate with stakeholders on what to do next, not just present. Keep it informal and honest about what is and is not done. Timebox it (up to about four hours for a one-month sprint, shorter for shorter sprints).
workshops.Where to Keep the Output: Keep the deck with your sprint artifacts; route feedback into the backlog.
workshops.Workshop Brief: This workshop produces the Sprint Demo Presentation and gathers Stakeholder Feedback. Grounded in Scrum's Sprint Review, it is more than a demo: the team shows completed work and collaborates with stakeholders on what to do next, not just a show-and-tell.

Create navigation-level site map and content outlines for new version
workshops.Workshop Steps to Complete:

2. PART 2: Design for your Personas - Answer key questions to identify how you want to design for the personas
3. PART 3: Build the Customer Experience - Identify how you will support personas through the customer experience lifecycle.
workshops.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?: This workshop is valuable because it helps to define a clear alignment in how you are going to approach a user experience. It helps get all teams on the same page, and helps your stakeholders buy in to the priorities that you need to decide. At the same time, you will be able to use this workshop to collect valuable insights from stakeholders that may know about your personas based on previous research they have done.
workshops.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Run this before a project starts to set direction. You can also run it later if the team needs to reset its approach. Revisit it as you learn more.
