workshop-steps.Do This Now: For each question, task, and observation, record what actually happened, for example "x of y people did Z."
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: What were the raw results of each question, task, and observation?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: Documented raw results across the test.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Capture what people did and said separately; do not interpret yet.
workshop-steps.Done When: The raw results are documented.

workshop-steps.Step Title: Cluster themes with an affinity map
workshop-steps.Do This Now: Group the observations into themes on an affinity map, and use a rainbow table to track which participants showed each finding.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: What patterns and themes repeat across participants?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: An affinity map of themes and a rainbow table.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: The rainbow table shows what is common versus a one-off.
workshop-steps.Done When: Themes are clustered and tracked.

workshop-steps.Step Title: Tie results back to each assumption
workshop-steps.Do This Now: Map the findings back to the assumptions you set out to test.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: What does the evidence say about each assumption we tested?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: Findings mapped to each assumption.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Stay honest; let the data speak, not your hopes.
workshop-steps.Done When: Each assumption has its evidence attached.

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Mark each assumption true, false, or undetermined, and assign an owner to the conclusion.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: Was this assumption true, false, or undetermined?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: A conclusion per assumption, with an owner.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: "Undetermined" is a valid, useful result; do not force a verdict.
workshop-steps.Done When: Every assumption has a conclusion.

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Write down the new assumptions and questions that emerged from this round.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: What new questions do these results raise?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: A list of new research questions.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Good research always breeds the next round of questions.
workshop-steps.Done When: New questions are captured.

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Place the new topics in a MoSCoW matrix, then feed them into the next Research Plan iteration.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: Which new topics matter most next?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: A prioritized set of next-round topics.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: This is the loop; research never stops in agile.
workshop-steps.Done When: The next round is prioritized.

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Bring the conclusions and themes from the Research Analysis workshop.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: What did our analysis conclude?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: Your findings, ready to shape into a story.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Present analyzed conclusions, not raw notes.
workshop-steps.Done When: The findings are gathered.

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Lay out the slides: background, goals, method, key findings, conclusions, recommendations, and next steps.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: What structure will carry the story clearly?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: A clear presentation structure.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: A consistent structure helps stakeholders follow and trust it.
workshop-steps.Done When: The structure is set.

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Put the main findings and what they mean up front.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: What are the most important things we learned, and why do they matter?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: Key findings framed for impact.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Lead with meaning; details support, they do not open.
workshop-steps.Done When: The key findings are clear and prominent.

workshop-steps.Do This Now: State who the data represents and the research's limitations.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: Who does this data represent, and where might it fall short?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: An honest framing of representation and limits.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Truthful limits protect the team from costly overreach.
workshop-steps.Done When: Representation and limits are stated.

workshop-steps.Step Title: Turn findings into recommendations and next steps
workshop-steps.Do This Now: Translate the findings into actionable recommendations and clear next steps.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: So what should the team do next?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: Actionable recommendations and next steps.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Findings without recommendations rarely change anything.
workshop-steps.Done When: Recommendations and next steps are defined.

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Drop in the audiences you want to storyboard for.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: Which audiences are we telling stories about?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: The audiences chosen to storyboard.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Focus on the audiences that matter most to this work.
workshop-steps.Done When: The audiences are listed.

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Add the current and future use case scenarios, per audience, that you might storyboard.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: What scenarios could we storyboard for each audience?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: A set of candidate use case scenarios.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Pull these from your segmentation and discovery work.
workshop-steps.Done When: Scenarios are captured per audience.

workshop-steps.Step Title: Prioritize and vote on the use cases
workshop-steps.Do This Now: Place the use cases in a MoSCoW matrix, then vote to choose which to storyboard.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: Which use cases are most worth storyboarding now?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: The chosen use cases to storyboard.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Use more than one voting round if the top is unclear.
workshop-steps.Done When: The team agrees which use cases to storyboard.

workshop-steps.Do This Now: In breakouts, sketch each chosen use case as an eight-panel comic of the experience today: what the user does, struggles with, feels, and wishes they had.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: What is the user's experience today, panel by panel?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: A current-state storyboard per use case.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Low-fi is perfect; the narrative matters, not the art.
workshop-steps.Done When: Each chosen use case has a current-state storyboard.

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Sketch the blue-sky future: how the experience works once the user's problems are solved. Be specific about the solution, not just "less confusion."
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: What could this experience be once the problems are gone?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: A future-state storyboard per use case.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Go wild here; this is your creative wish list.
workshop-steps.Done When: Each use case has a future-state storyboard.

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Regroup, walk the storyboards as a team, and fill in the connecting details.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: What do these stories tell us, and what's missing between the panels?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: Shared understanding and a fuller story.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Bring the whole team's eyes to each story.
workshop-steps.Done When: The team has analyzed the storyboards.

workshop-steps.Step Title: Reflect on good versus bad case studies
workshop-steps.Do This Now: As a team, capture what makes a case study strong and what makes one weak.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: What makes a good case study? What makes a bad one?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: A shared picture of what to aim for and avoid.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Look at examples if you have them; specifics beat generalities.
workshop-steps.Done When: The team agrees on what strong looks like.

workshop-steps.Step Title: Identify the team actions and events needed
workshop-steps.Do This Now: Name what the team must do, and what events must happen during the project, to produce a great case study.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: What must happen during the project for us to have a great story to tell?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: A list of team actions and events to plan for.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Capturing decisions and collaboration as they happen is the secret.
workshop-steps.Done When: The needed actions and events are named.

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Decide how you will work with other teams to produce your case study.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: How do we need to work with other teams to produce our case study?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: A plan for the cross-team collaboration.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Case studies are richer when they capture real cross-functional work.
workshop-steps.Done When: The collaboration plan is set.

workshop-steps.Step Title: Build a story-driven case study outline
workshop-steps.Do This Now: Outline the story your case study will tell, from background through outcomes.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: What is the story-driven outline of our case study?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: A story-driven case study outline.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Structure it as a story of growth, not a list of deliverables.
workshop-steps.Done When: The team has an outline to carry forward.

Workshop.label: Product and Service Development Milestones for Different Types of Projects Workshop Template

workshop-steps.Step Title: Learn the agile product and service development lifecycle
workshop-steps.Do This Now: Study the lifecycle and how its milestones flow, in parallel and repeating, not in a straight line.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: What are the milestones, and how do they actually flow?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: A shared model of the lifecycle.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: These milestones repeat and overlap; they are not sequential phases.
workshop-steps.Done When: The team understands the lifecycle.

Workshop.label: Product and Service Development Milestones for Different Types of Projects Workshop Template

workshop-steps.Step Title: Review each milestone and its deliverables
workshop-steps.Do This Now: Go milestone by milestone: what each one means and the deliverables it produces.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: What does each milestone mean, and what does it produce?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: Shared understanding of milestones and their deliverables.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Milestones are markers of progress, not fixed calendar phases.
workshop-steps.Done When: The team knows each milestone's deliverables.

Workshop.label: Product and Service Development Milestones for Different Types of Projects Workshop Template

workshop-steps.Do This Now: See which workshops produce the deliverables in each milestone.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: Which workshops produce each milestone's deliverables?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: A map from milestones to the workshops that feed them.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: This connects the training to the actual workshops the team runs.
workshop-steps.Done When: The team can map workshops to milestones.

Workshop.label: Product and Service Development Milestones for Different Types of Projects Workshop Template

workshop-steps.Step Title: Review project types and their deliverables
workshop-steps.Do This Now: Look at Tech Fleet's project types (business strategy, website, service design; discovery-only through full build) and how their deliverables differ.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: How do deliverables differ across our project types?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: Understanding of how project type shapes the work.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Not every project does every milestone; match the deliverables to the type.
workshop-steps.Done When: The team understands the project types.

Workshop.label: Personal Growth Vision, Scope, and Roadmap Workshop Template

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Capture your why, the people you grow with, your growth problems and opportunities (service leadership, teamwork, skills, communication), your goals, the value you will bring, what makes you unique, your barriers, costs, and KPIs.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: Why do I do this work, and where do I want to grow?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: The building blocks of your growth vision.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Be honest about the hard growth areas; that is where the value is.
workshop-steps.Done When: Your growth components are captured.

Workshop.label: Personal Growth Vision, Scope, and Roadmap Workshop Template

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Place your growth opportunities in a MoSCoW matrix by effort and value.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: Which growth areas are high value and worth the effort now?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: A prioritized set of growth opportunities.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: You cannot grow everything at once; choose a few.
workshop-steps.Done When: Your growth problems are prioritized.

Workshop.label: Personal Growth Vision, Scope, and Roadmap Workshop Template

workshop-steps.Step Title: Pick your top few to work on now
workshop-steps.Do This Now: Choose the top few growth opportunities as your near-term focus.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: What will I focus my growth on now?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: Your near-term growth focus.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Near-term is your MVP; the rest is your MMP.
workshop-steps.Done When: Your top growth focus is chosen.

Workshop.label: Personal Growth Vision, Scope, and Roadmap Workshop Template

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Build a near-term (MVP) and a longer-term (MMP) vision board for your growth: vision statement, audiences, problems, goals, value, uniqueness, barriers, costs, KPIs.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: What is my near-term and long-term growth vision?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: MVP and MMP personal growth vision boards.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Write your one-sentence vision statement last.
workshop-steps.Done When: You have MVP and MMP growth vision boards.

Workshop.label: Personal Growth Vision, Scope, and Roadmap Workshop Template

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Break your growth vision into epics, features, and tasks.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: What are the concrete pieces of my growth work?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: A backlog of growth epics, features, and tasks.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Small, concrete tasks make growth actually happen.
workshop-steps.Done When: Your growth backlog is organized.

Workshop.label: Personal Growth Vision, Scope, and Roadmap Workshop Template

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Sequence your growth epics and features into a roadmap over the year.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: When will I work on each part of my growth?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: A personal growth roadmap.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Keep it living; revisit and pivot as you grow.
workshop-steps.Done When: Your growth roadmap is built.

Workshop.label: Tech Fleet Sprint Demo Slide Deck Template

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Line up what is Done and not Done this sprint against the sprint goal.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: What did we complete this sprint, measured against our sprint goal?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: A clear picture of completed and incomplete work.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Be honest about what did not get done; that is useful information.
workshop-steps.Done When: The walk-through is prepared.

Workshop.label: Tech Fleet Sprint Demo Slide Deck Template

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Show the completed work to stakeholders.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: What does the completed work actually do?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: A demonstration of the increment.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: A demo is one way to show results, not the whole point of the review.
workshop-steps.Done When: The increment has been shown.

Workshop.label: Tech Fleet Sprint Demo Slide Deck Template

workshop-steps.Step Title: Share what went well and problems solved
workshop-steps.Do This Now: Walk stakeholders through what went well this sprint and the problems the team solved.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: What went well, and what did we work through?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: Shared understanding of the sprint's progress.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Honest reflection builds trust with stakeholders.
workshop-steps.Done When: The team has shared its progress.

Workshop.label: Tech Fleet Sprint Demo Slide Deck Template

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Collaborate with stakeholders on the value created and what matters next.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: What do stakeholders think, and what should we prioritize next?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: Stakeholder feedback and direction.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: This is the real purpose: collaborate on what to do next.
workshop-steps.Done When: Feedback has been gathered.

Workshop.label: Tech Fleet Sprint Demo Slide Deck Template

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Turn the feedback and next steps into backlog items and plan adjustments.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: How does this feedback change our backlog and plan?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: Feedback routed into the backlog and plan.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Feedback that never reaches the backlog changes nothing.
workshop-steps.Done When: The feedback is captured in the plan.

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Define the target personas and capture each one's traits and pain points (this readies the strategy).
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: Who are we designing for, and what are their traits and pains?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: A set of target personas with traits and pains.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Pull from existing personas and stakeholder knowledge where you can.
workshop-steps.Done When: The target personas are defined.

workshop-steps.Step Title: Define how you will design for your personas
workshop-steps.Do This Now: Decide the design strategy for each persona: how you intend to meet their needs and expectations.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: How do we want to design for each persona?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: A design strategy per persona.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Tie each strategic choice back to a persona's need or pain.
workshop-steps.Done When: The design strategy is defined per persona.

workshop-steps.Step Title: Define your customer experience funnel strategy
workshop-steps.Do This Now: Define how you will support each persona across the lifecycle funnel (awareness through loyalty), and how you will drive conversion and long-term engagement.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: How will we support and move each persona through the funnel?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: A customer experience strategy and funnel definition.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: Strategize the whole funnel, not just the first visit.
workshop-steps.Done When: The CX funnel strategy is defined.

workshop-steps.Step Title: Set the direction for the site map and content
workshop-steps.Do This Now: Define the content topics and navigation direction each audience needs, so the Site Map and CX Map workshops can build from it.
workshop-steps.Prompts / Questions: What must the site map, CX map, and content deliver, based on this strategy?
workshop-steps.Output of This Step: Strategic direction and requirements for the site map, CX map, and content.
workshop-steps.Tips & Pitfalls: This readies those workshops; it does not replace them.
workshop-steps.Done When: The direction for the site map and content is set.

Workshop.label: Brand Strategy and Identity Workshop Template

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Name a facilitator, scribe, timekeeper, and a tie-breaker. Post the current mission, vision, and values.
workshop-steps.Done When: Roles are set and the current mission, vision, and values are visible.

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Fill the Why, What, and How rings with sticky notes, starting from Why.
workshop-steps.Done When: The group agrees on the Why first, then What and How.

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Answer who needs to know, how they find out, and why they care.
workshop-steps.Done When: Each question has agreed sticky notes.

Workshop.label: Brand Strategy and Identity Workshop Template

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Vote each slider toward an end, list what the brand should not be, and pick four to five traits.
workshop-steps.Done When: Sliders, limits, and traits are agreed.

Workshop.label: Brand Strategy and Identity Workshop Template

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Shortlist from the twelve archetypes and vote a primary plus an optional secondary.
workshop-steps.Done When: One primary archetype is chosen.

Workshop.label: Brand Strategy and Identity Workshop Template

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Run fill, vote, decide for the metaphor, then the promise.
workshop-steps.Done When: One metaphor and one promise are chosen.

Workshop.label: Brand Strategy and Identity Workshop Template

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Fill each story line with the customer as the hero and read it aloud.
workshop-steps.Done When: The story reads like you and the group agrees.

Workshop.label: Brand Strategy and Identity Workshop Template

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Copy each agreed result into the one-page brief, read it aloud, and get a final yes.
workshop-steps.Done When: Everyone can live with the brief.

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Read the introduction: a nonprofit works toward no longer being needed. Set roles.
workshop-steps.Done When: The group shares the framing and roles are set.

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Fill the Golden Circle (Why, What, How) and write a one-sentence mission.
workshop-steps.Done When: A mission statement is agreed.

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Describe the world when you succeed and write a one-sentence vision.
workshop-steps.Done When: A vision statement is agreed.

workshop-steps.Do This Now: List values and explain each, then pick the set to hold true.
workshop-steps.Done When: The values and their meanings are agreed.

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Name audiences, problems, competitors, and what makes you unique, then write the positioning statement.
workshop-steps.Done When: A positioning statement is agreed.

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Dump the barriers, then break them into goals, interventions, and measures.
workshop-steps.Done When: The top barriers and the goals to beat them are chosen.

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Summarize into one commitment statement.
workshop-steps.Done When: A ten-year commitment is agreed.

workshop-steps.Do This Now: Turn the commitment into five-year strategic goals.
workshop-steps.Done When: The strategic goals are agreed.

Why this workshop exists: a mission-driven org works toward no longer being needed in the world, and starts from why it exists.
Use the Golden Circle to separate Why you exist, What you offer, and How you offer it. Then write a one-sentence mission statement: Our mission is to ___.
Describe the world when the mission is fully accomplished. Action-based, not theoretical. Write: We envision a world where ___.
Decide the values the organization and its members uphold, and explain each in your own words. Write: These are the values we hold true: ___.
Name the audiences you serve, the problems they face, the other orgs solving them, and what makes you unique. Write a positioning statement using the FOR / WE PROVIDE / THROUGH / UNLIKE format.
Name the barriers in your way, then the goals, interventions, and measures to overcome them. Write: In the next ten years, we're committed to ___ and we will do this by ___.
From the commitment, set the strategic goals for the next five years: Over the next five years, our strategic goals are to ___.

career-transitioning/Transitioning_into_.Summary of the Gaps: Academia trained you in the exact heart of this path: designing studies, running them, and making sense of what you find. Research Facilitation, Experiment Design, and Research Analysis carry over almost whole, so your gap is smaller than most. What changes is the pace and the purpose. Instead of research that stands on its own over months, you run lean studies that feed a product decision this week, and you share rough findings early rather than polishing a paper. The tools are new, mostly Figma, Dovetail, and FigJam, and usability testing will be a fresh method on top of the ones you know.
career-transitioning/Transitioning_into_.Training Recommendations: You already research well, so aim your energy at speed and application. Learn usability testing and how to choose a method quickly for the question at hand. Pick up Dovetail and Maze to run and analyze studies the way product teams do. Practice turning a study into a short, decision-ready summary instead of a full report. Learn an agile method like Lean UX to feel the faster rhythm. Lean on the rigor you already have while you adjust to working in days, not semesters.
career-transitioning/Transitioning_into_.A Day in the Life: On a cross-functional team, your day revolves around understanding users. You carry out and see through the research itself: planning studies, recruiting and interviewing people, running usability tests and surveys, and making sense of it all through analysis and heuristics. You turn that into research reports, affinity maps, journey maps, and clear findings the team can act on. Beyond the work you own, you are consulted across almost everything the team builds, weighing in on wireframes, prototypes, content, product strategy, and go-to-market thinking, since your read on real user needs sharpens other people's decisions. A typical day mixes focused sessions, a couple of interviews or a usability test, with synthesis in Dovetail and collaboration: a standup, a design critique where you carry the user's voice, and a working session to plan the next study. You share findings early and often, and you let evidence guide the team rather than opinion.

career-transitioning/Transitioning_into_.Summary of the Gaps: Accounting gave you comfort with numbers, logic, and turning data into a clear story, which is a strong base for the measurement side of this path. Data Analysis and Statistics transfer straight into surveys and analytics work. The newer ground is the human side: interviewing people, watching how they behave, and reading qualitative signals that do not reduce to a spreadsheet. The tools shift toward Figma, Dovetail, and Maze, though your spreadsheet fluency still helps with analytics. The real change is learning that the goal is understanding a person, not closing a number.
career-transitioning/Transitioning_into_.Training Recommendations: Start where your strengths already reach: the quantitative side, like surveys and analytics. Then stretch into qualitative methods, learning how to interview and observe without leading people. Practice usability testing on a small task. Pick up Dovetail to organize what you hear. Learn Lean UX for the team rhythm. Keep using your gift for clear summaries; research is only useful when others can act on it.

Because product management wears many hats, you are accountable for a very wide span of delivery, from requirements, design, and QA through architecture and launch, making sure the whole thing adds up to something users want and the business can sustain. You are consulted across nearly every part of the team. A typical day mixes strategy and planning in Notion, Trello, and FigJam with heavy collaboration: standups, stakeholder alignment, backlog refinement, and working sessions with design, research, and engineering. You steer in short loops, adjust as the market and users teach you, and keep everyone pointed at the highest-value work.

career-transitioning/Transitioning_into_.Summary of the Gaps: In this role your daily work is shaping brand identity, taking stock of content, and writing copy, and you both carry that work out and see it through to a finished, usable result. It rests on craft like Interaction Design and Information Architecture, and produces pieces like an Editorial Style Guide, Microcopy, and a Content Inventory. Academia set you up for the thinking behind it: Research Facilitation, Research Analysis, and Written Communication all transfer, and turning dense ideas into clear prose is close to good copywriting. What is new is the visual and structural craft, and the tools shift from papers to Figma, Notion, and FigJam. The real adjustment is rhythm, from long solitary study to short loops and shared rough drafts.
career-transitioning/Transitioning_into_.Training Recommendations: Your research and writing are strong, so aim early energy at the craft you will own. Start with Interaction Design and Information Architecture, the least familiar skills. Practice on the real work, drafting a small brand identity or content inventory rather than reading about it. Since you see this work through to done, learn to shape a full Editorial Style Guide, beyond a single paragraph. Pick up Figma and FigJam on a real task, and learn Lean UX for the team pace. Lean on your writing while the visual craft catches up.
career-transitioning/Transitioning_into_.A Day in the Life: On a cross-functional team, your day centers on the words and brand of the product. You carry out and see through the core content work: shaping brand identity, taking stock of the product's content in a content inventory, and writing the copy that guides people, from headlines down to the small microcopy on a button. Around that, you are pulled into a wide slice of the team's work as an advisor. You sit in on research sessions and design reviews, weigh in on wireframes, information architecture, and prototypes, and help shape strategy, positioning, and go-to-market thinking so the voice stays consistent everywhere. A typical day mixes focused making, drafting and refining content in Figma and FigJam, with collaboration: a standup, a working session with designers or researchers, and quick reviews where your read on clarity and tone helps other people's work land. You share drafts early and rough, expect feedback, and improve in short loops rather than polishing alone.
